#6737. Daydream’s New AI Agent Can Shop for You While You Sleep

Daydream wants to become a personal stylist in your pocket. The AI-powered fashion discovery platform, launched in 2025 by former Stitch Fix executive Julie Bornstein, is introducing a 24/7 AI shopping agent that can learn consumers’ tastes, assemble outfits and purchase products on their behalf — even while they sleep.

The new agent, which shoppers can chat with through Daydream’s app or by texting it directly via SMS, marks an evolution from the conversational fashion search engine the company launched just over a year ago. It can remember previous exchanges, put together complete outfits, offer virtual try-ons using an uploaded photograph and handle the steps leading up to checkout.

During an exclusive preview, co-founder and chief brand officer Lisa Yamner asks the agent to resume shopping for an upcoming trip to Mexico. Remembering her plans, it asks a few questions before assembling looks for beachfront dinners, complete with dresses, shoes and bags. Yamner swaps between pieces, tries them on using a virtual version of herself and uploads an influencer’s Instagram image to find similar items.

“Once you express a need or an interest, it can shop while you sleep,” Yamner explains. Shoppers can leave the agent to monitor products for price drops or continue working on a shopping request in the background, rather than repeatedly checking themselves. Any purchase still requires their approval. “We firmly believe that shopping doesn’t have to be a task, but there are parts of it that become that.” The aim is to take the drudgery out of shopping without losing the pleasure of discovery, she says.

At launch, the agent can shop across Daydream’s existing network of roughly 350 brand and retail partners, spanning more than 10,000 brands and three million products. Shoppers can ask it to purchase an item on their behalf, or check out directly with the retailer.

It comes as OpenAI, Instinct and Meta double down on shopping as a core use case and revenue stream for their newly launched ‘always on’ agents, and fashion retailers are now racing to build their own agents. Last week, Zalando announced plans for an AI agent that will purchase products on customers’ behalf from other retailers as well as its own catalog, from 2027. Meanwhile, brands including Ralph Lauren and J.Crew are building out their own branded AI shopping assistants, with J.Crew partnering with Anthropic on its new AI “Style Advisor”. Last month, Prada became the first luxury brand to launch an official plugin within OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

Daydream's answer is to sell its fashion expertise. The company has developed an internal “fashion knowledge graph” to enrich the information attached to products in its catalog, while human stylists help shape the agent’s recommendations. It recently appointed Francesca Sully as its first “stylist in residence”, tasked with teaching the technology to think more like a stylist and keep pace with trends.

Daydream recently appointed Francesca Sully as its first “stylist in residence”, tasked with teaching the AI agent to think more like a human stylist and keep pace with trends. Photo: Courtesy of Daydream.

Its founders believe a general-purpose AI agent, however sophisticated, will struggle to replicate the nuances of personal style. It comes back to the central question haunting fashion AI: can it mimic taste?

“We feel like a generalized agent is just not going to get fashion right,” Bornstein tells Vogue Business in an exclusive interview alongside co-founder Lisa Yamner. “Style is so nuanced. It relates to some very specific things that matter. So we need to know the right questions to ask, but also understand the product catalog of every brand out there — not just the price points, but also what the aesthetic of a brand world is, and how to connect that to other brands that align with that aesthetic and may be of interest.”

That expertise is also intended to help shoppers discover unfamiliar labels: approximately 97% of searches on Daydream contain no brand name, according to Bornstein. But in an increasingly crowded market, can that fashion expertise stand up as an independent AI shopping offering against the mass convenience of frontier AI agents and trusted retailers’ owned product catalogs?

When Daydream debuted last year, its proposition was to solve one of fashion e-commerce’s enduring frustrations: finding the right product across a fragmented universe of brands and retailers. Its conversational search engine allowed shoppers to describe what they wanted in natural language, rather than relying on conventional keywords and filters, encouraging users to “say more” about what they sought.

Although Daydream had already positioned itself around the idea of an AI agent, what it lacked was the ability to deliver the more involved, personalized service its founders envisaged — agents in their current form didn’t actually exist.

“We’ve been wanting to build from day one, but it took us a while to get there for a couple of reasons: one was that the agentic technology wasn’t yet there, and two is that the first version of the platform helped us really understand what consumers were looking for and what they wanted from an AI shopping assistant,” Bornstein says, explaining that Daydream was finding its original product couldn’t deliver the level of assistance shoppers wanted. Shoppers were asking very specific questions to find products for a need that included an occasion and their body type, and Daydream was showing them a page of search results, “when what they really wanted was more tailored help,” Bornstein adds. Conversational search might make finding fashion products easier, but it doesn’t necessarily solve the more subjective problem of deciding what to wear.

Bornstein recalls a similar challenge at her previous company, The Yes, where shoppers struggled to move beyond the conventions of traditional search. “We tried to get people to search by telling us a need and they would say, ‘Oh, I need a red dress for a Valentine’s Day party. I want to look sexy, but age-appropriate.’ And then you’d say, ‘Great, go ahead and type it into the search part.’ But then they would type in ‘red dress’, because their trust in search working was so low, and there was no mental model of being able to give a more detailed prompt.”

ChatGPT helped change that behavior, she says, making consumers more comfortable describing their needs in detail — and helping users understand how to use a product like Daydream. “Consumer expectations have started to change and people now understand what an agent is in a way they definitely didn’t two years ago when we started and no one understood what we were talking about,” Bornstein says.

The platform says it has amassed more than 2 million users since its June 2025 launch, with millennial women its largest audience, followed by Gen X and Gen Z. Bornstein describes two overlapping groups: fashion-savvy shoppers who appreciate having thousands of brands in one place, and time-poor consumers seeking more direction. But Daydream won’t disclose how many of its 2 million shoppers return or make purchases, making it difficult to gauge whether initial curiosity is translating into increased sales.

It comes just a week after Zalando announced an adjacent offering — a new AI agent feature, Zalando Extended, that will allow shoppers to discover and buy products from other third-party retailers without leaving the Zalando app, available from 2027. The European multibrand platform has 63 million active customers, extensive brand relationships and years of purchase and sizing data — assets that a much younger shopping platform like Daydream can’t easily replicate. Yet Bornstein argues the two companies are targeting different markets — Zalando solely operates in Europe, while Daydream is focused solely on the US. She also says the US retail landscape’s department stores and multibrand retailers generally have “more curated assortments”.

“The fact Zalando is going outside its own catalog makes a lot of sense because they’ve always tried to be extremely broad and like the higher-end ‘Amazon of fashion’ in Europe,” Bornstein argues.

But geography offers only a partial defence in a market where frontier AI models like ChatGPT and Claude are developing shopping capabilities that could eventually reach consumers across multiple countries, and gain more sophisticated fashion knowledge, via direct brand plugins like ChatGPT’s recently launched Prada plugin.

Asked what Daydream can offer that a much larger retailer can’t, Bornstein points to its first-mover advantage as the first cross-brand conversational search tool that’s “properly entrenched in fashion”, and the two years of data and prompts it’s collected from fashion-savvy consumers in that time. “I would also say we are solely focused on this,” she adds. “Having worked for other larger companies before in my past, I know how hard it is to build something like this on the side.”

There is also competition from fashion brands themselves. Ralph Lauren’s Ask Ralph and the launch of J.Crew’s new AI stylist last week suggest that brands increasingly want to provide personalized guidance within their own shopping environments.

Yet Bornstein says these brand-owned stylists can sit alongside Daydream’s ambitions. “When we launched originally, many brands asked us if we could build this AI agent for their sites,” she says. “And what we said to them is our initial goal is to have one place for consumers to go and see all brands — without having 10 tabs open.”

Daydream has also expanded into providing its technology to brands. Around eight brand sites are currently using its conversational search technology, Yamner says, and the company plans to bring some of its new agentic capabilities to those partners.

“Our feeling is if you know the brand and you go straight to the brand, there’s no reason why you wouldn’t want tools to help you shop that brand as effectively as you can,” Bornstein says. “So we’ll evolve the agentic product that we provide to brand sites to map to our core product, as it’s very portable to single brands too. But we are fundamentally focused on the B2C experience — it just also happens to work for B2B.”

One of Daydream’s potentially most valuable assets is the information it gathers from the way consumers describe their shopping needs. Traditional e-commerce search data might tell a brand that shoppers are searching for dresses or shoes. Conversational search can reveal the occasion, aesthetic and practical requirements behind those searches, as well as details like whether shoppers are searching for particular past collaborations or archive pieces — valuable data for brands’ product development and merchandising decisions, Bornstein says.

“That’s been the single best thing I think we’ve done for the industry over the last year — being able to surface really valuable and different insights for them, especially catalog intent,” she says, adding that they’ve found the same shopper tends to be entering complex conversational queries on Daydream but still be searching ‘red dress’ on brands’ own DTC sites. For brands, that information could can offer a more granular understanding of what customers want and why. For Daydream, it also creates a potential advantage over competitors that lack the same volume of detailed fashion-related prompts.

But the next stage of its personalization strategy requires shoppers to share considerably more. Daydream is developing integrations with Gmail and Google Calendar so its new AI agent can access this customer data and allow it to identify upcoming occasions and learn about previous purchases and marketing email subscriptions. Shoppers will soon also be able to share Pinterest boards with the agent to communicate their style preferences.

Users can set Daydream’s new AI agent tasks, like price comparison and stock checks, that it can carry out 24/7, even while they sleep. Photo: Courtesy of Daydream.

Daydream also operates on a commission model, yet Bornstein insists that commercial relationships won’t influence what the agent recommends — and it’s not pursuing advertising within the agent, at least for now. “There are no commercial incentives that go into what shows up for the customer,” she says. “Whatever they buy, we receive the same level of commission. So we are completely agnostic in what we’re showing and it’s about the customer’s preferences.” Brands will continue to receive customer information when purchases are completed through Daydream.

While Daydream is investing in a more complex and personalized experience, it’s not disclosed the conversion or retention figures needed to assess how effectively that experience translates into repeat purchasing. But Bornstein and Yamner remain convinced that fashion requires a different approach from the general-purpose agents increasingly being developed to manage everyday tasks.

“We’re watching the direction that the tech and customers are moving in, and we’re trying to get out ahead of it,” Yamner says. “We’re trying to say we get it. We get that this is what the customer’s expectations are going to become.”

#6736. Elizabeth Debicki Looks Angelic in All White at ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood Event

Elizabeth Debicki knows a thing or two about red carpet elegance. For ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood event in Beverly Hills tonight, the actress arrived wearing a sleeveless, silky white gown. The dress featured a minimalist silhouette, but she added a playful touch to the look with a feathered oversize clutch.

Earlier in the night, she stepped out at the Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth premiere at TCL Chinese Theatre, just a short drive away. For that event, she opted for a plunging black halter gown.

Debicki is among this year’s Women in Hollywood honorees. In her recent ELLE cover story, she reflected on the challenge of finding her next project after her buzzed-about performance as Princess Diana on The Crown.

“I was really looking for a while, after I did The Crown, for something I wanted to do,” she said. “It took a little while for me to find those jobs.”

She ultimately found two projects that excited her: Wicker, a fairy-tale comedy starring Olivia Colman as a woman who marries a man made of wicker (played by Alexander Skarsgård), and David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, in which she stars opposite Brad Pitt.

Debicki also opened up about the lessons she’s learned throughout her career, including the importance of maintaining a life outside of work.

“The thing that’s taken me the longest to learn is what to do with my real life,” she told ELLE. “When acting is the thing that you obsess over, that interests you most, that you’re the most driven to continue to do, it’s a bit of a compulsion, and your real life can get waylaid.”

#6735. GQ’s Men of the Year Dinner May Have Found the Next James Bond

Cocktail hour was drawing to a close; the traditional pre-party dinner for the 31st edition of GQ’s legendary Men of the Year event, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, was about to kick off. GQ’s Designer of the Year, Celine’s Michael Rider, and our Director of the Year, Denis Villeneuve, were already posted up inside the Chateau Marmont’s lobby lounge; the guests lingering just past the entrance included Odysseus himself, Matt Damon, building with his Ocean’s partner-in-crime Don Cheadle before pivoting to greet Chris Rock—like Damon, one of GQ’s three Men of the Year issue cover stars. (Andrew Garfield, subject of that third cover, had rolled in a few minutes earlier, resplendently coiffed, immediately gathering his After the Hunt co-star Ayo Edebiri and director Luca Guadagnino into a reunion hug.)

But among the Men of the Year veterans in attendance—like Rock, who scored his first MOTY cover in 1999, circa Bigger and Blacker—there were also plenty of first-timers from the new class of news-makers and paradigm-shakers celebrated in GQ’s 2026 Breakouts portfolio. And that varied mix—of longtime icons and undeniable up-and-comers, from Owen Thiele and Inde Navarette to I Play Rocky’s Anthony Ippolito and electro-rock duo Fcukers—made for a veritable particle accelerator of improbable collisions.

Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg in deep confab with Tinashe. Tony’s Stavros Halkias in an across-the-table comedy summit with Chris Rock. Journalist Pablo Torre, whose reporting on Kawhi Leonard and the LA Clippers salary-cap shenanigans shook the NBA, engrossed in conversation with GQ’s own Zach Baron and Villeneuve, who’d just signed off on the prints—for real this time—for his third and final Dune movie, soon to shake the walls of nearly every IMAX theater on Earth.

And Villeneuve wasn’t the only auteur on hand: Between the Dune mastermind, Misty Green writer/director/star Rock, Club Kid’s similarly slashed Jordan Firstman, the La Bola Negra writer-directors jointly known as Los Javis (Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrosi) and Guadagnino, who upon arriving had almost immediately located a cinematically moody lamplit corner to hold court in, the Chateau’s lobby was, quipped GQ Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi, “an incredible room to be an out-of-work actor in.”

Because journalism doesn’t take a night off—not even GQ’s biggest night—Baidawi also tried, during his opening remarks, to pry some info regarding the identity of the new James Bond (off the record, just between us) out of Villeneuve.

As the director politely demurred—hey, we had to try—another guest piped up from across the table. “Wait,” said Matt Damon, as Baidawi passed the former superspy the mic. “I have a question. Just a thought experiment. What if James Bond were older? And American?” (In the unlikely event that Damon just booked a second iconic-superspy role, you heard it here first.)

Toast time was upon us: Rosalind Eleazar, raising a glass to Chris Rock, recalled her Zoom audition with Rock for Misty Green, which was followed in short order by a missed call from an American number and the two-word text message that would change her life: “Chris Rock.” (That’s right—when Chris Rock calls you from an unknown number and gets your voice mail, he follows up with a text that just says “Chris Rock,” an absolute power-move that is, unfortunately, hard to replicate by the rest of us.)

“Thinking I was being rather witty, I replied, ‘Rosalind Eleazar,’” Eleazar said. “I waited eagerly for his response and—not so much as a laughing emoji. And I quickly realized that I am communicating with one of the funniest people on the planet and I should probably just leave the funny to him.”

Eleazar recalled Rock telling her on set, My movie—your character, giving her the freedom to discover Misty on her own. “And that’s a rare gift,” she said, “and one that I will always be grateful for.”

“Thank you, Rosalind,” Rock said. “The check will be there in the morning.”

Ayo Edebiri began by saluting “my dear friend, one of my favorite people in the world, one of the best actors ever, and a little bit of a role model to me if I’m being honest: Robert Pattinson.” She paused as the crowd fell out laughing. “Andrew! Andrew Garfield. I’m so sorry. This is a different speech for a different guy.”

“You never know what you’re going to get when you work with somebody,” Edebiri noted, but said the resolutely “normal” Garfield had put her immediately at ease on After the Hunt, making it “safe to be unsafe” in difficult scenes. “And, on that movie especially, we had tough stuff to do,” she said. “We were not nice to each other. Some of the boys these days, on Method, you never know.”

“If you ever see him in public,” Edebiri continued, “don't try any small talk with this man. Just don't do it. He's medically allergic to small talk. You get very deep, very fast. You will end up talking about esoteric poetry or the nature of masculinity in the modern world or just water, like the power and the mystery of water.” (This we can confirm.)

“I just love you so, so dearly,” Garfield responded, “and I hope we can be in each other's lives forever.”

And with that moment of open-hearted sincerity out of the way, it was time for Damon to hear from frenemy Jimmy Kimmel, who fired off weapons-grade roast jokes. “I fought for the First Amendment this year,” Kimmel said. “You fought a puppet cyclops.”

Damon, in response, mostly took the high road, offering up praise (for Edebiri’s speech) before getting the last word. “In closing, I would just like to repeat that I did not invite Jimmy Kimmel to this place. I’ve never invited him anywhere, and I never will. He is a horrible human being. And I thank you all for being here.” ✦

#6732. Is Zalando’s New AI Agent a Blueprint for the Future of Retail?

What happens when a multibrand fashion retailer starts selling products it doesn’t stock? European e-commerce giant Zalando is joining the AI shopping agent race with plans to let shoppers buy from other retailers through its platform. Its new offering, Zalando Extended, will use AI agents to complete purchases on customers’ behalf, potentially transforming Zalando into a shopping gateway beyond its own catalog.

Zalando is testing the service with premium home and living retailer Westwing. Its products already appear in Zalando’s search and browsing results, but shoppers currently have to click through to Westwing’s website to buy them. From 2027, Zalando’s AI agent will handle those purchases on customers’ behalf, allowing them to check out without leaving the Zalando app.

Retailers can join through a relatively simple integration, providing something similar to an affiliate product feed and entering into an additional agreement with Zalando. The company has not disclosed what commission or fee, if any, it will earn from these transactions. It's a notable move for a retailer that has spent years building its own assortment and relationships with thousands of brands, from Gucci to Burberry and Jacquemus. But as the likes of OpenAI, Google and Meta race to make general-purpose personal AI agents, the battle is increasingly over who controls the customer relationship, rather than simply who stocks the product.

Zalando’s AI assistant currently helps shoppers purchase from the multibrand retailer’s product catalogue. Photo: Courtesy of Zalando.

Zalando’s response is to position itself on both sides of that coin. Its three-pronged strategy aims to make its own platform the first stop for fashion discovery, expand its assortment through external retailers and also reach shoppers through third-party AI agents. It plans to offer checkout within Google’s AI Mode and Gemini app when its agentic commerce launches in Europe, and has tested advertising inside ChatGPT in the UK.

This also places Zalando in competition with specialist AI shopping platforms such as Daydream, which also launched a new AI shopping agent this week. Both are betting that fashion requires expertise beyond that of general-purpose AI agents. While Daydream operates in the US and Zalando in Europe, the latter enters the race with a significant advantage in scale.

But for rival luxury and multibrand fashion retailers, Zalando’s AI strategy raises a bigger question: is the future of fashion e-commerce about selling your own assortment, or becoming the gateway to everyone else’s?

At the Web Summit conference in Lisbon, Vogue Business sat down with chief technology officer Graeme Smith to discuss the company’s ambitions and who stands to own the customer relationship in the age of AI agents.

Vogue: Why allow Zalando customers to buy products from other retailers through Zalando Extended?

Smith: We’ve got over 63 million active customers at Zalando, and through our Lifestyle AI [Zalando’s umbrella term for its AI-powered personalization technology], we’ve really got to know their preferences — the brands they like, the price points they shop at, the brand values like sustainability they look for, and how their needs change over time. We can use all this to create a personalized experience that can even become proactive.

So we thought, why limit ourselves? We already have our wholesale and partner platforms, but with AI agents, we’ve found a really lightweight way to bring in other retailers whose products you wouldn’t normally find on Zalando.

Our first partner is Westwing. Today, you can discover its products on Zalando and click through to buy them on Westwing. But early next year, you’ll be able to buy that sofa or lamp directly on Zalando, using your existing account and payment details, without leaving the app. We’ll buy it on your behalf.

Imagine how much more assortment across fashion and lifestyle we could offer this way, without stocking it ourselves. We can then build that into our personalization, learning more about customers’ interests beyond our existing catalog and helping them discover more products.

Vogue: With general-purpose AI agents increasingly capable of shopping on consumers’ behalf, are you competing directly with the likes of OpenAI, Google and Meta? Why would shoppers choose Zalando instead?

People are going to use a variety of agents, but our mission is always to make Zalando the best place to start the fashion and lifestyle shopping journey. That comes down to the customer experience we can provide that others can’t, which starts with data.

We’ve been using AI for over 15 years, including for personalized shopping recommendations, and we’ve invested heavily in size and fit. We get tens of thousands of body measurements a week, and we have so much data from customer returns about which items run small or large. So we’ve got over 10,000 size charts, and we’ve put AI on top of that. No third-party agent has got that. So if you care about getting the fit right the first time, Zalando’s agent will be the place to come.

We’ve also invested in recommending whole outfits based on our understanding of trends, how people shop for different occasions and years of customer behavior at scale.

Vogue: How quickly do you expect Zalando Extended to grow? Are you planning to onboard lots more retailers in the coming months, or is this more of a test-and-learn phase?

It’s a little bit of both. We’re testing and learning, but it’s not a particularly complex thing we’re doing, and we’re very excited by what we’ve seen so far. Assuming it’s successful, this has the potential to scale very fast because the integration is so lightweight.

Most of these retailers already produce an affiliate feed, which is essentially what we need. We can make the sign-up and operations very simple for them, and it’s very light for us too. So there’s potential to scale this massively.

Vogue: Trust is fundamental to AI agent adoption, and attitudes vary between markets. Why would consumers trust Zalando Assistant more than a general-purpose AI agent?

Zalando is a brand that people trust, and we’ve worked very hard to earn that trust. The company has just turned 18, and we’ve built that trust through how we look after the customer experience, including how we handle their data. We’re a European company, so the data we hold is subject to high European standards for data protection.

We’ve seen customers enthusiastically adopt Zalando Assistant. Interestingly, questions about what we know about them haven’t been a big part of the conversation — people have just started using it. We’ve had 22 million customers engage with Zalando Assistant this year, including 13 million in the last quarter.

Customers are twice as likely to buy something in a session where they use Zalando Assistant compared with one where they don’t. And of course, we have all the consent mechanisms required in Europe. Customers can also request that their data be deleted.

Graeme Smith, Zalando’s CTO. Photo: Courtesy of Zalando.

Vogue: Is there a risk that Zalando could lose its direct relationship with customers by bringing other retailers onto its platform?

No, we don’t think of it like that. We want people to come to Zalando more and more, and for it to be the place where they start their shopping journey. We’ve got 70% organic traffic, which is very high, and we work hard to maintain that.

We think we can do that by building really great experiences tailored to fashion and lifestyle shopping. Bringing in more retailers actually gives people more reasons to come to Zalando, because they know they can access a wider variety of products. They can buy a sofa on Zalando, as well as everything else. So we think this could actually drive more traffic.

Now, could someone go directly to Westwing to buy their next sofa? Of course, and that’s fine. We don’t sell sofas on Zalando. What matters is that we’re the best place to discover fashion and lifestyle products, wherever they come from.

Vogue: You’re also piloting advertising in ChatGPT and preparing to participate in Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol. How does that fit with your ambition to make Zalando the starting point for shopping?

There are three strands to our strategy. The first is getting people to keep coming back to Zalando as the best place to start their shopping journey. The second is what we call inbound agentic commerce, and the third is Zalando Extended, which allows us to massively expand the assortment available through outbound agentic commerce.

Inbound agentic commerce is what most people talk about when they discuss AI shopping agents. People are using ChatGPT, Google’s AI-powered search and other platforms. We had to decide early on how we felt about that, and we saw it as an opportunity. Our customers are going to use these services anyway, so we want Zalando to be there and meet them where they are. We also want to reach new customers.

We’ve become very good at generative engine optimisation (GEO) — we’re the number one fashion destination in Europe referred to by AI agents. But we haven’t stopped at organic visibility. We’ve also piloted advertising inside ChatGPT in the UK, and we’re now looking at the results and deciding where to go next.

With Google, it’s even more interesting. When Google launches agentic commerce in Europe, Zalando will be there from the start. Customers will be able to discover Zalando products and even check out within Google if they want to.

But they’ll still need a Zalando account. That’s very important to us. We want to engage with these AI platforms on our own terms and maintain the customer relationship.

Vogue: Fashion shopping is often emotional and highly considered. Do you think consumers will really want to complete purchases through AI agents, rather than visiting a retailer’s website?

We don’t know how this is going to play out. I’m very excited by it, but fashion is very personal and emotional.

What we see is that when customers arrive at Zalando from another channel, whether that’s an AI agent, Instagram or TikTok, they often don’t buy the item they landed on. They explore three or four more products, look at similar items and browse around before making a purchase.

It’s another signal that fashion is different, it’s a high-consideration purchase. So if I had to bet — and it’s always difficult to make predictions — I think people will use agents to research products, but they’ll still want to click through to the retailer, like Zalando, to ask: is this item quite right for me? What more can I learn about it? What similar products are available? And then maybe they’ll buy from there, but let’s see.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6730. Buying Your First Pair of Selvedge Jeans? Start Here

We’ve got bad news for white couches: Crunchy, indigo-dyed, raw selvedge jeans are back. People might say they never left, but as someone who literally edited a daily web series about denim fades from 2015 to 2018, I can assure you that across the almost-decade since, the category has taken something of a back seat as jeans with interesting washes and nostalgic cuts (Our Legacy’s Third Cut, GAP’s 90s Loose) surged in popularity.

But while it, ahem, faded from the public eye, the raw denim market was still tended to by the true believers among us. And we owe them a great debt, because their stewardship means we’re not just picking up where the last trend left off. Instead, we’re jumping into an elevated timeline. The best makers in the world have only gotten better, the cuts have gotten more diverse, and a whole bunch of stuff that was once incredibly hard to find in the United States is now readily available.

So available, in fact, that the selection can be overwhelming. Which is where I come in! Because while there are now thousands of pairs of raw denim jeans to choose from, I can tell you that only a precious few specific cuts have consistently dominated Subreddits, YouTube roundups, and my text message history for the best part of this century. Ten of them are below, starting with five approachable icons, and moving through to five more legendary deeper cuts. Let’s get faded.

The company behind Sugar Cane, Toyo Enterprise, has been making hard-wearing garments since the mid-’60s, but Sugar Cane didn’t come around until 1975. Ever since, they’ve been making some of the most considered, sturdy and timeless jeans and workwear on the planet in Japan, all of it aging more beautifully than a fancy barolo.

If you’re looking to dip your toes into the Sugar Cane pool, the 1947 model brilliantly recreates one of the most well-loved iterations of the most well-worn model on the planet (we won’t name names, but they’re in here too), and comes in a four-season, 14.25oz. selvedge denim fabric that will produce some preposterously good fades.

For anyone who’s fallen in love with a pair of old old vintage jeans, and wondered what they felt like when they came off the production line, it’s hard to get closer than a pair of Fullcounts. The brand was started in 1993 in Osaka, Japan, with the express purpose of reverse engineering the wonder of those vintage pairs, down to the all-cotton threads and long-staple cotton.

They sure figured it out, and still make everything in Japan. And while the classic 0105 is an absolute knockout, the Wide Straight iteration gives you a little more comfort with the same break-in potential. And if you’re just getting yourself into the raw selvedge game, a little comfort never hurts.

The only Canadian entrant on this list—partly because Henry’s hasn’t restocked yet—Naked & Famous has been around since 2008. And as you might expect from a brand whose hallmark fit is called the Weird Guy, they’re a little quirky. In a good way! For not only are they rigorously dedicated to sourcing the sickest raw denim on the planet, but that denim often has some funky detailing as well, like a green weft or some galaxy-like imperfections.

The True Guy cut is technically a relaxed straight (don’t confuse that for baggy) and this particular pair has kevlar woven into the fabric, for those into literal bulletproof denim.

If you’ve ever spent time on denim message boards, you’ve probably seen the name “Iron Heart” associated with some of the heaviest denim known to man. (If you’ve never been, steel yourself before entering.) And while it is true that the Japanese brand pushes the definition of heavyweight to its absolute limit, it also makes a damn good pair of regular jeans.

In fact, the mid-weight fare is as good as any on the market, will produce some HOF-worthy fades, and won’t require a title fight to soften up. Within that weight class, the straight leg of the 634S-142 is the kind of timeless silhouette that should outlast most trend cycles. (Also, for the record, “mid-weight” is a relative term. This is the lightest-weight denim that Iron Heart will entertain.)

While the US quite literally invented jeans as we understand them (denim as a fabric is another story, for those keeping very detailed score), you’d be forgiven for thinking otherwise, considering the lack of US-made options on this list. But thankfully, 3Sixteen is doing the work of like six companies at this point, sourcing the world’s finest denim—we don’t really make that here anymore—and stitching the 5-pockets up back home in the USA.

Every cut they make has a legion of fans, but the semi-recent, semi-baggy RS is the one tearing up the charts at the moment. And for great reasons. It’s got the aforementioned room, has a top block (re: the area that houses the waistband, fly and pockets) that doesn’t get all bunched up and funky, and a higher rise that’s flattering on just about everyone. As a result, it’s a pair that both denimheads and denim rookies appreciate with the same kind of zeal.

When it comes to details that will turn a denimhead into a living meme—Vince McMahon Progression, Guy Turning Around, you pick—few brands can execute them like Oni can. From the denim itself, which is milled in Japan and feels more handmade than small-batch sourdough, to the period-accurate details like flat-felled seams and linear bar tacks, every pair starts as a work of art and develops into a wholly separate work of art as they’re worn.

The only issue, really, is finding them, because hand-making just about everything isn’t exactly a scalable process. When they’re around, (and they currently are!) they’re worth more than just a gander, particularly the Wide Straight, which has a loose, straight leg and a healthy, fairly forgiving rise. This pair in particular is made with lighter-weight 12oz. denim, but don’t mistake that for lightweight denim—it’ll hold up year round, and could always handle some longjohns during a cold-snap, if you feel so inclined.

Those familiar with the Osaka 5—the loose collection of denim brands that sprouted up in Osaka in the ‘70s, ‘80s and ‘90s and redefined the very notion of raw denim specifically and the idea of what “jeans” could be, more broadly—will know that Warehouse was the fifth and final member, founded by two alums from a different member, Evisu. And for roughly 30 years the brand’s pumped out intricately detailed, vintage-indebted jeans that some of the pickiest people on the planet have sworn by, even going so far as sourcing American cotton to keep the look and feel as close to the source material as possible.

This pair in particular is based on one of the most popular pairs of 501s Levi’s ever made, the 1966 model, which had a straight leg and a high rise and a slightly twisted seam after a few washes, giving it a slow-developing signature—all present and accounted for here in 2026 via Warehouse.

These aren’t for the faint of heart. Let’s get that out of the way. 21oz. denim is almost armor, especially if your previous denim reference point is something with a wash, a rinse or some stretch. But for anyone looking for a challenge, absolutely electric fades and a pair of jeans that might outlast horseshoe crabs, look no further.

That’s because Samurai, another Osaka-based brand (but not part of the Osaka 5, for whatever it’s worth), makes some of the hardest-fading, hardest-wearing, most-revered jeans anywhere, and that includes the ultra-heavyweight numbers. And who knows, all that extra (fabric) weight might be nice with winter incoming.

Levi’s offers some great raw selvedge 501s at a pretty reasonable price, a pair that will age well and (with proper care of course) last for years. The 501, however, isn’t a standardized cut. In fact, it’s tweaked every few years to reflect the prevailing sentiment of the time a little bit better. And as a result, different eras have different hallmarks—for instance, the 1947 is a bit slimmer, the 1954 is the first pair with a zipper and the 1901 is the first pair with two back pockets.

Levi’s Vintage Clothing, a sub-label under the broader umbrella, still makes a bunch of these pairs and while the aforementioned are killer, the 1933 feels paradoxically relevant to 2026: it’s got a healthy, wide leg, a healthy rise and a couple cheeky details to differentiate it from the rest of the pack, like a back cinch and suspender buttons.

We couldn’t make this list without including a pair from the first member of the Osaka 5, in part because it’s hard to imagine any of this would be possible without Studio D’Artisan and in part because the brand still makes some of the best jeans in the world. Founded in 1979, Studio D’Artisan kicked off the obsession surrounding raw selvedge denim and bygone detailing, doubling down on craftsmanship and material quality in an era defined by synthetics and acid-washing. And they never really strayed, ultimately adding some more timeless staples to the denim assortment, all of it made in Japan with commensurate care. The SD-801 is a classic straight leg fit, made in Japan from a rope-dyed natural indigo 15oz. denim fabric and armed with a host of cheeky details, like a selvedge hit at the coin pocket and a goat leather patch at the back.

Of course, trying out any new look comes with the eternal question: How do I style these things?

Well, one of the best things about raw selvedge denim is that it wears well with pretty much everything. With that in mind, don’t overthink it. But if you do grab yourself a pair of elite-tier jeans and feel like upgrading the supporting cast around it, we have some recommendations for you. For instance, a pair of sturdy leather shoes—whether some Tyroleans, a work boot, or the like—has a multiplying effect beneath some rope-dyed indigo. The same goes for a vintage-inspired, well-proportioned t-shirt or hardy flannel. Of course, as is the case with the jeans above, not all of these items are created equal. The below eight, however, have the GQ seal of approval.

#6728. 3 Ways To Defrost Chicken Without Spreading Salmonella, According To An Expert

Your dinner plans aren't ruined just yet.

Forgetting to take chicken out of the freezer is an all-too-common occurrence that can bring your dinner plans to a screeching halt. To get things back on track, your gut instinct may be to thaw it as quickly as possible. But there are more important things to worry about than a delayed dinner.

Raw poultry can carry Salmonella, so how you handle it matters. Nothing is less appetizing than giving your whole family a foodborne illness.

But before you give up and order takeout, we’re here to help. We chatted with Ellen Steinberg, PhD, RD, LD, and food safety specialist, to find the best (and safest) methods to thaw chicken. Whether you plan ahead or need to defrost it fast, here’s what you should do.

Defrosting chicken isn’t as simple as taking it out of the freezer. Salmonella is real, y’all—according to FoodSafety.gov, roughly 4% of chicken packages at American grocery stores are contaminated with the bacteria. That bacteria can multiply rapidly in the temperature danger zone, between 40°F and 140°F. Translation: Leaving your chicken out on the counter can actually make you sick.

To prevent that, choose the right method and protect the surrounding environment from cross-contamination. Even with supposedly airtight packaging, the plastic may have holes, or chicken juice may transfer from other packages at the grocery store. It’s especially difficult to spot when the meat is frozen, so Steinberg says it’s better to be safe than sorry.

“You should put your [raw] chicken in a roasting pan or a baking sheet so the juices won’t spread,” she says. Everything that touches raw chicken should be thoroughly cleaned with hot, soapy water. If you want to take food safety even further, Steinberg suggests keeping a separate cutting board in a different color that you use exclusively for raw meat. And above all else: Wash your hands!

If you’re not in a rush, thawing chicken in the fridge yields the most consistent results. Because refrigerators should stay at 40°F and below, frozen chicken can gradually defrost without entering the temperature danger zone where bacteria multiply more rapidly.

Because of this, Steinberg says it’s the only USDA-approved thawing method that lets you refreeze raw chicken without cooking it first. “If you end up deciding that you don’t want to cook the chicken or you only want to use half of it, you can place it back in the freezer,” she says. There is a caveat, however: Once your chicken has fully thawed, you should either cook or refreeze it within one to two days.

If you opt for the refrigerator method, keep these safety measures in mind. Beyond keeping your meat contained on a plate or tray, place it on the bottom shelf. If juice drips, it’ll contaminate the fewest ingredients. Steinberg also suggests storing the chicken toward the back of your refrigerator. “The temperature is more consistent, unlike the areas closest to the door,” she says.

If you need to defrost chicken fast, one of the best ways is with cool, running water. Unlike fridge air, water conducts heat much more effectively. Keeping the water moving also helps maintain consistent thawing conditions. But you don't necessarily need to leave the faucet running: The USDA also recommends submerging chicken in cold water and changing it every 30 minutes.

So if cold water thaws meat quickly, would hot water do the job even faster? It might, but the potential food safety risks aren't worth it. "If you thaw chicken under warm or hot water, the outside of the meat can enter the temperature danger zone while the center is still frozen,” Steinberg says.

For the running-water method, place the chicken in leak-proof packaging in a bowl and run cool water (70°F or lower) over it. Thawing times depend on the size and thickness of the meat, but smaller packages may be ready in an hour or less. Once thawed, cook the chicken immediately before considering refreezing it.

The final USDA-approved method involves using your microwave’s defrost setting. While it’s certainly faster than letting meat thaw in the fridge, we suggest relying on this method only if you have no other option.

Steinberg says this technique leaves the least wiggle room for planning your dinner. “You have to cook it immediately,” she says. “You can’t defrost it and then decide to cook two hours later.”

The need to cook immediately is certainly one downside of the microwave method. However, another compelling argument against using the defrost setting is that it can make your chicken taste worse.

Microwaves heat food unevenly, especially with thicker pieces of meat. Some areas can start warming up or even cooking before the center fully thaws. It's not a big deal when reheating leftovers, but it can nearly ruin frozen proteins.

By the time the center is fully defrosted, the outer edges may already be partially cooked. Can you imagine chicken that tastes worse than unseasoned microwaved chicken? We can't.

It’s a safe and fast defrosting method when followed by immediate cooking—but at what cost? So we'd only vouch for this technique if your chicken will end up shredded or submerged in enough sauce to mask the texture.

#6727. Lights, Camera, Action! An Exclusive Look Inside ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood Celebration

Florence Pugh, Julianne Moore, Penélope Cruz, and more were honored at our annual event.

Los Angeles has no shortage of awards shows, but ELLE’s annual Women in Hollywood event has always been about something more: putting the spotlight on the women whose work makes the industry worth watching. On Monday night, eight of film and television’s most talked-about talents came together to celebrate their collective achievements, with plenty of oohs, aahs, and well-deserved gushes along the way.

This year’s honorees—Carrie Coon, Elizabeth Debicki, Rosalind Eleazar, Julianne Moore, Samantha Morton, Inde Navarrette, Florence Pugh, and Penélope Cruz—gathered at the Four Seasons Hotel Los Angeles at Beverly Hills for an evening hosted by ELLE editor-in-chief Nina Garcia.

Presented in partnership with Ralph Lauren and Bulgari, with support from Evian, the soirée drew familiar faces from across Tinseltown. Matt Damon, Seth Rogen, Bryce Dallas Howard, Alexander Skarsgård, and Louisa Jacobson were among those who took the stage to present the honors, while Morton accepted hers remotely from her home in London, where she was sick with the flu.

Beyond the eight honorees, the guest list included Lily James, Ashley Park, Elsa Hosk, Madison Beer, Jackie Tohn, Molly Sims, and more.

Champagne and yuzu mocktails flowed as guests mingled before making their way into the ballroom, where a three-course dinner awaited: beet salad, Chilean sea bass, and chocolate tortino.

Garcia kicked things off by celebrating a banner year for moviegoing, while reminding the room that there’s still work to be done when it comes to creating opportunities for women. “We need roles for women that are messy, complicated, funny, and real—and sometimes even older than 50!” she said.

She pointed to the eight honorees as a reminder of what’s possible when those roles make it to the screen. “You are all proof of what happens when these roles are written—you knock it out of the park. These women we are honoring? The characters they have played? They are not decorative. They’re not supporting a man’s journey. They are women in full.”

Scroll through below for an exclusive look inside the event.

Moriel is the editorial and social media assistant at ELLE.com, covering celebrity, culture, and fashion. She previously wrote for The Daily Front Row. When she's off work, you can find her with her nose in a book, taking a dance class, or online shopping.

#6726. What’s It Like to Be Tennis’s World Number One? Daniil Medvedev Lets Us Into the Club

The ATP Finals—the most important men’s tournament on the tennis calendar outside of the Grand Slams—kicked off on Sunday in Torino. Founded in 1970 as a season-ending competition pitting the highest-ranked players against each other, the current iteration features the world’s top eight men—Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Ben Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli, Arthur Fils, Frances Tiafoe, and Rafael Jodar—facing each other first in a round-robin group format and then in elimination stages. (It’s similar in format to the women’s WTA Finals, which concluded Sunday in Indian Wells, with Mirra Andreeva taking home the big trophy.)

Ranking, of course, is everything—it’s what gets you invited to the finals—and the summa achievement of the world’s top ranking is the subject of a new book, ATP No. 1 Club: Icons of Men’s Tennis, just out from Phaidon. It features iconic photos of each number-one player since 1973—the men’s game has seen only 30, including Alcaraz, Zverev, and Medvedev—along with text by the late award-winning tennis writer Mark Hodgkinson.

We sat down with one of those iconic players—Medvedev, one of the five current or former number-ones still competing—to ask him, you know, what it’s like to do something better than anyone else in the world.

Vogue: Do you remember, from your earliest years playing tennis, who was number one at the time?

Daniil Medvedev: I started playing tennis when I was six, in 2002, but I was not yet a tennis fan, let’s say. By the time I started to understand tennis a bit more, Roger [Federer] was there already, and I think for most of my childhood it was Roger at number one, and then Rafa, who from time to time took the top spot. And then came Novak—who, as we know now, took the leading spot for a longer period of time. One time, years later, I made a game of it—I think I named, not all of them, probably 27 of them.

Did you have a tennis hero when you were a kid?

So I have to be honest here: I’m still probably a bit like this, but when I was young, whoever was winning too much—doesn’t matter which sport—I stopped liking them. I’m like, Okay, he’s only winning. So at one point I was supporting anyone against Roger—I don’t say it in a bad way, it’s just how I am. At one moment it was Barcelona with [their former coach] Pep Guardiola and they were beating everyone, and I was like, Okay—give us something new.

But it changed from tournament to tournament: I supported Marat [Safin in 2005] when he won the Australian Open. This was incredible—we, as kids in Russia, were waking up early in the morning to watch his matches. Andy Roddick—I loved his serve; sometimes I was copying it. Novak as well, when he just came in, before he started beating everyone and I was cheering for the underdog. I never had one hero.

When you were dreaming kid dreams, was it about winning Wimbledon or another tournament? Was being the world number one ever part of that?

I never was thinking about number one or a Grand Slam. Of course, when I grew up and started playing better tennis, those kind of goals came into place. But when I was really young, I remember hitting against the wall, and because the wall never misses, I was thinking that I’m playing against Roger, Rafa, Novak. I was trying to beat them, but of course you cannot beat the wall. Those were fun memories—and I think, probably, in the back of my mind, I knew that if I’m playing them, it means that I’m somewhere in the top rankings.

My dream was to become a great tennis player, and I feel like I achieved it. I’m happy about it: Every day you go to practice, you work hard, you fight for the matches, and you don’t think about it. But when I talk to someone like you and put myself back there, I’m like, I actually achieved my dream. It’s just that the dream constantly changes, because you want more.

Did you feel different when you first became the ATP number one player in 2022?

Yes and no. Maybe there’s a tiny bit more pressure and attention paid to you, but it’s also just such a nice feeling. I mean, you are the best in the whole world, and everyone else is just trying. And it was not easy, but I made it. [Medvedev became the first player outside the so-called Big Four—Djokovic, Federer, Nadal, and Murray—to hold the top ranking in 18 years.]

Did that put a kind of target on you that hadn’t been there before?

For sure, especially in the world we live in now, that happens. Whenever you lose: “Oh, he’s not good enough to be world number one.” But I didn’t care, because I’m like, “I’m number one,” and it felt so good. People would ask me after a loss, “Maybe the ranking put more pressure on you? Maybe that’s why you didn’t perform.” I’d just say, “Maybe yes,” but I didn’t care. It was such a good feeling. Anyone who has been there, I think, will tell you the same: It’s a nice feeling. I want to try to be there again, of course—it’s going to be super tough, especially with Carlos and Jannik [Sinner] winning so much.

Did people—either inside or outside of tennis—treat you differently when you were number one? Did things come to you more easily?

For sure, when I was the world number one—I was on a big stretch of winning the 2021 US Open, playing some Masters finals, winning some Masters—I got some, whatever you call it, invitations. I remember going to Los Angeles before Indian Wells after I became world number one, and I went to some restaurants and I would ask for the bill and they’re like, “Yes—someone took care of it.” So stuff like this—when you are world number one, people talk a bit more about you; you’re on TV more. These are things which come with, let’s call it fame, which also can have a downside: Some people do this kind of thing just for pleasure, but maybe someone else pays and thinks that you’re going to sit and talk to him for 30 minutes. And I don’t want to be obliged to do something because someone did something for me—that’s just how I live. Especially if I’m rushing somewhere, you know: I’m okay to pay, man. As I say, there are some upsides, some downsides. If you get invited to a football match and you meet some players, or a baseball match: fun.

Ah, game. Okay. I didn’t know this. In any case: I just enjoy life. I’m number one, I enjoy life. I’m number 10, I enjoy life.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6724. The 12 Best-Dressed Stars at the GQ Men of the Year 2026 Party

The GQ Men of the Year 2026 party is a wrap, and what a time it was. Where else but on menswear’s biggest night could you see Stavvy rocking a chartreuse suit, get some potential dirt about the next James Bond straight from the source, and witness Matt Damon learning that “body count” has two meanings? Now that’s Hollywood, baby!

As per usual, the evening really started cooking on the step-and-repeat, where the celebs took the “modern red carpet” dress code to heart. We’re talking swaggy suiting, fantastic gowns, and yes, even a very good pair of khakis. Scroll on to see our favorite looks of the night.

Now this is how you wear a suit. The Emmy-winning star of The Bear rolled up in an impeccably tailored pinstriped look by London-based designer Conner Ives, which was punctuated by a bright green shirt, a forehead curl, and a deep burgundy tie that matched the MOTY backdrop. As GQ’s former fashion critic Rachel Tashjian put it on Instagram: “She always looks cool, but this is the coolest she’s ever looked.”

For Garfield, no look is complete without his flowing mane of hair. It doesn’t hurt to have a crisply tailored Edward Sexton suit and an all-time classic watch from Breguet on his wrist.

Andrew Garfield in Edward Sexton. Watch by Breguet.

In Mowalowa sparkles and a Donna Summer-esque ’do, Tinashe looked every bit like the Popstar she is.

The Tony star sexed up the classic shawl lapel-jacket with a high-voltage shade of green. This is what the GQ Men of the Year party is all about: pulling off a fashion risk with A-lister-level confidence.

Stavros Halkias in Alan David, Cego, and Bottega Veneta.

The writer-director duo behind this year’s hit international film, La Bola Negra, brought their own flowers last night. In addition to rocking coordinating roses, Los Javis—made up of two Javiers, Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo—put a sexy spin on the classic red-carpet suit by way of leather mesh and exposed undies (courtesy of Haider Ackermann’s Tom Ford) and perfectly tousled curls (subjects’ own).

Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo in Tom Ford.

Naturally, as GQ’s 2026 Designer of the Year, it makes sense that Rider (wearing his own Celine clothes) would be one of the best dressed of the night. Have you ever seen an undershirt peek out of a sweater with such unpracticed rakishness? Or a pair of khakis look so at home on a red carpet? Take notes.

Two episodes into the return of HBO’s Gilded Age, Louisa Jacobson cruised off a successful season premiere in a sultry McQueen moto jacket. She’s been on a style streak over the past year, with several covetable jackets and menswear-inspired outfits in her repertoire—and this leathery number is keeping that streak strong.

Louisa Jacobson in Alexander McQueen. Jewelry by Azlee.

The Off Campus breakout has spent plenty of time on red carpets this year, but a wonky striped suit by Vivienne Westwood—featuring some truly humongous lapels—is a major fashion leap forward.

Belmont Cameli in Vivienne Westwood. Watch by Audemars Piguet.

A fringed glove? A pom-pom heel? A knockout of an outfit, all courtesy of Sarah Burton’s Givenchy.

What’s better than one head full of wicked micro-whisps? Two heads full of wicked micro-whisps, as seen on GQ Breakouts Shanny Wise and Jackson Walker Lewis, of the NYC DJ duo Fcukers. They each wore all-black designer duds, punctuating their looks with cut-outs and patches of leather.

Shanny Wise in Jordan Lea Allen and Haider Ackermann. Jackson Walker Lewis in Dior and Balenciaga.

#6722. Is This the Greatest Fashion Auction of All Time?

3,000 fashion items from a personal collection are up for sale at Maurice Auction in Paris.

Who owns four vintage Dior Maasai necklaces? Not very many people, except for, of course, one of Paris’s most mysterious women and deeply devoted collectors of fashion. The anonymous French clotheshorse is now the subject of an upcoming multipart, 3,000-piece sale at Maurice Auction. “It’s not someone who is known by the industry, it’s just someone who was very wealthy and that could afford such a collection as a true and passionate collector for more than 30 years,” Salomé Pirson, co-founder of Maurice Auction, tells ELLE.

Dubbed the Infinite Wardrobe, the multipart auction contains haute couture, ready-to-wear, handbags, and accessories from the likes of Chanel, Dior, Hermès, Valentino, Roberto Cavalli, Fendi, and Ungaro. The Infinite Wardrobe will kick off with a live auction on November 18 in Paris, followed by eight different online-only auctions sorted by brand or subject (Chanel, Italian fashion, Dior, bags, for instance). Even with the growing interest in auctions recently spurred by a younger demographic, it’s certainly one of the most extensive fashion auctions that has happened in recent years. Earlier this year, Maurice Auction broke records when it sold rare haute couture from the collection of couture queen Mouna Ayoub.

Much of the Infinite Wardrobe is unworn or only worn once, pristinely preserved like a time capsule for decades in one closet. Some of it even still has tags attached. “What’s unusual is the volume,” says Marie-Laurence Tixier, co-founder of Maurice Auction. “The client was really someone who collected, and when she liked a look or a pair of shoes, she would buy all the colors.” For the auction, that means Hermès Oran sandals in every shade of the rainbow and every iteration of vintage Chanel Gripoix necklaces. Some of the items will be sold in more than a dozen variations.

When the duo first encountered the collection, it was stored in a single Parisian apartment, all exhibited by color, type of accessory, and brand. “I’ve heard that people, when they went to have dinner at her place, they visited the closet, because it was a piece of art itself,” adds Tixier. It’s by far the biggest auction the company has ever done since it was founded in 2022, and also the biggest undertaking of their careers in terms of cataloging, researching, and organizing all of the pieces. “It’s like going into a fantasy closet where you realize it’s not gonna be a dream, it’s gonna be a real job for three months,” says Tixier. The rarest items were researched in collaboration with Kerry Taylor, fashion’s favorite London auctioneer.

If you love designer fashion, it’s a great opportunity to pick up a vintage luxury just before the holidays. But for the real fashion freaks, there are some ultra-rare gems that rarely come to market, too. Think: Jean Paul Gaultier-designed Hermès crocodile jackets, Emanuel Ungaro haute couture, and incredible, lightweight vintage Fendi furs. “She had exquisite taste, it’s very elegant, very, very refined,” says Tixier. “There are no logos.”

Roberto Cavalli beaded trousers, Christian Dior by Gianfranco Ferré mini bustle dresses, and Gianni Versace embroidered jackets are just a few of the treasures available in the first part of the auction. In other words: the dream closet is real, and soon, it will be up for grabs.

#6720. The Vogue Business AI Tracker

The Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most important AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week. From venture capital investments and startup launches to product drops and regulatory updates, we’ll make sure you never miss a beat when it comes to the AI news that matters.

The news: J.Crew launches AI stylist built on Anthropic’s Claude.

Why it matters: J.Crew is the latest luxury brand to introduce an AI-powered shopping assistant. Built on Anthropic’s Claude, its new “Style Advisor” helps customers put together outfits based on occasions, personal preferences and specific items, drawing on the brand’s styling archives and campaign imagery.

The launch reflects a growing push among fashion retailers to make online shopping more conversational and personalized, as brands look to keep customers within their own digital ecosystems, rather than lose product discovery to third-party AI platforms. It comes a week after Prada became the first luxury brand to launch a dedicated plugin with ChatGPT, and follows Ralph Lauren’s push into branded AI personal styling last year with its “Ask Ralph” white-label AI styling tool.

The news: Natural Cycles launches its own fertility-tracking smart ring.

Why it matters: Natural Cycles is launching its first smart ring, moving beyond its existing partnership with Oura into its own wearable hardware. The new “NC Ring” measures body temperature overnight, feeding data into the company’s AI-powered fertility algorithm, which uses machine learning to calculate daily fertility status for its hormone-free contraceptive app.

The move puts Natural Cycles into competition with Oura, whose CEO Tom Hale told Vogue Business that women’s health features have been a significant driver of growth as the company moves towards a much-anticipated IPO. Unlike the Oura integration, which requires subscriptions to both services, NC Ring works with a Natural Cycles subscription alone. The company says around 80% of its active users already track their temperature using a wearable, giving it an established customer base for its own hardware.

The news: Pre-orders for Gentle Monster’s Google smart glasses are already sold out.

Why it matters: All 16 styles of Gentle Monster’s new AI smart glasses, developed with Google and Samsung, have sold out their initial pre-order allocations just days after launching, despite prices starting at $449. It’s a surprising sign that fashion-forward design could help win over consumers who might otherwise be reluctant to wear a computer on their face. Notably, most of Google’s more conventional Warby Parker styles remain available.

Gentle Monster’s sellout suggests that distinctive design could be a powerful draw, even as the surveillance debate remains unresolved. The caveat? Neither Google nor Gentle Monster has disclosed how many pairs were available to pre-order, making it difficult to gauge the scale of demand.

The news: Gentle Monster taps Joaquin Phoenix to front its Google AI Glasses.

Why it matters: Gentle Monster unveiled a campaign starring Joaquin Phoenix for its forthcoming AI-powered glasses, developed with Google and Samsung. Directed by filmmaker Jonathan Glazer, the short film will debut in mid-November, ahead of the collection’s December launch. (Pre-orders open on November 12.) The glasses, first previewed at Google I/O in May, run on Google’s Android XR platform and integrate its Gemini assistant, offering features including real-time translation, navigation and hands-free photography.

The launch marks a significant step in Google’s return to smart eyewear, adding competition to Meta’s established Ray-Ban partnership. Google has also teamed up with Warby Parker, while Kering is developing AI glasses with Google for Gucci. Gentle Monster’s decision to enlist Phoenix and Glazer is yet another sign that fashion credibility and cultural positioning are central to Big Tech rivals’ attempts to win the smart glasses race.

The news: Amazon launches SMS-based AI shopping agent after blocking Meta’s Muse.

Why it matters: Amazon has begun testing an expanded version of its AI shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping, among a small group of US customers over text. The new SMS feature lets shoppers search for and compare products, send photographs to find similar items, track prices and complete purchases without opening Amazon’s website or app.

The move reflects a broader shift toward making every consumer touchpoint shoppable, from social media and search engines to messaging. As AI agents become accessible through everyday interactions, the distinction between browsing, asking for advice and making a purchase could become increasingly blurred. For luxury brands, the challenge is not just where their products are sold, but how they appear in shopping conversations that take place beyond their own channels.

Amazon’s decision to block Meta Muse from accessing its marketplace in September also suggests that retailers want to extend their own reach without necessarily ceding control of discovery to competitors.

The news: Zalando unveils plans for AI shopping agent that can buy from other retailers.

Why it matters: Zalando has announced plans for a new AI shopping agent that will allow customers to purchase products from other retailers without leaving its app. Called Zalando Extended, the service is being piloted with homeware retailer Westwing, with AI-powered checkout scheduled to officially launch in 2027. The agent will eventually be able to complete purchases on shoppers’ behalf, expanding Zalando’s offering beyond the products it sells directly. The move builds on its existing conversational AI assistant, which has attracted more than 22 million unique users this year, according to Zalando’s Q3 earnings update.

The retailer’s plans follow a similar move by Amazon, whose Buy for Me feature allows customers to purchase products from external retailers through its shopping app. Both point to a potentially significant change in the marketplace model: rather than requiring brands and retailers to list their products on a platform, AI agents could facilitate purchases directly from their own websites.

For brands, this could open up new routes to customers without the usual marketplace integrations, while raising questions about who controls product discovery and the customer relationship. For Zalando, it offers a way to expand its assortment without holding additional stock, while keeping shoppers within its own ecosystem.

Why it matters: Prada has launched a ChatGPT plugin allowing users in the US, the UK and Italy to discover products, explore collections and find stores using information sourced directly from the brand. As AI assistants become a gateway to product discovery, the move gives Prada a more authoritative presence in conversations it might otherwise struggle to influence. “Conversational experiences represent a natural evolution of traditional e-commerce,” said Prada Group digital director Laura Campanella. “Through this pilot initiative, we are exploring a new territory for customer engagement.”

The news coincides with the launch of Prada’s Christmas campaign this week, featuring hand-drawn animation by Disney veteran John Pomeroy. These two contrasting moves reflect a broader distinction emerging in luxury: AI for product discovery, and human craftsmanship for consumer-facing brand storytelling.

The news: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals the huge costs and risks of the AI boom.

Why it matters: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO filing offers a rare look inside the economics — and extraordinary risks — of the AI industry. As the Claude AI maker prepares for a potential $2 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reports that its revenues exceeded $33 billion in the first nine months of 2026, while its computing costs have fallen dramatically relative to sales, all suggesting a path to profitability. Yet Anthropic has also committed more than $800 billion to computing infrastructure through 2045, much of it supplied by technology giants including Amazon and Google, who are also major investors.

Crucially, the prospectus devotes 92 pages to risks, warning that future AI models could resist shutdown, manipulate information or cause harm too large for insurers to cover. For businesses embedding AI into everything from creative production to customer service, the filing exposes a central contradiction: the technology is becoming commercially indispensable even as its developers acknowledge profound uncertainty over its long-term risks.

The news: Anthropic plans European AI consultancy.

Why it matters: Anthropic is reportedly partnering with private equity firm Hg to launch a European consultancy that’ll place AI engineers and advisers in external businesses to help them integrate Anthropic’s technology, according to the Financial Times. Expected to launch by the end of 2026, hubs are currently planned in London and Berlin, with the Claude developer likely using the venture to accelerate corporate AI adoption — and even capture some of the work traditionally handled by consultancies such as Accenture and the Big Four.

Fashion and luxury businesses, many of which are still grappling with how to deploy AI, could be fertile ground for these services. But the model raises an obvious tension: while companies may welcome direct access to AI expertise, how independent can the advice be when the consultancy is backed by a company with a commercial interest in driving adoption of its own technology?

The news: Anthropic launches Claude Duet AI agent to rival OpenAI and Meta.

Why it matters: Anthropic has released Claude Duet, an AI agent rivaling Meta’s consumer-focused Muse and OpenAI’s more enterprise-oriented Dots; the Duet has both brand and consumer use cases for fashion. It can purchase products on consumers’ behalf using Shopify’s Shop Pay and Stripe Link, while merchants can instruct the agent to set up, design and manage their Shopify stores, including inventory and orders, Anthropic announced in a blog post. Meanwhile, a “richer visual editor” — which allows brands to design and preview their storefronts within the agent’s interface before anything goes live — is “coming soon”.

It was only a matter of time until Anthropic followed Meta and OpenAI in launching a personal AI assistant. Now, the battle is on between these tech companies to capture both consumer and brands’ trust, so that the integration these agents depend on across stores and payment providers is realized. The growing competition here signals a shift towards AI-mediated purchases, potentially reducing direct customer interactions for brands and making product visibility and seamless checkout across AI platforms increasingly important.

The news: Major banks and retailers block AI shopping agents like Meta Muse.

Why it matters: A growing list of US banks and retailers are blocking AI agents like Meta Muse and Instinct from acting on their websites. Amazon and Ebay have both prohibited these models from browsing or purchasing items on their respective marketplaces, while Citigroup, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Charles Schwab have each moved to prevent outside agents from logging into customer accounts and transacting on their behalf.

“We have to make sure we protect our customers in the right way [and] we’re building tools to do that,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week. “In the meantime, we’re not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company, because that’s too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.”

While much of the fashion industry runs its direct-to-consumer sites via platform providers like Shopify — which has opened its network to AI agents unless a brand explicitly opts out — the growing calls from prominent banking officials to introduce legislation point to a bigger unresolved question: when an AI agent makes a purchase that a consumer later disputes, who is responsible for putting it right? For now, experts say much of that burden may still land with the retailer.

The news: OpenAI UK employees received £2.3 million on average in pay and shares in 2025.

Why it matters: OpenAI employees in the UK received an average of £2.3 million in pay and shares last year, according to newly filed UK accounts. The ChatGPT developer distributed £255 million in salary and equity compensation among 110 staff — more than double the previous year’s average package. The figures reflect fierce competition for specialist AI talent, although remuneration varies significantly between employees, with leading researchers commanding the largest pay.

It’s another sign that the AI bubble is far from bursting, with these salaries incentivizing employees for longer and reflecting the budgets of the venture capitalists funding the company. (OpenAI’s most recent funding round reached $122 billion in March 2026, at an $852 billion post-money valuation.)

OpenAI’s UK revenue more than tripled to £293 million in 2025, as London becomes an increasingly key international AI research and commercial hub.

The news: Pinterest launches AI-powered beauty guides.

Why it matters: Pinterest has launched Beauty Guides, an AI-powered feature that analyzes hair and nail Pins to generate personalized salon instructions, at-home tutorials and product recommendations. Available first to US iOS users, Pinterest says the tool aims to close the gap between discovering a beauty look and recreating it.

While competitors like Google Lens already use AI-powered visual search to identify and shop products, Pinterest is extending the concept to practical beauty advice. The move reflects a broader shift from AI-powered discovery to AI-assisted decision-making, while helping Pinterest turn its vast repository of visual inspiration into greater shopping intent and potential commercial opportunities for beauty brands. It also builds on the platform’s recent push into visual search advertising, giving it more ways to connect inspiration with purchases.

The news: OpenAI releases virtual try-on in ChatGPT.

Why it matters: OpenAI is introducing AI-powered virtual try-on and product-saving features to ChatGPT, deepening its push into fashion e-commerce. Users can upload photos of themselves to visualize how clothing and accessories might look on, while a new Favorites feature lets them save products and try-on images for later.

Powered by ChatGPT Images 2.5 (OpenAI’s latest image generator, released in September) the tools will roll out globally across consumer plans, with purchases still completed on merchants’ websites. The launch puts ChatGPT in more direct competition with visual shopping platforms such as Google and Pinterest, as AI assistants evolve from product discovery tools into personalized shopping destinations.

For fashion brands, it raises the prospect of ChatGPT becoming an increasingly influential touchpoint in the customer journey. Luxury brands have been hesitant to adopt virtual try-on on their own channels, largely because the tech hasn’t met their visual standards — but the latest advances in AI are rapidly improving the realism of these digital models.

The news: TikTok launches AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout.

Why it matters: TikTok has launched an AI-powered shopping assistant that provides personalized product guidance, answering questions about sizing, availability and delivery directly within the app. Alongside this, a new one-click checkout feature allows users to purchase directly from brands on their FYP, without leaving TikTok.

Developed in partnership with commerce and payment providers including Shopify, Salesforce and Stripe, the features mark an expansion beyond TikTok Shop’s existing marketplace model, more deeply embedding AI-assisted shopping and direct brand purchases into the social platform. Its aim is to create a more seamless journey from inspiration through discovery, to purchase.

The launch comes against a wider shift towards AI-powered, end-to-end shopping experiences, alongside Meta’s Muse AI agent, Pinterest’s growing shopping investment, and ChatGPT’s new virtual try-on capabilities. For brands, the challenge becomes how to surface in these AI products, where checkout is handled outside their own channels.

The news: Trump orders the US government to stop calling AI “AI”.

Why it matters: President Donald Trump has signed an executive order instructing the US government to replace “artificial intelligence” and “AI” with “super intelligence” and “SI” across all official communications and policy documents, arguing that the new terminology better reflects the tech’s rapidly advancing capabilities and economic potential.
