#6693. Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond

After a whirlwind month of speculation, unsubstantiated rumors, and endless Kalshi prognostication, white smoke has finally emerged from the Amazon MGM chimney. There’s a new James Bond—and his name is Robert Pattinson.

The announcement ends the long-running—and quite frankly, exhausting—mystery over Daniel Craig’s successor and starts a new creative era for the 007 franchise, which Amazon acquired from longtime Bond custodians Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in February 2025, four years after No Time to Die was released. Now, Pattinson will tux up as the seventh cinematic Bond under the stewardship of super-producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal and the vision of GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, marking arguably the biggest role of the 40-year-old London-born actor’s career.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Rumors of Pattinson’s selection caught fire in October, when delays on The Batman Part II gave him a window to audition for Bond at Berkshire’s Bray Studios, alongside peers Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, and an unnamed fourth actor. The chatter heightened a couple weeks later when various British tabloids suggested that Turner, O’Connor, and Lowden were each the preferred choice to satisfy the demands and responsibilities of the beloved British action hero—heightening suspicion that a final decision was looming. According to THR, the finalists were judged “based on stunts, camera presence.” But Pattinson’s last-minute arrival clearly tipped the scale.

“Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007,” said Villeneuve in a statement to THR. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”

It’s both a particularly inspired and obvious choice. Pattinson’s physical traits and characteristics hue close to Ian Fleming’s original Bond—tall and slim, with dark hair. He’s already a bona fide movie star, the current face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise; meanwhile, the selection catches him at the tail end of another booked-and-busy year. Unlike his auditioning peers, the acclaimed actor will enter the franchise well-experienced working in IP and with big-name directors. After co-leading this spring’s The Drama, he chewed up scenes as Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey (the second time working with Nolan after Tenet), made a creepy turn as Chris Hansen in Primetime, and will close 2026 as Scytale in Dune: Part 3—now the first of future Villeneuve collaborations, a relationship that surely helped him acquire his license to kill.

“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” Pascal and Heyman stated jointly to THR. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit, and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

The decision to hire a movie star isn’t a risky choice, but there’s not much precedent within the franchise—especially recently. When he succeeded Pierce Brosnan as Bond in 2005, beating out Clive Owen, Michael Fassbender, and Henry Cavill, Craig boasted an under-the-radar resume. He’d just come off Matthew Vaughn’s crime thriller Layer Cake, but otherwise had played supporting roles in Road to Perdition, The Mother, and Enduring Love. His only big-budget studio experience came several years earlier as Angelina Jolie’s love interest in Tomb Raider.

Naturally, the British press drew its fangs upon his selection, critiquing everything from his general obscurity to his physical features, which stood in stark contrast to previous Bond actors. “The Mane’s Blond, James Blond,” chirped The Irish Times, while The London Daily Mirror played with the same pun: “The Name’s Bland … James Bland.” At his official introduction to the press along the Thames, Craig arrived on a speedboat wearing a life vest, attracting instant mockery—the first of several digs about his less-than-sleek aesthetic and physical abilities. (One tabloid insulted an on-set sunburn and his inability to drive a stick shift car.)

Pattinson, however, has mostly conjured genuine excitement—not in spite of, but because of, his extreme familiarity with moviegoers, dating back to his Young Adult days in the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises. Since then, over the last decade-plus, his eccentric characters and commanding screen presence immediately qualifies him as someone “stirring and exciting and different,” descriptors that Pascal said she prioritized in their methodical search.

Thanks to director Martin Campbell, Casino Royale returned the Bond franchise to earth and established Craig as a grounded, gritty action star in the mold of Jason Bourne. The movie ended up raking in $616 million globally, the highest earning Bond film to date, and launched Craig into four more sequels. Similarly, Pattinson will have the benefit of a highly-respected, Oscar-nominated director in his corner with experience shepherding IP into new places and eliciting compelling performances about tortured male protagonists.

With Villeneuve at the helm of this 26th installment, don’t expect another hard creative pivot; the man behind Prisoners, Blade Runner 2049, and Dune wasn’t hired to bring back the colorful, absurdist, gadget-heavy era that Austin Powers parodied throughout the 90’s. Still, new leadership means a new direction—a clean slate for Pattinson to burnish an already diverse, robust career and prove his chops again at the highest level of scrutiny.

#6692. Nara Smith’s Mom’s Pasta

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

This is my mom’s recipe, and it taught me what simple abundance really looks like. She’d grate tomatoes and spoon the sauce over her native South African pap (a dish made from cornmeal, similar to grits or polenta), rice, ground beef, or almost anything that needed a little love. I couldn’t believe something so good could come from a handful of ingredients, and she showed me that with this dish it’s not about adding more, but how you handle what you have.

The magic is in the grating. It separates the sweet tomato pulp and leaves the skins behind, giving you the pure heart of the fruit. Please don’t skip the beef bouillon—it gives the sauce its deeper savory backbone. I love this tossed with freshly made spaghetti or tagliatelle, though dried pasta works beautifully, too—exactly like my mom makes it. You can enjoy this year-round, but it’s especially delightful in summer, when tomatoes taste like the sun.

#6690. Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Announcement Is Already Brewing Some Watch Drama

Throughout the years-long process of casting the new James Bond, I tried to follow the watches to an answer. When Aaron Taylor-Johnson joined the Omega family in May 2025, it felt like watching the 007 Vatican spit white smoke from its steeple. Just this past weekend, fans were still pinning red strings on their bulletin boards between Jack Lowden and the MI6 superspy when images resurfaced of the Slow Horses star wearing Omega. Since 1995’s Goldeneye, Bond has been an Omega man—a relationship later canonized in one of cinema’s most iconic line readings, when Daniel Craig confirmed his brand of choice in three stretched-out syllables: Oh-Mee-Guh.

If, like me, you were only basing your predictions on what the reported pool of potential Bonds wore on their wrists, Robert Pattinson would have been an easy name to cross off. The newly announced 007 only signed on as an ambassador for the Swiss luxury brand Jaeger-LeCoultre two short months ago! When I interviewed Pattinson about the appointment over the summer, he was effusive about his new partner: “I very rarely even wear watches, but when I tried it on, I was like, ‘That’s my favorite watch.’ I wanted to just buy it.”

Now, in addition to juggling his other iconic role as Batman, Pattinson will presumably need to balance his existing commitment to JLC with his new gig’s long-held ties to Omega. (Reps for both brands did not immediately respond to requests for comment, though JLC conspicuously posted a photo of Pattinson on Instagram a few hours after the announcement.)

During our conversation earlier this summer, Pattinson revealed what he looks for in a watch. He caught the collecting bug in March, when he wore JLC’s Master Control Chronometre Perpetual Calendar to the Oscars afterparties. “All these other actors with their fancy watches on asked me, ‘Hey, what are you wearing?’” Pattinson recalls. “It was one of those moments where I’m like, ‘It’s kind of badass having this thing on.’”

If it’s attention-grabbing badass watches Pattinson is after, he’s in good hands with Omega. The brand is best known for supplying the watches Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin wore when they landed on the moon in 1969. Omega has been happy to create special versions of the Speedmaster for its current partners to dial up its profile. And, of course, the Swiss house continues to expand its Bond-inspired offerings: The maker recently added a “Spectre” version of the Seamaster, 007’s preferred model, to the lineup. And whenever Omega needs to drum up buzz around soon-to-be-released models, they tend to show up on former Bond Craig’s wrists during public appearances.

Speculators trying to pin down the next Bond would have had better luck if they’d read some less recent watch tea leaves. Back in 2020, Christopher Nolan released Tenet, his inscrutable but enthralling time-warp thriller in which Pattinson plays a mysterious, dapper, and charming spy involved in a high-stakes mission to save the world—about as good a preview of what the 40-year-old actor will look like as 007 as you’ll find in his filmography. And the watch on his wrist in that flick? An Omega.

#6687. Taylor Swift Swaps Her Signature Red Lipstick for “Cinnamon Latte Lips”

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The old Taylor can’t come to the phone right now

Over the years, Taylor Swift has changed her hair often, switched up her style, and gone through many eras, but one constant has been her iconic red lip. Swift has worn the notable blue-red color for decades—through multiple tours, relationships, and possibly even at her wedding—but more recently, she’s branched out and ditched her signature red for something a bit juicier.

On Monday, the Recording Academy announced the 2027 Grammy nominations, and Swift made a surprise appearance on the livestream to announce two of the categories, “Album of the Year” and “Song of the Year,” but her appearance wasn’t the only surprise. Instead of her classic red lip, Swift wore “cinnamon latte lips”—a burnt-orange shade that may be our favorite hue for the fall season. One might assume “cinnamon latte lips” would skew more brown, but the way Swift wears it, the color has a bit of orange. The lipstick shade also resembles the one Swift wore when announcing her recent single “Patient Zero” back in September.

Although Swift swapped her red for a warm brown-orange hue for the Grammys announcement, she still wore her classic winged eyeliner and bangs—two other staples of her beauty look. This isn’t the first time she’s shaken up her lip look. More recently, Swift has leaned more neutral, with a petal-pink lip at the sixth annual Academy Museum Gala and the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards. But she’s not completely forgoing her red lip, as it still seems to be a staple look, especially at her husband Travis Kelce’s Kansas City Chiefs games.

Swift hasn’t explicitly shared what lipstick she is wearing in the video. However, her makeup artist, Lorrie Turk, has previously confirmed that she often wears the Nars lipstick in Morocco, a warm, neutral cinnamon shade with an orange undertone, so she may have worn the same shade during the Grammys announcements.

#6686. Rosalind Eleazar Thanks Chris Rock for Making Misty Green ‘Messy’ and ‘Difficult’ in Her ELLE Women in Hollywood Speech

She thanked her co-star and director for “writing a story with a heavy dose of discomfort.”

After delivering standout performances this year in Slow Horses and Misty Green, Rosalind Eleazar was honored at ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood event. During the celebration—which took place at The Four Seasons Beverly Hills on November 16—she used her speech to thank Chris Rock for choosing her to star in Misty Green, and explained that she pulled strength from her mother for the role.

“I want to thank Chris Rock for writing a woman like Misty and writing a story with a heavy dose of discomfort,” she said. “She’s messy. She’s contradictory, she’s difficult, she’s funny, and at times she’s really quite ugly in her behavior. But underneath all of that is someone in tremendous pain. Someone who has become so accustomed to surviving that she’s almost lost touch with herself and become numb.”

Eleazar took a moment to spotlight her mother’s own achievements, and praised her for being self-sufficient, determined, and tenacious. “When I was little, I thought my mother was some sort of superwoman,” she recalled. “She worked in a male-dominated industry. She achieved things that are still beyond my wildest dreams, and somehow managed to raise a child at the same time.”

Such accomplishments led Eleazar to have “a rather naive understanding of what was possible for women.” She explained, “I didn’t really see the barriers, because I had this extraordinary woman in front of me who seemed to walk straight through them.”

She added, “I think what we often perceive as strength can sometimes be a form of armor. A way of protecting something much more vulnerable underneath. And whilst my mum and Misty Green are very different people, I am drawn to characters that are full and have multiple facets, and are human, and are flawed.”

In addition to thanking her mom, Rock, and her fellow nominees, she also thanked Daniel Kaluuya—her Misty Green co-star, who also introduced her for the honor—for offering her a source of support. “He’s been one of my greatest champions and such a wonderful friend. Someone that I can call and have called at any hour of the day with some existential question about this sort of weird journey we’re on,” she concluded her speech. “Daniel, your generosity, your friendship, and your extraordinary talent mean so much to me. And I feel incredibly lucky to have worked alongside you.”

#6685. Cranberry Cream Cheese Spread

Of all the incredible dips we’ve created over the years, our cranberry whipped feta dip is an internet and personal favorite—so much so that I just had to come back with an equally luxurious variation: this cranberry-topped whipped cream cheese spread. With the holiday party season just around the corner, this spread is begging to be included in your party spread. Plus, it's as easy to make as it is delicious—a tangy, sweet cranberry sauce gets finished with brandy, then is spooned atop a lemony whipped cream cheese for a guaranteed winning combo.

Fresh Or Frozen Cranberries? I used both while testing, and they both work interchangeably. I found the fresh cranberries broke down a little more than frozen, so it depends on whether or not you’re looking for more or less texture in your sauce.

What temperature should the cream cheese be? Make sure the cream cheese is chilled and softened but not super cold. It should be somewhat pliable when whipping to avoid lumps; this will ensure the mixture is light and airy. A little heavy cream will loosen the mixture if it's too thick.

The lemon zest: I found that the cream cheese layer needed a little more oomph. If you get a bite of cream cheese on a cracker, it shouldn’t be one-dimensional. Adding a touch of lemon zest makes it more palatable.

Storage:Store the cream cheese spread, with or without cranberry sauce, in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

#6683. David Duchovny on Books, Band and ‘The X-Files’

David Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive. From 1993 to 2002, The X-Files made government conspiracies a staple of primetime television. Duchovny’s FBI special agent Fox Mulder, with his skeptical counterpart, Gillian Anderson’s agent Dana Scully, personified the imminent breakdown of consensus reality in the coming century, delivering the paranoid fringe into 20 million American living rooms. The show belongs to a world of monoculture that no longer exists, and it launched Duchovny into a realm of visibility that’s hard to imagine now, when famous people are produced and consumed at an industrial rate. A few weeks ago, as my boyfriend shopped for a suit jacket at Crowley Vintage in Brooklyn and I edited this story on my phone, I watched a college-age boy put on a long, gray trench coat and announce to his girlfriend: “Mulder mode.”

Duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s. Many viewers interpreted Californication as a kind of autofiction, although Duchovny did not write for the show. The actor has written a number of novels, but it’s apparent to anyone who has spent 30 seconds with him that this soft-spoken, reluctant celebrity has nothing to do with the character Hank Moody. Still, Californication did anticipate something about art, celebrity, and self-commodification: Anybody who writes today must contend with marketing an artistic persona for a public that does not, as a rule, read.

In addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films. He greets the degraded state of American arts with a charming blend of rigor and self-deprecation. “I’m not Jonathan Franzen,” he says of his fiction-writing process. “But if I work on something every day, it deepens. And eventually, hopefully, I can achieve one tenth of what Jonathan Franzen achieves.” But he has an aversion to the sort of publicity that might make his various artistic ventures more lucrative. He tells me he finds it “spiritually impoverishing.”

I meet Duchovny with his band—millennial slackers half his age—at their practice space in Carroll Gardens, where they’re preparing to tour their fourth LP, Prince of Pieces. He wears a white Hanes T-shirt, tight underneath his athletic arms, and he has a tattoo on his ankle—a compass pointing west, something he got when his daughter, West, was hospitalized as an infant. (She’s 27 now, an accomplished actor. “She wanted to be a doctor,” he says. “I was so happy when she told me she was going to pursue acting. Thank God.”)

The albums are composed of subdued, easy-to-listen-to folk-rock tracks, not dissimilar from early Kurt Vile. It’s the band’s first rehearsal in ages, and one of their only chances to prepare in advance of a European tour. In person, they play the songs harder and heavier, sprinkling in crowd-pleasing covers: “Godzilla” by Blue Öyster Cult, “The One I Love” by REM, and—“sadly only one time,” Duchovny says—“Hotline Bling.” The energy in the room is high. These men like one another. Duchovny’s manager offers me a beer from the cooler I’m perched on. I gesture to the tallboy in my purse. He looks disappointed. “You didn’t trust us,” he says. Duchovny steps aside to take a sip of water and picks up the microphone.

“You can sing along,” his keyboardist, Colin Lee, says.

At 66, David Duchovny remains a sex symbol. He’s in better shape than he was on The X-Files. He’s in better shape than the boys in the band. The night after practice, during a Q&A for a screening of his 2023 film Reverse the Curse, he mentions that the wardrobe department had to fashion a “BDSM harness” for him to wear under his clothes to remind him to hunch like an old man. He plays a Red Sox fan who bonds with his estranged son over baseball, marijuana, and their shared lust for a beautiful, young death doula. Duchovny’s character has terminal cancer. “I’m in my dying era,” he tells the crowd. “I die in every film. ”

For the most part, the audience at Westchester County’s Irvington Theater is old enough to have watched The X-Files as it aired. At least two esoteric-looking old men carry David’s poetry collection like a prayer book. There are a handful of young people. A college-aged girl in a KN95 mask raises her hand to ask about Bucky Fucking Dent, the novel adaptation of the Reverse the Curse screenplay, which Duchovny wrote while the movie was in production purgatory. “In the book, Ted and Marty’s last name is Fullilove. In the movie you change it to Fullaker. Why did you do that?”

“Good question,” Duchovny says, stalling. “Full of love. Full of shit. It’s all the same.”

Inevitably, someone asks about the new X-Files. Ryan Coogler is rebooting the show for Hulu. Duchovny will later suggest to me that Chris Carter, the show’s original writer, has designs on a reboot of his own—“He has plans, and wants to end with the original show.” As for Coogler’s version, he says, “I know he said he wants me to come do something, but we haven’t figured out what yet.” During the audience Q&A, Duchovny seems to have misheard the question, and spoils the ending for The Exiles, his forthcoming Taiwanese crime film: “I die in that one too.”

Duchovny’s latest book, About Time, a collection of poems published last year by Akashic, is also largely about dying: the death of his father, the death of his first marriage, the ambient death that hung in the air at the beginning of the decade. He started writing the poems when his therapist encouraged him to talk to dead people. “He was talking about Rudolph Steiner’s belief that you can talk to the dead. And he said: You can talk to your father and you should. My dad and I didn’t connect like we might have,” Duchovny says. “When you’re younger, you think you have all the time in the world to get the relationship you want. But the relationship doesn’t end.” In conversation, he is cerebral without being annoying. “There’s a power struggle when you read a really good novel,” he says. “Somebody’s mind is taking over your mind. I think about language a lot and how we take it for granted as being an accurate signifier. When I was younger I thought communication was possible. I’m not so sure now. But it’s fun to try.”

Duchovny’s humility complicates the sexual charisma that still lives at the center of his public persona. His introduction to About Time begins, “I know what you’re thinking: Just what the world needs now—a bunch of poems from an actor.” There’s a sense that he wants to get ahead of the reader’s skepticism. But there’s also plenty of perceptive lines in the poems themselves: “You dreamt you wrote something so good, / so ambivalent and destructive, so creative, / so lacking in morals, decency, or instruction, / so sad and so funny, / so useless and old, / so familiar and new, / so full of theft and power / that they had to name a god after it.” I ask him if good writing is necessarily amoral. He says, “Probably. Which is why any politically correct work of art is usually super successful and really bad. Usually artists are difficult people, and I have no problem separating the art from the artist. But people do now.”

In college, Duchovny wanted to be a poet. “I thought it was an actual occupation you could have,” he says. When an underclassman turned up in his workshop who was better than him, he quit writing poems on the spot. “It was actually Walter Kirn,” he says. “He showed up at 16-years-old. He was a genius. I was like okay—I’m not a poet.”

The two men have become close in the last decade. Kirn, who wrote Up in the Air and founded the newspaper County Highway, tells me what Duchovny was like at Princeton: “He was golden. He had an aura. I was a little starstruck by him.” Duchovny has agreed to play a character inspired by paranormal radio host Art Bell in American Nights, a film that Kirn is developing alongside director Alex Lee Moyer. Bell’s Coast to Coast, a cult AM show during the ’80s and ’90s, was beloved by long-haul truckers and compound preppers alike, who called in to report UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, and crop circles. “I, like the rest of my generation, grew up on The X-Files,” Moyer tells me. “It made a massive impression on me, and I’ve been a fan of David ever since. The synchronicity of him being a part of this is not lost on me.”

I ask Duchovny if he always needed to be the best. “I at least needed to be the best in my class,” he says.

In LA, I meet Duchovny in a quiet restaurant to talk about his books. He describes his first novel as “an act of cowardice.” Holy Cow is narrated by an anthropomorphized barnyard animal who uncovers the conspiracy theory that is factory farming. “I thought: Well, they’re not gonna cut me off at the knees on this. Because I’m clearly not that serious. It was calculated. I didn’t want to try for the great American novel the first time as an actor.” The books that followed are more ambitious, each one better than the last. By the time he was promoting his fourth book, 2021’s Truly Like Lightning, he made his ambition plain. “I want to be taken seriously,” he said on Marc Maron’s podcast. “That’s my weakness. I want that book to be taken seriously.”

“You don’t want people to be like the guy from The X-Files wrote a book,” Maron said.

“That’s what they’re gonna say,” Duchovny said, “but I hope and I believe that eventually people will see that I mean business.”

Truly Like Lightning centers on a Mormon polygamist family forced to enter the godless world of Los Angeles when their homestead is upended. “When I started to read about Mormonism, it struck me as super optimistic. Everyone’s gonna get their own planet and everyone’s gonna be able to propagate souls. As opposed to a European perspective, which was always about the end of something, being 2,000 years removed from this thing. The Mormons said no, this is still happening.” The novel takes cues from the literary critic Harold Bloom, who wrote that Mormonism was an “American original” and called its founder a “religious genius.” Duchovny studied under Bloom at Yale, where he earned some of an English PhD. “Everything goes back to Bloom,” he says. “And you never really leave grad school. I’m not sure I’ve left grad school. They might still be waiting for my dissertation.”

But Duchovny did leave grad school. He signed with a talent agent one summer to try to earn some money acting in commercials. His agent told him that if he wanted to go out for theater or film roles, he’d have to get into an acting class. “I said: I’m not doing anything. When I stepped into acting class, something happened. I wasn’t a demonstrative person—I was an intellectual person. So it was like: Yeah, be unreasonable. Be irrational. It opened up a different world, a world of fiction, a world without consequences. I’m doing a scene, and I’m yelling at this person and I’m going to murder them, but I don’t have to go to jail.”

For someone with half a dozen good books and an enormous public profile, it’s surprising there haven’t been more reviews. Johnny Temple, who published Duchovny’s two most recent books on Akashic, tells me, “It’s certainly frustrating that there hasn't been more review coverage of David’s books. For any well-known actor, musician, or other type of public figure, there’s always going to be obstacles to being taken seriously in a different medium.” Kirn tells me, “That makes writing fiction a much purer achievement in my mind. You’re doing this because you love it, and you know that two thirds of your fans will only remember you as a TV character. It’s a brilliant, Sisyphean task. Also, he’s a superb writer.”

I ask Duchovny whether he still thinks about being the best. “I think now I can acknowledge that it’s a hollow designation,” he says. “Especially in the arts. Even though we give awards, which is silly. Holy Cow made the Times bestseller list. Ever since, everything I write sells less and less.”

“It’s hard for someone to champion it,” he adds. “If I wrote a memoir, I’m sure it would get reviewed in the Times.”

Talking to Duchovny, one is reminded that wanting to be taken seriously and being in on the joke aren’t mutually exclusive. As band practice winds down in Brooklyn, the guys are excited to cover Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day.” Duchovny crosses his arms in front of his lap like a schoolboy as he sings. To my ear it sounds just fine, but Lee, the keyboardist, asks the mixer to lower the reverb on David’s voice.

“Maybe lower David’s mic in general?” the bassist, Mitchell Stewart asks.

“Lower than zero,” Duchovny says. “Less than zero.”

A few days later, he texts me. He just screened an early cut of Soapbox, a Hollywood satire he wrote and stars in opposite Laverne Cox. At first, he’s bummed that the test audience has decided that his character shouldn’t get killed in the final moments of the movie. But a couple hours later, he writes me again: “People don’t want me to die. I guess I should be flattered.”

#6682. Netflix’s ‘The Body’ Is The Most Fun Teen Drama We’ve Had In Years

The following article contains minor spoilers for The Body.

It’s been a big few years for the teen drama, from Off Campus and Sterling Point to The Summer I Turned Pretty and Heartstopper. Nothing ever truly bad happens, but emotionally there’s always something at stake.

Quinn Shephard’s The Body, which came out on Netflix this month, is also a teen drama—but don’t confuse the latter with other iterations of the genre. The Body is winking, sapphic, and totally deranged. It has more in common with Mean Girls and Cruel Intentions, by way of Carrie and The Crucible, than the gentle high school stories of late. (Already there’s a Christian petition to cancel it that has gathered 90,000 signatures, so you know it’s good.)

Our story begins on Halloween in 2004, at a Catholic high school in a small town (we’re not told where, though filming took place around Ontario, Canada). Everyone’s in Juicy Couture, lips glossed to the nines, Chloé Paddingtons and Balenciaga Le City bags slung over their shoulders (never mind that the former was released in 2005; you’ll discover that The Body plays fast and loose with historical accuracy). In the opening episode, the school’s dance troupe, the Lions, throws a big party at an abandoned convent and everyone’s invited: even the weird outcast, Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros). But when they all take ecstasy and engage in a Satanic initiation ritual—leaving one of the dancers, Grace (Sofia Wylie) unconscious—the balance of the group is thrown into disarray.

What happens next is part mass psychogenic hysteria (when some of the girls’ hands start shaking, followed by seizures and visions, it brings to mind the 2011 story out of LeRoy, New York, in which 20 girls at a high school developed “conversion disorder”), part possible supernatural occurrence; we’re left hanging in the balance. What’s more interesting, though, is the idea of repression and religious guilt, compounded by the attitudes of the era (everything lame is described as “gay,” so extra points for accuracy there). Sapphic thoughts and feelings bubble beneath the surface, threatening to spill over. Burgeoning sexuality fizzes throughout these high schoolers’ lives. The series is an excellent portrait of girlhood; more times than once I was transported back to being 15 or 16 and acting like a girl possessed.

Yet while plenty of the themes are gritty (religious trauma, crystal meth addiction, internalized homophobia), this isn’t a serious show. The humor is dark and a little twisted (at one point, the girls are all screaming their confessions, which range from “I’m not a natural blond” to “my brother killed seven people in Afghanistan”). The fashion is a sort of Gen Z-ified version of millennial style (all J’adore Dior tank tops and bejewelled XXL shades, rather than, like, greasy side-bangs and knit hats with flames on them). The latter is fun rather than annoying or erroneous; much like in Mean Girls and Cruel Intentions, we’re given a slick and sexy version of high school. In many ways, that’s the most 2004 thing of all.

Of course, the eight-episode series is not completely flawless. There are moments when the pace sags a little, and a few plot points arise that are either hard to make sense of, or that disappear into the ether. Even so, in this era of mild-mannered and overly earnest YA shows, The Body stands out as deliciously knowing and mischievous—even a little off-color. (In the opening minutes, as the teen girls stretch each other in the grass, the brilliantly wry Elise, played by Sara Boustany, comments, “Holy fuck, you guys look like a bunch of dykes.” Again, historically accurate.) In fact, I haven’t had this much fun watching a teen drama since the first season of Yellowjackets, or early episodes of Riverdale.

As is often the case with Netflix, the ending leaves room for a second season, without there being any indication as of yet that there will be one. Reddit threads are already alight with fans stressing out over whether they’ll axe the show (my instinct is that a second season is a no-brainer, though that doesn’t really mean anything). Regardless, it’s been a truly addictive first outing. And the streamer would be possessed—nay, demonic—not to green-light another.

#6679. Mashed Potatoes

No holiday table—or really any dinner table, for that matter—is truly complete without a substantial side of creamy, buttery mashed potatoes. While it may seem like simple, classic comfort food, there are a few ways to take mashed potatoes from good to great. That's why we retested this recipe again and again until we achieved potato perfection.

What People Are Saying:"So good! I don’t typically like sour cream on its own but it was a huge improvement for basic mashed potatoes. Will definitely be making this again." – PurpleStrawberry

"Easily my go-to mashed potato recipe. I've made it for Thanksgiving, and got requests to make it again. It's so good, doesn't even need gravy." – kitkat123

Really, the only chopping you'll have to do is cut up the potatoes. I do suggest peeling them (more on that later), and be sure to try to cut the potatoes into equal-sized pieces so they cook evenly. Around 1" chunks are ideal. Time to cook 'em! In testing, I found that covering the potatoes with cold water first yields the best consistency and ensures the potatoes don't become too mushy. Don't forget to add a pinch of salt to the water! Let the potatoes cook until softened—the best way to test is to use a paring knife and make sure it can be inserted with no resistance. This should take about 20 minutes. Make sure to drain when they're done so they don't overcook.

Now comes the fun part: Mashing the potatoes until smooth. You can use a masher, a ricer, or even a handheld mixer for this step. I think the smoother, the better, but you do you, of course.

On to what makes these potatoes the best ever: Heat up some whole milk and butter until the butter is melted in a pot.

Then, pour over the still-warm potatoes and mix to combine. Then add the sour cream, some salt, and pepper, and you're basically good to go! Mix everything well, transfer to your prettiest serving bowl, and proceed with the finishing touches: a couple of pieces of butter to melt into the potatoes, plus fresh parsley for some color and brightness. Brace yourself for the compliments.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

#6678. Robert Pattinson Might Be the Most Fashion-Forward Bond Yet

From Sean Connery’s immaculately tailored suits in Dr. No to Daniel Craig’s thigh-bearing trunks in Casino Royale, each man who has played James Bond has brought a new aesthetic sensibility to the role. For Connery, this meant soft-shouldered Savile Row tailoring, polo shirts, and knit ties to suit the era of Ivy Style, while Roger Moore’s wardrobe of safari jackets and nylon ski suits embodied the sporty hedonism of the 1970s. In the 21st century, Daniel Craig’s Bond was built around a timely blend of Brioni, Tom Ford, and stalwart British brands that complemented the contemporary #menswear scene. Today’s news that Robert Pattinson—a longtime Dior ambassador and one of the most consistently thrilling dressers in Hollywood—has been cast as 007 suggests Bond’s most fashionable era may be yet to come.

Daniel Craig is no slouch in the clothing department, but before donning the tux for Casino Royale, he was primarily known as a stage actor with a penchant for distressed jeans and Chuck Taylor high-tops. Pattinson, meanwhile, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for a decade, during which he’s established his impeccable taste and a willingness to take big swings with his outfits—not to mention a reputation for wearing the absolute heck out of a gray suit. Now, with fellow Brit Jonathan Anderson (who cast Craig in Loewe’s quirked-up fall 2024 campaign and posted this heartwarming pic today) running the show at Dior, the stage is set for a Bond with a taste for capital-F fashion.

Tradition dictates a vibe shift whenever a new Bond is chosen, but whatever James Bond wears has an outsized impact on menswear. Pierce Brosnan’s era had structured Brioni suits and made the Omega Seamaster a star, while Daniel Craig helped cement Tom Ford’s tailoring as a red-carpet staple and juiced sales of N.Peal ribbed Army sweaters and Drake’s suede chukkas. As GQ’s Cam Wolf noted in a 2018 article about Skyfall, Daniel Craig’s Barbour jacket, sweater, jeans, and brogue boots from that film—a classic but fairly unremarkable outfit—became the aspirational template for untold numbers of men on r/malefashionadvice. A few years later, when Craig wore a Rag & Bone slim-fit henley in No Time to Die, the brand sold out of the unassuming undershirt in a matter of days.

It’s been five years since No Time to Die’s release, and it will likely be at least a couple more before Pattinson’s first outing as 007 hits screens. That’s a long wait to see how the next Bond era aesthetic comes together, but given Pattinson’s distinctive approach to fashion, it should be well worth it for the clothes alone.

#6677. LuxExperience Reports 8.5% Sales Growth Amid Turnaround

LuxExperience — owner of Mytheresa, Net-a-Porter, Mr Porter, and Yoox — grew net sales 8.5% on a constant currency basis in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, generating €604.7 million. This marked the fourth consecutive quarter of growth since the group formed in April 2025 following Mytheresa’s acquisition of Yoox Net-a-Porter (YNAP) Group.

“[It was a] super quarter considering that it’s still a mixed picture out there for luxury,” group CEO Michael Kliger tells Vogue Business. “It shows there is demand in multi-brand and digital.

The group’s adjusted EBITDA improved year-on-year, climbing 590 basis points to 2.1%, up from -3.9%. LuxExperience also honed its outlook for fiscal 2027 to 6-9% growth, up from a mid-single-digit to high-single-digit range. The company increased its adjusted EBITDA margin to 2.5-3.5%, up from 2-3%.

Kliger described the quarter as the group’s strongest so far since the LuxExperience inception. “We are ahead of plan with these numbers. That’s why we upped the guidance,” he says.

By brand, Mytheresa’s sales grew 10%, generating €250.8 million, bolstered by a 9% climb in the US. Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter together grew 7.2%, generating €231 million, attributing this to a 24.3% jump in the US. Carried by strong performance in Europe (excluding the UK), Yoox — the group’s off-price retailer — also grew 8.2%, reporting €128.6 million in net sales.

Despite the group’s online foundation, each business invested in IRL events during the quarter. Mytheresa delivered 18 premium customer activations across Europe, the US, and Asia, continuing its one-of-a-kind VIC clienteling strategy. Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter also executed seven and 10 “extremely important person” (EIP) experiences, respectively, across the US and Europe. Yoox continued its focus in Europe, unveiling 14 community events in the region.

“This customer on the luxury side [Mytheresa and the Porter brands] is resilient,” says Kliger. “On the Yoox side, we see that in the lower and middle class, people prefer good offers, having not so much discretionary spend and still loving luxury. Whereas on the Mytheresa and the Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter side, we really speak to those that have the means to buy the latest [product] as soon as it hits the market.”

Mytheresa increased its adjusted EBITDA by 128.1%, while Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter upped theirs to 0.3%, marking the second quarter of profitability post-acquisition. Yoox remained unprofitable; however, it reduced its quarterly loss from €-19.1 million to €-6 million, taking adjusted EBITDA margin from -16.1% to -4.6%

Kliger says that Mytheresa is leveling out its marketing investment, shifting focus from digital to premium physical events, citing the two-week yacht voyage across Monte Carlo and St. Tropez, as well as upcoming pop-ups in the French Alps and Florida.

Both Net-a-Porter and Mytheresa will keep their focus on top spenders, Kliger affirms. What distinguishes Mytheresa and the Porter brands? “Mytheresa is very focused on the womenswear side,” Kliger says, noting that it only offers around 220 brands. “Net-a-Porter [offering around 500 brands] is broader and is for the customer that looks for editorial advice and brand discovery.”

For Net-a-Porter and Mr. Porter, the company is investing more in marketing and ramping up the editorial output and video production. “So we invest more to really inject energy into these brands,” Kliger adds.

Between Net-a-Porter and Mytheresa, customer overlap remained at 12%. (The figure has not changed in the last 18 months.) “The brands themselves have really carved out different personalities,” says Kliger. “If anything, we want that to become even sharper. The growth both businesses show does not come at the expense of one of the other. They’re growing into the market.”

Kliger attributes LuxExperience’s continued growth to a handful of core factors. First, the company is digital, and the digital market is expanding. Second, the group is positioned on both sides of the market, offering high-end and off-price. Lastly, the business isn’t heavily exposed to the luxury slowdown in China. “Our China business — we have good representation in APAC — but it was never oversized, and therefore we don’t suffer overly from the sluggish demand.”

Looking ahead, Kliger doesn’t foresee any major obstacles to the continued growth and predicted return to profit for Yoox, which he expects to realize between the last quarter of fiscal 2027 and the first quarter of 2028.

#6676. I Tried The Great British Bake Off’s Most Controversial Recipe—Here’s How It Went

The “technical challenge,” a blind-baking test where contestants receive the same recipe and ingredients, often with minimal or deliberately sparse instructions, is a staple of The Great British Bake Off. And contestants have seriously struggled with it over the years. But according to Paul Hollywood, this season’s challenge featuring blue cheese and roasted grape flatbreads was the worst yet. After 60 minutes of kneading, grape-roasting, and undercooking, the bakers produced trays of thick, raw flatbreads that Paul and Nigella could barely eat.

After bakers argued that an hour wasn’t enough, Paul said, “There’s plenty of time.” But fans, critics, and former bakers alike have been plenty vocal about their feelings. The popular opinion? The bakers were set up to fail—and also that the flavors seemed a little weird.

With all the controversy, I was curious to see if the challenge was even possible—so I tried it myself. While I purposefully did NOT watch the episode before my attempt, I did print the full recipe from the GBBO website. This recipe was definitely WAY more helpful than the one the bakers were given, and I followed it to the letter.

Here’s how it went: the good, the bad, and the very ugly.

The beginning? Very smooth. I put the grapes in the oven (the online recipe told me to roast them as a whole bunch rather than cutting them up) and made the bread dough, kneading it for the five minutes specified before letting it rest.

As soon as I set the dough aside to rest, I discovered how absolutely torturous technical downtime is. I was at an absolute loss. I had nothing to do…except read the recipe over and over again and make sure I knew what 8 cm and 23 cm looked like.

Interestingly enough, the bakers on the show didn’t have this downtime; they were busy cutting and roasting their grapes by then. That said, I don’t think that order was necessarily better; with the time spent slicing the grapes, they wouldn’t have had much time at ALL to roast—and not nearly enough to cool.

The grapes came out of the oven. They weren’t very roasted—as one of the bakers said, they just looked like “raw grapes”—but the recipe said 20 minutes and gave no indicators for how roasted they should be (and also I knew they needed to cool before stuffing), so I just went with it.

I dumped out the dough (a rude awakening after its 15-minute rest) and chopped it into eight pieces. Immediately, I realized I should have weighed the larger ball and divided it by eight so I could make sure all the pieces were equal, but I didn’t have much time to fuss, so I tried to make them roughly the same weight and moved on.

The recipe said to roll out each portion of dough into an 8 cm circle, fill it with five roasted grapes and one-eighth of the blue cheese, lift the edges of the circle up to pinch them together, then turn the little ball seam side down and roll the whole thing out into a 23 cm circle.

To begin, I cut my dough into wedges from the larger ball, and it was hard to roll them out into a circle to fill. But that was nothing compared to the problems I had rolling out the filled dough. First, the dough wasn’t rested enough, so it kept springing back at me as I tried to roll it out. But the bigger issue was the grapes. Since they were still pretty juicy, they started bursting as I rolled out the flatbread, flying to the edges and tearing holes in the dough as they oozed out.

After over 15 minutes of stuffing and rolling, my workstation was littered with burst grape guts. None of my flatbreads were 23 cm wide (I think the widest they got was 18?) and I still had three to roll out, but I also knew I needed to start cooking or I was going to have eight totally raw flatbreads at the end of time.

Cooking the flatbreads wasn’t a total disaster—I guess—but grape juice oozed out of the holes where they burst and left black patches of burnt sugar on the pan, which I had absolutely no time to clean out since I was still racing the clock. Fortunately, the flatbreads didn’t seem to need the full 90 seconds per side. In fact, they seemed to need constant attention to prevent them from burning, which was bad news since I was still trying to roll out the remaining three flatbreads on the side.

Time was up, and I had five cooked (burst) stuffed flatbreads on my sheet tray, three totally raw ones on the countertop, and a smoking pan. I now know how the bakers feel at the end of such challenges: slightly insane and utterly defeated.

Looking back on the challenge, I can honestly say that it was difficult and somewhat impossible. Ultimately, I couldn’t get all the flatbreads cooked in time, even though I was rolling them out much thinner than the bakers were. But while timing was definitely a problem, the bigger issue was the impossible stupidity of stuffing juicy grapes inside a flatbread and then trying to roll it out without the grapes bursting out and ruining the dough.

Since I managed to cook five flatbreads, I could (unlike Paul and Nigella) taste the finished result—but honestly, I wasn’t a fan. The blue cheese was WAY too strong, and the grapes felt like random pockets of juice in an otherwise savory flatbread. Overall, I wouldn’t recommend trying this challenge yourself—unless you want to be scrubbing the burnt bits of grape sugar off your pan for the next week.

#6673. Is Jeremy Allen White Playing Wolverine? His Mutton Chops Say Yes

Marvel has filled most of the seats for its new X-Men film. Sadie Sink is Jean Grey, Kit Connor is Cyclops, Christopher Abbott is Professor X, Samara Weaving is Emma Frost, Inde Navarrette is Rogue, and Maya Boyd is Storm. But there’s still one grizzly gap in the line-up: Wolverine.

Earlier this month, Jeremy Allen White was linked with the role after insider Jeff Sneider reported that he had met with Marvel about a small part that could become much bigger later on. Nobody has confirmed that the part is Wolverine (and Sneider has since stressed that White isn’t officially in talks) but the internet did the math pretty quickly. And now there’s a smoking gun: facial hair.

While walking around the Studio City Farmers Market over the weekend (because, of course), The Social Reckoning star was spotted carrying a bouquet of flowers bigger than his torso and wearing some extremely Wolverine-y mutton chops. Normally, growing out your sideburns wouldn’t count as casting news. But when you’ve just been linked with Logan and suddenly look ready to join the X-Men, people are going to ask questions.

White would make a lot of sense. He’s 5’7”, which puts him much closer to the comic book Wolverine’s famously stocky 5’3” frame than Hugh Jackman ever was. He also spent months getting absolutely massive for The Iron Claw, so the muscle is already there. And after years of watching him play Carmy in The Bear, we know he can do angry and exhausted and permanently one minor inconvenience away from losing it. That’s basically three quarters of the Wolverine job description.

Jackman has owned the role since the first X-Men film landed in 2000. He’s played Wolverine across 10 movies, most recently returning for 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine. His version became so definitive that it’s difficult to picture anyone else with the claws (other than the time Troye Sivan briefly had them in 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine), even though the 6’2" actor looked very different from the shorter character drawn in the OG comics.

Maybe White just fancied some giant sideburns. Maybe the flowers are covering three adamantium claws. Either way, Marvel should probably give him a call—assuming it hasn’t already.

#6671. Classic Stuffing

While traditional stuffing is technically supposed to be stuffed inside the turkey to cook, that isn’t actually the ideal or even recommended way to cook your Thanksgiving turkey (or stuffing). I've found that you’ll achieve much better results by cooking them separately. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath. It's my perfect version of the holiday side—I tested it again and again, so it was worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

What People Are Saying:"[It's] an excellent recipe you can tweak it for taste. I like to up the onion by half again and use a lot more fresh sage." - GreenClover

"Using a [mandoline] made the final preparation fast and easy. It was a big hit over a lovely meal. The dressing brought high praise from two trained chefs." - RedFish

As I mentioned above, sourdough bread is my go-to for stuffing. The first step is to bake it! You'll need 2 sheets, or do this in batches. You want to dry it out, so bake for 15 to 20 minutes.

While that's toasting, it's time to cook the aromatics. Melt some butter, then cook the onions, leeks, and garlic until your kitchen smells amazing and everything is softened.

Time for the liquids: Simply whisk eggs, broth, milk, and some fresh herbs in a large measuring cup. You can use a touch of red pepper for a hint of spice, which I highly recommend, but if you have a spice-averse crowd, you can skip it.

When the bread is done toasting, turn the oven temp up to 375°. Prepare a 13" x 9" baking dish by coating it with a thin layer of butter.

Time to combine it all together: In a large bowl, mix the bread, aromatics, and liquid ingredients and toss until combined. You can let this sit at room temperature for up to 1 hour if you're planning ahead. Dot with even more butter, then bake until crispy. You can serve this stuffing warm or at room temperature.

#6668. 40 More Million-Dollar Watches Just Sold at Auction

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

Back in June, I reported on the bonanza of watches crossing the million-dollar-plus mark at auction. What once felt like a unicorn price for watchmakers, auction houses, and the industry as a whole no longer feels so magical. “I joke with people that $1 million is like the new $250,000 of five years ago,” Paul Boutros of Phillips auction house said over the summer.

In just the first half of 2026, the number of million-dollar watches sold nearly eclipsed the total from all of 2025. Now, after a raft of high-profile auctions in Geneva a couple of weeks ago, the industry has set yet another record. In just the last month alone (including Monaco Legend Group, which kicked things off in late October), 40 million-dollar watches hammered, according to numbers provided by EveryWatch. That’s more sold than in any entire year before 2020.

If you’re keeping score at home, we’ve seen 133 watches sell at or above seven figures this year. And we’ve still got plenty of year left.

The question is: How much steam does the auction world have left? And what’s driving this radical spike in big-ticket timepieces?

A $10 million Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar Chronograph ref. 2499

Mike Nouveau, WatchTok King and dealer, has told me that if more kids knew how much growth potential there is in the vintage market, they’d put down the creator-style tiny microphones and start studying reference numbers. The vintage market spiked in the middle of the pandemic, when prices on sport watch grails like the Patek Philippe Nautilus and Rolex Daytona went crypto-mode as a new wave of speculators flooded the high-end collecting scene.

But while the steel sport watch craze has cooled—or at least leveled off—the market has continued riding a remarkably durable wave, helped in part by the arrival of a previously quiet category: the insiders-only independent brands. “For many years at auction, we always said, ‘You have Patek Philippe and Rolex. What’s the third brand that can compete?’” Alexandre Ghotbi, a deputy chairman at Phillips auction house, told me in 2024 for a story on the beloved watchmaker Rexhep Rexhepi. “Today’s third brand is not a brand—it’s a genre: independent artisanal watchmakers.”

Think F.P. Journe, Berneron, Phillipe Dufour, Rexhepi’s Atelier Akrivia—companies helmed by watchmaking auteurs turning out hyper-limited runs, most of which sell out long before a perfectly-lit product photo ever hits the web. Oftentimes, the only way to get your hands on one of their wares—if you haven’t yet achieved friend-of-the-brand status—is by raising a paddle at auction.

When I asked dealer Eric Wind if he thought the indie insanity would remain strong, he was unequivocal: “At the top end, yes.” The dealer Zoe Abelson, of Graal Watches, actually believes we haven’t reached the peak yet. “I do think there's still room for the pieces that are actually rare to continue to grow in value with a continuance in new interest in collecting watches and the yearning to build the most impressive collection,” she said.

Two weekends ago, a new independent brand joined the list of million-dollar watchmakers. Sylvain Pinaud cut his teeth restoring antique watches and established his eponymous brand in 2018. He’s known for showing his work—the instrumental components of his watches are often highlighted on the dial. A unique version of his Origine, a model that only launched in 2022, sold for 1,011,200 Swiss francs (roughly $1,211,500).

Pinaud’s success is indicative of what happens to the elite independent brands that hit the big time. Compared to many of the heavyweight Swiss makers working at scale, independent watchmakers are seen as artisans who hand-produce their designs in extremely limited quantities. It’s why a watchmaker like Kari Voutilainen, considered a master of his craft, has sold more million-dollar pieces this year than many of the big fellas getting rap lyric shoutouts. “There's a growing appreciation for what these watchmakers are producing,” said Ben Horesh, EveryWatch’s CEO. “It’s great to see more independents challenging the old guard."

Look at that list above. Voutilainen ranks just after Rolex and Patek Philippe but ahead of Cartier for the most million-dollar watches sold at auction in 2026. The list is heavy on independents, including Rexhepi’s Akrivia, George Daniels, Philippe Dufour, and Vianney Halter. The real headline, though, is seeing F.P. Journe—the godfather of the indie scene—at the very top. If one area of the market doesn’t feel entirely sustainable, it’s the inferno around FPJ’s pieces. For deep-pocketed newcomers to the “hobby” of catching big-ticket whales, the Geneva-based maker has come to represent the grailiest of grails. Nearly every Journe piece that comes to auction sells for multiples of its estimate. And I mean everything: an empty watch box made for a set of FPJs sold for $230,000 at Christie’s! “The less rare—or in Journe's case, current production—pieces that get swept up in the overall market growth will slow down soon,” Abelson said. “I don't think it's sustainable; at a certain point the values will price out enough people that there should be a correction.”

A $13 million F.P. Journe Chronomètre à Résonance "Régence”

If six-figure watches were once rare, 10-million-plus pieces were true spectacles. Between 2020 and 2023, not a single watch crossed that threshold. In the last decade, from 2015 to 2025, there were just seven 10-million watches total. But with some time still on the clock, seven watches have already topped that threshold in 2026. A solid chunk of that is thanks to the wild one-of-one Daytonas that Rolex made for a charity auction—three out of the four sold for seven figures—but it’s still an astounding feat. The rest of the list is filled out by:

These days, it’s hard to find a category of watches that isn’t doing well at auction. Cartier hasn’t fallen off—in fact, the brand keeps setting records: a very cool clock known as Portico No. 4 hammered for approximately $5,768,400 at Phillips the weekend before last, becoming the most expensive Cartier ever sold in the process. Breguet is, rightfully and finally, on the rise. And after relaunching just last summer, Urban Jürgensen’s vintage pieces are hotter than ever. A super sexy pink-gold version of the brand’s Reference 2 went for 358,400 Swiss francs (about $430,000) at Sotheby’s.

To put a fine point on all this, just look at how overall sales are soaring. Last year, Phillips set the record with $83,018,538 worth of timepieces sold in a single auction. It only took 12 months to shatter that number. This month saw Phillips reset the record with a $112.3 million auction. I would say 2026 is an inflection point for the industry…if I didn’t anticipate that we’ll be back here talking about even more record-setting sales every year for the foreseeable future.

#6666. Green Bean Casserole

Green bean casserole belongs on every Thanksgiving spread. If you're scrambling to figure out how to perfect the classic side dish, look no further. I ditched the cream of mushroom soup for a homemade cream sauce and fresh sautéed mushrooms, but don’t worry—this dish is still super-simple to make. You only need 8 ingredients and a little over an hour to make it. Keep reading on for my top tips to make this classic side dish the best it can be:

What People Are Saying:"Once you have this, you'll never be able to go back to the Campbell's gray sodium laden sludge & soggy canned green beans recipe! This is amazing! Your whole family will change their minds about green bean casserole." - CyanCarrot

"This is the best green bean casserole I've ever made! It was easy enough that I could read it through twice, and then just make the dish without having to refer to the text of the recipe! It turned out great, my family ate it up! Without using a can of condensed soup, I could control the amount of salt...this made from scratch sauce tastes more mushroomy than a can of condensed soup!" - GreenBike

The very first step is blanching the green beans. This may seem a little fussy, but it's the best way to start cooking the beans to preserve their crispy texture and bright green color as they continue to bake in the oven. It's easy, but just requires a little setup. Cook the beans in salted water for a few minutes, then immediately transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking process. That's it!

On to the aromatics! This is what takes this casserole truly over the top. Cook sliced onions in butter until just starting to soften, anywhere from 7 to 10 minutes.

Add the mushrooms and let everyone get to know each other. Make it even better by adding some garlic; in my opinion, the more, the merrier. Your kitchen will smell amazing. Pour the aromatics into the bowl with the blanched beans.

Time for the sauce. No need to wipe out the pot, just melt a stick of butter, then toast the flour.

Slowly pour in the milk and whisk, letting the sauce come to a simmer, until nicely thickened. Be sure to taste for salt and pepper.

Add to bowl with beans, stir to combine, then transfer to a 13" x 9" baking dish. Spread in the dish, then bake until everything is bubbly, which should take just 30 minutes.

Time for the fried onions! Return to the oven and bake until the onions are just warmed through, about 5 minutes more.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Save some time (and oven space) on the busy holiday by making this Thanksgiving side ahead of time. Simply assemble the casserole (without the fried onions), cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for up to 4 days or until you're ready to bake!

Some tips: Make sure to let it cool to room temperature before baking, or add a couple of minutes to your timer to adjust to the colder temperature. Whatever you do, DON'T forget to add the fried onions until after the first round of baking. If they're added before refrigerating, they'll get soggy instead of having that signature crispy crunch.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container (or cover your casserole dish with storage wrap) before refrigerating. This side will last up to 4 days refrigerated (look through our Thanksgiving leftovers ideas for some creative inspo for what to do with them), and leftovers can be reheated in the microwave or oven.

#6665. Best Harrington Jackets 2026: Preppy, Punk, and Ultra-Functional

Few jackets have managed to cross as many style tribes—and decades—as the Harrington. In fact, if you were to enroll in Classic Menswear 101, the Harrington jacket would be a prerequisite. The transitional season staple—a favorite of Elvis, James Dean, Steve McQueen, and every member of The Clash—is constantly found across lookbooks and style Instagram accounts, because it does so many things so well.

For one, it's incredibly practical: Water-resistant, pocket-forward, lightly insulating, and ever-adaptable to the day's conditions thanks to its full-zip and collar. But the almost-cropped length—and popped collar, if you so dare—is also a style swerve that makes every wearer feel one dose cooler than they did before. No wonder it’s been embraced over the decades by everyone from golfers to preppies to A-Listers and punks.

The original Harrington—a Baracuta G9—is still available almost a century on from its release, and still excellent. But if you’re looking to broaden your horizons, today’s Harrington jackets aren’t resting on their laurels. Below, the standout versions worth adding to your rotation before we’re into parka territory.

The classic Baracuta G9 golf jacket is as British as beans on toast. This is the original tartan-lined, ribbed-cuff Harrington, the jacket you picture when you think of Steve McQueen or Paul Newman, and the brand that insider-y menswear favorites like Engineered Garments and Noah have collaborated with when they wanted to make Harringtons of their own. Baracuta got its start making raincoats for other brands—Burberry included—before branching out with its own designs, and the G9 is still made in England today. Crafted from a water-resistant cotton-poly blend, and featuring the signature Fraser tartan lining and iconic umbrella back yoke (which keeps rain off your back while letting air circulate) it really doesn't get any better than this.

Uniqlo delivers a whole Harrington jacket without sacrificing anything, and in fact saves you some precious dollars along the way. We’re talking a slightly cropped, slightly relaxed silhouette, a touch of stretch, classic slant pockets and even a genre-affirming plaid lining. And while it’s not water-resistant like some other options, it makes up for it with a durable cotton fabric that’ll dry off in no time, and still keep you protected from a few unforeseen raindrops. If you’re after the workaday Harrington aesthetic without spending a lot, this one gets the job done and then some.

If you're looking to purchase a Harrington jacket that'll serve you for seasons to come, but don't particularly want to spend half your rent check on it, J.Crew's faithful take on the Harrington is as true as it gets. And this is no compromise pick: It still comes with plenty of details to get excited about, from the handsome, buttoned interior chest pocket to the warming full lining, leather zip tag, and 10-ounce cotton twill that's already been washed a few times by the brand to make it feel lived-in and well-loved from the jump. It also comes in multiple colors, partly because J.Crew is confident you'll be back for more. Oh, and if you want a winterized Harrington, check out the corduroy iteration, which also has a quilted, Primaloft-stuffed lining.

A pared-down, easygoing take on the classics, Quince’s Harrington strikes a smart balance of polished and sporty, without even the faintest fuss. Offered in khaki, navy and black, this one is the modern minimalist’s Harrington—a clean, contemporary style that does what a staple should do: make you look good without causing a scene. Oh, and that twill outer will break in wonderfully over time, in case you were wondering.

One of the best parts about a Harrington Jacket is that the idea is fully formed. As such, it can be a hard style to riff on, mostly because the source material is so dialed in that it’s often best to leave well enough alone. Ernest W. Baker designers Reid Baker and Inês Amorim, however, couldn’t care less about that tradition and went nuclear with this one: it’s a true-blue Harrington complete with a cropped fit, ribbing at the waist, barrel cuffs and a point collar. But then the inclusion of a leather collar and Western-inspired yoke details in lieu of the classic back vent turns it into something else entirely, without changing the fit one bit. And they nailed it. It’s transformative without being performative, utterly distinct and eminently familiar and, most improbably, contradiction free.

This has most of the trappings of your classic Harrington—stand collar, cool back vent, functional cuffs—but it also eschews the classic ribbed hem for a cinched waist, which adds a little bit of drama to the notoriously no-drama silhouette.

Todd Snyder often plays it straight—Ivy-ish classics with just the right details. Here, they’ve ditched part of the trad playbook and leaned into the modern with water-resistant tech cotton-nylon blend, but it's also a bit cropped and fits very much like you'd remember. And now, it's also on sale.

A Harrington is already pretty pared down, but Barbour trimmed every ounce of fat on this one, leaving us with a slightly longer silhouette, all the *essential* bells and whistles and a brown cotton outer that gets to take center stage.

We could get into the buttery leather collar or the insane Italian wool serge fabric that Wanze deployed on this stunner, or even lock in on that two-way RiRi zipper, but that'd be burying the lede because you're not going to get a red like this anywhere else.

We wouldn't typically include different versions of the same style in one guide, but when our Best Overall version also comes in a buttery suede, exceptions are made.

Stone Island traffics in the unexpected, so, in a way, it should come as no surprise that the Italian label's take on the classic is a Gonzo, teched-out one—one made with a garment-dyed fabric that's been treated with an "anti-drop" finish.

The Harrington is an icon of preppy style, so of course Ralph Lauren has blessed us with its lightweight cotton take, complete with the signature Polo pony on the chest. It’s preppy, American, and exactly the kind of jacket your kids will proudly say “This used to be my Dad’s” about.

You might not think of a Harrington as a "winter jacket," but hear us out: it can be. This Percival joint, for instance, is made out of a hardy birdseye wool blend that will hold up to some chilly weather and layer up nicely when calling things "chilly" is understatement.

The funniest thing about the Harrington? It wasn’t originally called a Harrington at all. The original—and, as you've read above, our favorite—was called the “G9.” It was cooked up by Baracuta in 1937 in rainy old Manchester, England, as a golf jacket—the “G” stands for “golf.” (The idea was to make a garment that could take a beating from British weather without cramping your backswing.) But the jacket earned its now-iconic name thanks to Rodney Harrington, a character from the 1960s TV show Peyton Place, who wore one so often that the name just stuck.

The traditional Harrington jacket fits close to the shoulders and chest, but still has enough room for a full range of arm motion—it is a golfing style, after all. The hem then typically sits either at the waist, or for a more stylized look, just above the belt line. It should be easy to spot from product shots whether the designer in question has stuck to this traditional shape, or elongated the style a touch. From that point, the only thing left to consider is whether you plan to wear it over thick sweaters, or lighter T-shirts and shirts. If it's the former, you may want to consider sizing up.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)
