#6663. Explore the year 1 final projects created by our 2025/26 CondéFuture students

In October 2025, 12 students joined the CondéFuture programme where they gained an exclusive insight into the media industry from Condé Nast professionals who then, through various workshops, encouraged them to explore their passions in photography, video, social media, fashion, digital design, and more. This cohort of CondéFuture students split into three teams, each one building a full magazine issue the way a real editorial team would. Each team picked one or more Condé Nast titles to design an issue around. They developed a theme, then tackled every part of getting an issue out into the world — from finalising layouts, reporting, conducting photo shoots, building a social strategy, to creating both short and long-form videos.

After months of ideating, designing, shooting, and writing content, then weeks spent rehearsing their presentations, the three teams were ready for the showcase. It opened with a student Q&A before each team walked the audience through their magazine, cover to cover, explaining specific choices along the way. Let’s take a look at what they created!

The Allure x Wired team, consisting of Creative Director Ava Gholson, Design Director Amalia Pena, Features Editor Camilla Spillmann and Digital Director Ian Kim, took on one of the more unresolved questions in beauty media right now: what happens to beauty standards when the images shaping them are increasingly AI-generated? The cover carried that concept through the visual of a model's face broken into panels with dotted facial-recognition-style scan lines laid over a beauty shot. The cover story, "We Can't Take Our Eyes Off Iyan Moon Yang," profiled a model through that same lens of tech, beauty, and representation, written by Camilla.

The team chose this theme to highlight a new wave of white supremacy ideology embedded into AI algorithms. Databases are fed the idea that beauty standards should align with white, Eurocentric features, thus perpetuating a harmful cycle in both the beauty industry and the social fabric of America. The Allure x Wired team “find it important to shine a light on this issue, as Gen Z and Gen Alpha have unprecedented access to technology and can be easily influenced. [They are] sometimes made to feel insecure by a system designed to manipulate how they see themselves without even knowing it”.

Inside, the issue is the "Sea to Skin" advertisement, a fictional sustainable skincare brand created by the students, as well as "Is It AI?”, a quiz-style spread testing whether a reader can tell AI-generated beauty content from human-made. "Authenticity in the Age of AI," also by Camilla, was a reported piece on AI beauty influencers.

"I Like Girls With Fair Skin", written by Ava, took on colorism and Eurocentric beauty standards directly. When describing her reason for writing this piece, Ava described the article as her “experience with colorism within society”, “this essay argues that Eurocentric beauty standards are a legacy of colonialism and capitalism, designed to enforce oppression and homogeneity. It calls for a critical examination of these standards and their impact on self-perception, culture, and society”.

On this same theme, they created a video that took the form of a Wired-style autocomplete piece, with young people responding on camera to search-bar prompts about modern beauty standards and AI's impact on creativity and trends.

"Our team decided on combining the two magazines because we liked the idea of "traveling through Bon Appétit" and exploring different cultures in NYC through food, especially immigrant-owned businesses” explained Jerniya Jones, Digital Director of this project. Jerniya, along with teammates Elaina Klein, Design Director, Kevin Lin, Creative Director and Alice Popovych, Features Editor, “wanted to show that New York City has more to offer than just the touristy side of Manhattan."

The cover story, "Traveling Through the Boroughs," explored the city's ethnic communities through food, profiling spots like Veselka, 5 Boro Cafe, New Asha Sri Lankan Restaurant, and Fish 'N' Ting. Two articles ran alongside it: "Locals Know Best," highlighting fifteen spots recommended by actual New Yorkers, and "Affordable + Healthy," promoting ten specific healthy restaurants that don't cost a fortune, including Happy Zoe Vegan Bakery in Greenpoint and Motley Kitchen in the South Bronx.

"The City of Art and Culture" paired an interview with two working PhotoVogue photographers, Chiemeka Offor and Andrew Kung, on how New York City shapes their work and their sense of identity and place.

"A Local's Tale", written by Alice Popovych, profiled Tai Garcia, Community Program Manager at CondéFuture. It followed her into the penthouse of the Brooklyn Museum of Art's director, whose walls happened to be covered in work by the artist Kehinde Wiley, who she unexpectedly got to meet in person! "Turns out that we walked into the home of the man that runs the entire Brooklyn Museum of Art," Garcia said. "There was the most beautiful artwork, paintings, sculptures, all on his walls, and you could get so close to them, closer than you could get in a regular museum."

Other spreads included "A Day in the Life," a Polaroid-style photo collage of what the students describe as the real New York experience, and "Afterschool Activities," a guide to where city kids actually go to eat or hang out after 9th period (though for this cohort, that's sometimes the Condé Nast office at the World Trade Center). One spread was a parody ad, a riff on the city's old Dunkin' campaign reading "NYC Runs on Dunkin'." Their video was an interview with the owner of one of the city's legendary frozen dessert stands — Delicioso Coco Helado — who told the story of how her father got the idea after seeing similar stands in Puerto Rico, and how they've since become a quintessential piece of New York City childhood, bringing people together across different neighborhoods.

Dawn, the senior copy editor who worked with several teams on their drafts, had high praise for this project. "I'm a lifelong New Yorker, and one of the pieces I loved so much was a story about getting to know New York, all the different boroughs, through food and the authenticity of food as culture. Not only did I get a list of restaurants to check out, I felt like the flavor of that story jumped off the page. They were teaching me about a city I've loved for decades." She'd read it as an early draft and saw it through many edits. "It started strong and ended stronger," she said, pointing to how the team tied in Veselka and the way that community has rallied around the restaurant since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Creative Director Olivia DiGennaro, Digital Director Ryan Martinez, Design Director Jasmeryn Reynoso and Features Editor Sydney Liu built this special edition around the theme "Everlasting, Evergreen." Their own mission statement opened the issue: Vanity Fair has covered culture, fashion, and current affairs since 1913, and the team wanted to explore how style today continually draws on and reimagines the eras before it, while pushing back on the idea that only certain kinds of faces belong in a magazine.

Ryan explains the group’s interest in this particular theme: “late 1900s Hollywood celebrity culture has left us with a cycle that is visible and present in today's youth in the form of their interests, inspirations, and most importantly, styles. Our Vanity Fair special edition covers exactly how this evolution takes shape, noticeably in our present society. Just like the brand's heritage, it explores the shift in culture, fashion, and current affairs within our generations (and especially Gen Z) in the past few decades”.

Beyond this, the issue included a story on how modern pop stars like Sabrina Carpenter and Olivia Dean have drawn on old Hollywood fashion and style ("The Golden Age: Luxurious, Tragic, Longing, the New Sound of Old Hollywood"). The cover story itself interviewed seven NYC teens about how they see their own fashion choices in relation to the eras before them, drawing a line between 20th-century style and how their generation reinterprets it now. The piece was careful to note the difference between influence and imitation: their inspirations, while important, stay that way – just inspirations, not guidelines. The issue closed with a spotlight on Alexandra Dautel, a Paris-based photographer whose work the team said shaped their own photo direction.

The students’ work over year 1 culminated in an end of year showcase. Their work was presented in a gallery format, with their covers and spreads laid out for guests to browse through. Amongst these guests were alumni from CondéFuture's earlier cohorts who came back to see what the new group had accomplished.

Students were also able to present their work to the guests, talking them through their journey. Walter Doyle, Senior Education Manager, explained that “the CondéFuture showcase highlights all that the students have absorbed in such a short time. The presentations were incredible, with each capturing the spirit of the brand they were representing”.

As students head into their second year, they are faced with a different kind of project ahead of them: rather than working in teams, each will be paired one-to-one with a mentor for an individual capstone project, applying what this year taught them about how a media career actually works.

#6662. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6661. I Tried Taco Bell’s New FLAMIN’ HOT Menu Items To See If They Really Bring The Heat

One of these could've used a few extra sauce packets.

I'll try just about anything Taco Bell puts on its menu, and whatever I order usually ends up drenched in hot sauce. So when I heard the chain was adding a new FLAMIN' HOT offering (and bringing back a punchy fan favorite), I was curious whether they'd finally give me enough spice to leave those packets alone. I like my food hot enough to get a few beads of sweat forming on my nose, and with a name like FLAMIN' HOT, I don't think that's asking too much.

There were two contenders: the returning FLAMIN' HOT Grilled Cheese Burrito ($5.49), which I'd missed during its first run, and the brand-new FLAMIN' HOT Mini Taco Salad ($2.49). Both feature Fritos FLAMIN' HOT, so I figured I was in for some decent spice. Here's how that worked out.

I love a good taco salad, especially when the bowl itself is edible. But my first impression of this mini version was that it looked like a pretty ordinary Taco Bell salad. And after a few bites, I wasn't finding much to convince me otherwise.

You've got seasoned beef, refried beans, lettuce, tomatoes, cheddar, and Creamy Chipotle sauce tucked into a crispy flour tortilla bowl. Beneath everything was a layer of reddish rice, which Taco Bell says is seasoned with FLAMIN' HOT Fritos. I could definitely see the color, but whatever was making that rice spicy wasn't doing much for my taste buds.

And speaking of Fritos, I'm still trying to figure out where mine went. They're supposed to be in there, but I genuinely couldn't tell whether they'd been included in my particular serving. I would've loved more of the chipotle sauce, too, because the other ingredients seemed to overpower whatever heat was hiding underneath.

The shell itself was fine, although a little bland and greasy. I’m still pro-taco salads, but I just wish the spice had been more noticeable—especially with a name that makes such a big promise.

The returning burrito is stuffed with seasoned beef, spicy rice, crunchy FLAMIN' HOT Fritos, nacho cheese sauce, sour cream, and Creamy Chipotle sauce. And because Taco Bell clearly believes there's no such thing as too much cheese, the entire thing gets a three-cheese blend grilled onto the outside of the tortilla.

I took a pretty substantial first bite, making sure to get into those Fritos and all its FLAMIN’ HOT components. The nacho cheese had that gloriously gooey, movie-theater quality (complimentary), while the rest of the fillings worked together much better than they had in the salad. There's a lot happening inside this thing, and I was enjoying every bit of it.

Most importantly, I could actually taste the heat. There was a satisfying punch of spice, followed by that little tickle at the back of my throat that tells me something's doing its job. I wasn't desperately reaching for a drink, but the burrito had enough kick to make me happy.

I even went back for another bite of the mini taco salad afterward, and it tasted better with the burrito's lingering heat still in my mouth. Who knew it needed a little help from its menu companion?

Ultimately, the burrito is the one I'd order again. The mini taco salad has potential, and for $2.49, I wouldn't be opposed to giving it another shot. But next time, I'm bringing the extra hot sauce packets it should've saved me from needing.

#6660. John Mulaney Wore Joe DiMaggio’s Watch to Host 'Saturday Night Live'

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

Between sniffing out paternal autism and perfecting his Robert F. Kennedy impression, you may have noticed that John Mulaney was wearing an extraordinary watch while hosting Saturday Night Live this weekend. It’s a beauty—a gold vintage Patek Philippe with swoopy Breguet numerals—but its backstory is even more impressive. On December 12, 1948, New York Yankees legend Joe DiMaggio purchased this timepiece and owned it until his death in 1999.

The Patek Philippe, a ref. 130 circa 1947, is already a rare bird before you add in its Joltin’ Joe provenance. The model is one of just 180 made in yellow gold with Breguet numerals, and only 55 with this same combination have ever reached the secondary market. In late October, dealer Eric Wind of Wind Vintage put this specific watch up for sale with a $1.2 million asking price. “I think it’s the greatest Patek that’s known and tied to any athlete,” Wind told Robb Report last month.

For his seventh time hosting SNL, Mulaney came to Wind in search of “an important watch,” the dealer explains now. After surveying Wind’s entire catalog, the comedian landed on this piece, whose ties to a legendary New Yorker felt right for helming one of the city’s most hallowed institutions. To be clear, Mulaney only borrowed the watch for the show, which means its legend will have only grown by the time it reaches an eventual buyer. Talk about an illustrious provenance: A DiMaggio-owned Patek that also appeared on Saturday Night Live. “It was a very special moment and another cool moment of history for this important Patek Philippe,” Wind says.

As a known history buff and devoted baseball fan, the watch likely appealed to Mulaney on several levels. But its eggshell-hued dial also happened to go perfectly with the brown suit Mulaney sported during his opening monologue. “John has classic styling,” Wind says, “and the Joe DiMaggio Patek Philippe was the chef’s kiss on his wrist.”

Over the past several years, Mulaney has emerged as one of Hollywood’s most prolific and tasteful watch collectors. He is an eager and omnivorous admirer, bouncing between his beloved Rolex Air-King, loud Chopard chronographs, and glamorous Grand Seikos.

Mulaney, styled by Michael Fisher, wearing Cavour

During our watch-focused interview last May, Mulaney told me that he steers away from more obvious models like your garden-variety Rolex Submariner. “I don’t ask any questions about it, I know what it is,” he explained. “And I’m just more interested in watches that [are a little more] mysterious.” As an example, Mulaney specifically referenced a Patek Philippe Calatrava his wife Olivia Munn bought him.

The DiMaggio Patek is full of intrigue. The watch obviously has important provenance, but it’s historic on its own accord, too. The ref. 130 is named for the movement inside, known as the Calibre 130. That engine was the basis for Patek’s 1518, the first serially produced watch to combine a perpetual calendar and chronograph.

Funnily enough, this isn’t the first Mulaney, DiMaggio, and SNL crossover. In his 2018 special Kid Gorgeous at Radio City, the comedian explained what it was like working with famous SNL hosts during his time as a staff writer. “It’d be like if you went into your childhood bedroom and Joe DiMaggio was sitting there,” Mulaney quipped. “Yeah, he’s Joe DiMaggio, he’s a legend, he had sex with Marilyn Monroe, but only you know where the bathroom is.” And only Mulaney has had DiMaggio’s watch on his wrist, for now.

#6657. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6656. Drinking Tea Too Hot Could Be Bad For Your Health—Here's What To Know

Your morning cup might benefit from a little patience.

There’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health. A recently published study followed nearly half a million adults in China for almost a decade, examining how tea-drinking habits related to their health. Researchers found that regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of vascular disease than non-tea drinkers. But one major caveat emerged: Those who reported drinking their tea “burning hot” had a higher risk of vascular disease.

According to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease. But don't give up your daily tea habit quite yet. “This study is interesting, but we don't have a proven biological explanation yet,” Dr. Niraj Patel, medical director at Clara, says.

Dr. Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.

“It doesn’t look like this study has any proposed mechanism for why burning hot tea would increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” she explains. “However, we do know that drinks that are too hot can increase the risk of esophageal cancer by creating local injury and damage.”

That concern is supported by the World Health Organization's cancer research agency, which has classified drinking beverages hotter than 149°F as probably carcinogenic to humans. The classification specifically concerns esophageal cancer, though, so it doesn't explain the connection to vascular disease identified in the new study.

The study didn’t identify a specific temperature at which drinking tea becomes detrimental to vascular health. And although researchers found an association between drinking extremely hot tea and vascular disease, that doesn't necessarily mean one causes the other.

ScienceDaily also notes that drinking tea at extremely high temperatures may diminish some of the health benefits associated with regular tea consumption.

Azarcon believes further research into tea's chemical makeup and how it may change at different temperatures could help answer some of the remaining questions.

"I'd say enjoy your tea, but don't feel like you need to drink it while it's scalding hot,” Patel suggests. “There's a difference between brewing tea with hot water and actually drinking it at that temperature. Letting it cool for a few minutes is an easy precaution and doesn't require giving up something you enjoy."

So while I don’t plan on giving up my tea habit any time soon, I am definitely making extra sure that I let my cup sit out a little longer before taking that first sip.

#6655. Pamela Anderson Is a Sentimentalist at Heart

The actress on holiday traditions, motherhood, and the sentimental value of giving with Pandora.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

For Pamela Anderson, the holiday season is less about elaborate celebrations and more about appreciating life’s quieter moments. “I love the fall. I always say fall is the season of the soul,” she tells ELLE. Whether she’s tending to her garden on Vancouver Island, cooking vegetarian dishes for her family, or watching her sons establish traditions of their own, Anderson has found a new appreciation for the simple pleasures that make this time of year so special.

It’s a philosophy that extends to her approach to gift-giving. A self-described sentimentalist, Anderson prefers presents that carry a personal meaning, from family photographs to jewelry passed down through generations. And through her partnership with Pandora (Anderson is a face of the brand), she’s found a way to celebrate those connections with pieces that feel both personal and accessible.

I love the fall. I always say fall is the season of the soul. I think that’s a Virginia Woolf quote. Even in a garden, you focus more on the little things instead of being overwhelmed by so much abundance. It feels like a really special time of year. I love the fall weather and the leaves changing. It’s beautiful, especially here on the East Coast. Where I’m from on Vancouver Island, it actually looks very similar.

I absolutely love gardening. When I was home, I was cleaning up a bunch of leaves, and it feels like a workout, too. It’s nice to be outside, even in the rain. I don’t shy away from the rain, or nothing would ever get done where I’m from. I love being outside and getting my hands dirty. In this part of my life, I’m really gravitating toward that, but I’m also working a lot, so it’s a really good balance. I get to do really glamorous things, work on film and onstage, and then I go home, put my boots on, and get in the garden.

Now, the boys are usually with their wife and fiancée over the holidays. They’re building their lives and their own traditions, so I always say, “Don’t worry about me. I’m always around.” It’s nice to see them building those traditions. I’ve done a lot of hosting and party planning in my life. I’m a decorator, so I love all of that. But this year, it’s really about seeing all the traditions and things my sons have soaked up and watching them start their own lives. I’m not a pressure planner. I don’t want them to feel pressure to include me. I just say, “You guys do your thing. I’m watching, I’m observing.” It’s really special as a mom to see them so happy with their significant others. The women in their lives have great taste and love to share that with them and me.

I love cooking. I always cook all the sides, the vegetable dishes. It’s been a while since we’ve all been together for a big meal. Time is just flying by. My sons are such great cooks, too. We all have our specialties. I think I actually prefer decorating to cooking, because you set the stage. Then you can have a potluck!

I’ve given a lot of my jewelry from my lifetime to my kids and to their wife and fiancée. I like more sentimental gifts. I’m a sentimentalist, I guess. I love flowers, and this year, one of my sons just got married, but they don’t have wedding pictures of themselves. So they’re getting wedding pictures, engagement pictures, just a bunch of really sentimental things from me.

I just give my kids everything. I like to give those pieces to them so they can appreciate them while I’m here. I don’t hoard a lot of things. I’m always changing, always trying new things, and I don’t think I’m a big consumer anyway. I have special pieces that I’ve already passed on.

My mother always wants my Pandora jewelry. Every time I go anywhere, she’s asking, “Do you have Pandora? Do you have any earrings?” She loves it. My mom’s sisters and everyone just love Pandora. She loves both gold and silver, the jewels, the colors. Some of the beautiful pieces they have around the holidays, she would go crazy for. She loves it all.

I definitely wear more jewelry than I used to. It depends on what I’m wearing or where I’m going. I like to recycle jewelry. A lot of my Pandora pieces I’ve worn on different red carpets or to different special events. It’s nice for jewelry to be attainable, cruelty-free, and sustainable. Those things are so important to me. Jewelry isn’t just for the few. It’s for everybody.

When I align with somebody, I like to know that we have similar philosophies. I think it’s the small-town girl in me who never felt jewelry was in the cards for her. It’s nice to know there’s a jewelry company that’s forward-thinking and sustainable, thinking about recycling and also making it affordable. It just feels more like me. I love glamour and I love fancy things, but I think my kind of fashion is more inspirational.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6654. The OG 'Thomas Crown Affair' Is an Essential Menswear Movie. How Will the Reboot Stack Up?

Between a stacked roster of Hollywood icons in their prime (Newman, Poitier, Redford) and a cadre of auteur directors on the come-up (Kubrick, Peckinpah, Coppola), the late 1960s produced some of the 20th century’s most stylish movies. Right up there with the best of them is The Thomas Crown Affair, a 1968 caper film directed by Norman Jewison and starring Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway. Fast-forward a few days and the same could be said about the 1999 remake starring Bond-era Pierce Brosnan, which is worth watching for the suits alone.

Now, in other news of a formerly Brosnan-led, menswear-centric franchise being rebooted: Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan is the producer, director, and star of a third riff on The Thomas Crown Affair, as he announced at CinemaCon back in April. Judging by the first trailer that dropped last week, the film aims to uphold the sartorial reputation of its forebears.

Hitting theaters in March 2027, Jordan’s The Thomas Crown Affair remake follows the same premise as the 1968 and 1999 versions: a wealthy playboy businessman plots art heists for fun while being pursued by a sexy insurance investigator, played in this iteration by potential future Wonder Woman Adria Arjona. There’s crime, there’s glamour, there’s sexual tension—but most of all, in the spirit of the Thomas Crowns before him, there appears to be plenty of high-octane menswear. The movie’s style credit is bolstered by Ruth E. Carter, the two-time Oscar-winning costume designer of the Black Panther movies, who also dressed Jordan for his Oscar-winning turn in Sinners.

But how will MBJ’s high-fashion Thomas Crown land? In the trailer, he can be seen wearing a stiff gray shirt with a matching tie and trousers by Bottega Veneta. The shirt, marked by the luxury brand’s signature triangle pocket detail, had an odd fit: taut around the torso yet puffy around the biceps. Here’s hoping we’ll see some sharper tailoring in the next preview.

Still, to understand Thomas Crown’s legacy as one of the best-dressed guys in film, and why the forthcoming reboot will likely be a smorgasbord of big-time menswear, it’s worth looking back at what made the original such a gem of classic American style. Beyond Jewison’s use of Mondrian-esque split-screen and a very cool soundtrack by French composer Michel Legrand, McQueen’s wardrobe is a perfect embodiment of late 1960s cool, and a how-to for anyone looking to capture it.

Equal parts finely tailored and adventurous, Crown is the ultimate man’s man: He closes million-dollar deals by day, but also flies planes, plays polo, and does donuts on the beach in a juiced-up dune buggy. Likewise, his wardrobe is split between incredible tailoring and a supremely dialed-in lineup of casual pieces. Crown’s suits are a primer on old-school Savile Row: structured, traditional, and precisely tailored, and his shirts, ties, and pocket squares are equally on point. Crown’s double-Albert style watch chain (attached to a Patek Philippe pocket watch, naturally) is a decidedly advanced swerve, but his Cartier Tank Cintrée looks as good in 2026 as it did in 1968 (or 1928, for that matter).

Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway in The Thomas Crown Affair (1968).

Off-duty Crown’s casual looks include a parade of hall-of-fame menswear pieces like the Baracuta G9 Harrington jacket (classic navy blue with a red tartan lining), brown suede desert boots, and Persol aviators he wears while piloting his glider (gliders—also extremely cool). Club rules be damned, he plays golf in a non-regulation long-sleeved tee, whacks polo balls in an outfit straight out of a Ralph Lauren campaign, and later dons an Aran sweater for a romantic evening clambake at his beach house. It’s often said that Steve McQueen could look good in anything, and that might be true, but the clothes in this movie hit hard enough to make anyone look several orders of magnitude cooler.

Set to the funky bars of Fela Kuti’s “Gentleman,” the trailer for Jordan’s forthcoming Thomas Crown Affair offers several tantalizing tidbits of what’s in store, including a Ferrari F40, several razor-sharp tuxes, and a glimpse at a watch that’s almost certainly a vintage Piaget. That monochrome Bottega look aside, between Jordan’s leading man chops and Carter’s knack for high-concept menswear, we’re assuredly in good hands.

#6653. Applications for the 2027 LVMH Prize Are Now Open

Each year in Paris, promising young designers present their work to industry legends, hoping to distinguish themselves as part of fashion’s rising new guard—and to secure a cash prize of €400,000. Today, applications for the 14th edition of the LVMH Prize are now open.

Over the length of the Prize, the event has served as an invaluable launchpad for independent designers, including two former contestants who are both set to make historic debuts. Grace Wales Bonner (winner, 2016) will present her first collection for Hermès men’s in January, 2027, and just last week, Martine Rose (semifinalist, 2017) was confirmed for the top job at Balenciaga following Pierpaolo Piccioli’s departure. Meanwhile, this year’s Karl Lagerfeld prize winner, Zane Li of Lii, also snagged the top prize at the 2026 CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund.

Jury members, who this year included newbies Michael Rider of Celine and Louis Vuitton CEO Pietro Beccari, are interested in fostering designers with promising businesses. “The jury this time around was very focused on where people produce, where they distribute, and who the final client is,” said Delphine Arnault in an interview following Julie Kegel’s 2026 win. “They were interested in designers who [could talk about] who their [customers] are.”

Designers can submit their application on lvmhprize.com from now through April 4, 2027. Winners of the Karl Lagerfeld Prize and Savoir-Faire Prize, will each take home €200,000, while the three winners of the LVMH Prize for Young Graduates will join the creative studios of the Group’s Houses on one-year contracts. Both the graduate winners and their schools will also receive a €10,000 allocation. Applicants must be between the ages of 18-40 and have created at least two ready-to-wear collections. The semifinals will take place in Paris on March 3 and 4, 2027.

#6652. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6650. This Buzzy New Wellness Retreat in Kerala Blends Ancient Traditions With Modern Medicine

As the birthplace of yoga and its sister science Ayurveda, India certainly has no shortage of wellness retreats. The country is quite literally filled with spiritual centers, located everywhere from the foothills of the Himalayas to the beaches of Goa to the sacred riverbanks of Varanasi. I’ve been fortunate enough to visit a fair amount of them over the past decade, thanks to both my work as the author of Destination Wellness, an exploration of ancient health traditions around the world, and the fact that my husband is a born-and-raised Delhiite. We live in New York, but go to India regularly to stay with family and travel around the rest of the country together.

That’s why I was immediately intrigued when I heard about Tulåh Clinical Wellness, a longevity-focused wellness center in Kerala that opened earlier this year and blends ancient Ayurveda with more modern diagnostic testing. While some wellness retreats in India are already known for their mix of global healing traditions (Six Senses Vana and Ananda in the Himalayas come to mind), Tulåh’s blend sounded new to me, closer to a clinical European med spa—albeit one steeped in traditional medicine. Its location stood out to me, too, given Kerala’s long history as the epicenter of Ayurveda in India. I’ve done two very traditional Ayurvedic retreats in Kerala myself, so as I read Tulåh’s extensive list of modern medical offerings—from MRIs to mammograms—I became increasingly curious about its approach. How would all that new testing and technology fit into the longstanding wellness scene in Kerala? And what would that mean for India at large?

To find out, I booked a weeklong program at Tulåh in early September, right at the tail end of monsoon season (actually considered one of the best times for Ayurvedic treatments in Kerala). It was drizzling when I got off the plane in the coastal city of Calicut, but by the time I arrived at the property half an hour later, the rain had stopped and the air smelled fresh—and not just because of the post-shower skies. Tulåh is set on 30 acres of rewilded forest and medicinal gardens in the Western Ghats, a lush mountain range whose abundance of healing herbs and plants perfumes its air with a consistently earthy scent.

My stay began with a watermelon elixir welcome drink and a tour of the property, which felt even more global than I expected—almost like an international wellness campus with a serious Indian pedigree. That’s partly because “the sanctuary,” as the staffers lovingly call it, is modeled after Auroville, an experimental, spiritually-minded community just north of Pondicherry in Tamil Nadu. Auroville brings people from different countries and cultures together with the goal of living in harmony, and Tulåh—which means “balance” in Sanskrit—has that same world-blending vibe. Designed by Dubai-based firm Lami Architects, the 65-suite property is built on the site of a former cotton mill and looks strikingly modern from the outside, with sleek, flowing curves inspired by the legendary Zaha Hadid. Yet inside its nine main buildings, the minimalist interiors focus largely on Indian craftsmanship, featuring smooth terrazzo floors sourced from artisans in Rajasthan, handwoven earth-toned rugs and marble from Uttar Pradesh, and plush furniture from a design studio in Kerala. Strolling around the grounds after my initial tour, I even heard the upbeat “Qui Es-Tu?” from the French electro-pop duo Poom playing on speakers placed throughout the tropical gardens, followed by a bamboo flutist performing peaceful South Indian Carnatic meditations in the lobby just a few minutes later.

This deliberate mix of influences is the brainchild of founder Faizal Kottikollon, an entrepreneur, engineer, and philanthropist who was born in Kerala, studied in the US, and later settled in Dubai. “Yoga and Ayurveda are India’s IP, but Ayurveda often gets siloed,” he told me one afternoon over a cup of herbal tea. “It gets marketed as an alternative therapy in the medical world, when it should be in the mainstream alongside other modern practices.”

He, of all people, would know. Back in 2022, Kottikollon was diagnosed with spinal cord compression, and his doctors recommended a very risky spinal surgery. He didn’t want to do that, so he turned instead to the traditional Ayurvedic practices he’d grown up around in Kerala. Ayurvedic practitioner Dr. Vishnuraj Prakash, whom Kottikollon later hired as the first doctor at Tulåh, suggested he do a 21-day panchakarma treatment along with mamsa kizhi massages with warm cloth bundles of goat meat, milk, rice, and various herbs. In Ayurveda, goat meat is thought to strengthen muscle tissues—and by all accounts it did. Kottikollon’s next MRI showed that his compression was healed. Today, he says he is 99% recovered.

“When we did the MRI after my panchakarma, my modern medicine doctors had to believe in Ayurveda, because the proof was right there,” he told me. “And that’s when I said, ‘Oh my god, this is the future of healthcare.’ Ayurveda had the solution to my problem for thousands of years, but my modern doctors never knew. That’s why it should be integrated with modern medicine rather than working on its own. People don’t talk to each other, because human beings are blocked by egos—but all doctors need to work together. And that’s what I’m trying to change.”

His plan (and his $100 million investment) seems to be working. At Tulåh, my days were filled with a true mix of traditional Ayurvedic practices and modern longevity diagnostics. It all started, as these sorts of retreats so often do, well before my stay, when I sent in various samples for the medical team to assess just a few months after their February opening. Then I went straight into two full days of diagnostic tests and consultations the day after I arrived. A nurse took my blood sample on my first morning, followed by a BCA (body composition analysis) and an Ayurvedic consultation with my designated practitioner, Dr. Urvashi Naithani. She read my pulse, asked some lifestyle questions, and ultimately identified a kapha imbalance in my system that was making me sluggish. In Ayurveda, everyone has a unique constitution shaped by three doshas: vata (air and space), pitta (fire and water), and kapha (earth and water). The goal in life is to keep all three doshas in balance at all times, though as I can attest, that’s very hard to do.

A shirodhara treatment on a Vichy Shower Bed.

My program continued with a couple of kapha-reducing Ayurvedic treatments interspersed with more modern longevity testing. That included a chest X-ray, a CAC scan, a DXA scan, an MRI (quite an accomplishment for a claustrophobe like me), a dental appointment, a psychological assessment, and a slew of mobility and fitness consultations. At times it felt a bit jarring to go from a soothing ancient therapy like shirodhara to a terrifying 45-minute scan in a metal tube, but I always knew it was all in pursuit of self-knowledge—and that made me feel really good. It was almost like being back in school, only the subject was myself.

Everything eventually culminated with the big “MDM meeting,” or the multidisciplinary team meeting, on my third full day. This meeting is essentially Kottikollon’s vision of integration come to life: when representatives from Tulåh’s nine departments (Ayurveda, functional medicine, modern medicine, Chinese medicine, fitness, physiotherapy, psychology, clinical yoga, and dental) convene to discuss your results and put together a custom plan for the rest of your stay and your routine after you leave. Back to the school metaphor, I couldn’t help but think of it as all my teachers from different subjects gossiping about me in the conference room… but with only my very best interests in mind.

If the team had determined I needed serious medical attention, Tulåh has an on-site ICU and operating room, as well as access to a nearby hospital that Kottikollon also owns. But in my case, the consensus across the board was that I simply needed to boost my energy and get much, much stronger. One of the biggest subjects the MDM team discusses is your Tulåh Life Index, a proprietary number they calculate to assess your body’s overall function based on your bloodwork, body composition results, lifestyle questions, and more. My score was 71 out of 100, which was not terrible (70 and above is the goal), but not great either—thanks largely to my lack of muscle mass. In my defense, there was a good reason for that. As I told the doctors during my consultations, I stopped strength training regularly during a five-year period of IVF treatments, when fertility doctors advise against lifting weights because of the risk of ovarian torsion. Though I could’ve done more strength training between IVF rounds, I was still a bit too scared for my ovaries to fully get back into it. Now that I’m finally emerging from the IVF tunnel thanks to turning to surrogacy, the doctors recommended I make regaining my muscle mass a top priority—especially since I’m now 41, when these things begin to matter even more. I knew this already, technically, but hearing it from a team of professionals based on my own numbers made it feel extra real to me—and all the more urgent.

What followed was a few more packed days of treatments and meals customized to my new high-strength, high-energy lifestyle. My meals were delicious—lots of high-protein South Indian fish curries and North Indian specialties like chicken tikka and chana masala, all made with predominantly organic and locally-grown ingredients. And unlike my past Ayurvedic retreats in Kerala, where the plan mostly revolved around oil treatments and yoga, therapies at Tulåh also included aquatic fitness, personal strength training sessions, clinical yoga with a focus on alignment, and daily sound baths in the incredible Sonorium (I fell asleep every time). Throughout it all, the staff was so caring and lovely as well. During a qawwali performance in the Sonorium one night, I even saw a young teacher offer an older Indian uncle a pillow for behind his back without him ever asking.

My Ayurvedic treatments were still my favorite, though. In a plot twist that will undoubtedly delight all Ayurveda lovers, Kottikollon and his team have combined the Vichy shower—named after the thermal spa town of Vichy, France—with a traditional Ayurvedic massage bed to create the recently patented Vichy Shower Bed, which has six showerheads directly above the heated, ergonomically designed table. This means that, rather than shuffling you to the shower after your treatment so you can rinse off all the medicated oil, practitioners do it for you right there on the bed—including a shampoo and condition. In my experience, Ayurvedic oil is often near impossible to get off, so this perk was absolute bliss for me. And it’s one that Kottikollon hopes will make Ayurveda more accessible to the mainstream as well. “Traditional wooden Ayurvedic beds can be slippery and leave you with oil all over, and I believe this is part of the reason why Ayurveda has not been adopted in the current world,” he told me. “But Ayurveda can solve so many problems—which is why I want this bed to be at all the spas and hospitals in the world along with all the other options.”

A treatment room with a Vichy Shower Bed.

I’ll co-sign that. While I wasn’t sure how it would feel to combine Ayurveda with all things modern, I ended up loving the 360-degree approach. Not having to pick a lane (or a century) was so convenient—like one-stop shopping for longevity. If anything, seeing the ancient practices I’ve come to love used as part of a diagnostics-informed treatment plan even helped me appreciate them in a new, deeper way.

I’m also happy to report I’ve followed through on my strength and energy mission, at least somewhat, since I checked out of Tulåh a month ago. As a frequent traveler, it’s hard for me to get into a super steady routine, but I did lift weights at my hotel gym in Japan last week as opposed to just running on the treadmill—and that felt like progress to me. At home in New York, I’ve also been consulting Tulåh’s Home app, which provides personalized recipes, workout plans, yoga poses and meditations based on my medical results. I don’t use it every day (maybe you’ve heard of a little thing called the NYC restaurant scene?), but I’ve made enough of the recipes to tell you they’re easy and good. And the yoga nidra meditation has become my new go-to for getting out of an afternoon slump.

We have a saying in my family of journalists: “Everything’s been said, but not everyone has said it.” And so, in the grand tradition of honoring your roots, allow me to state the obvious: Knowledge really is power. It feels so good to know exactly what I need to do. Now I just need to keep doing it.

#6649. Exclusive: The World’s Top Players Look Back on a Wild Year in Men’s Tennis

It was Friday the 13th, and Turin, Italy, the site of the Nitto ATP Finals, glowed with cobalt light as a fingernail moon hung in the air. It looked almost like a Tintoretto painting.

At the Piazza San Carlo, a blue carpet had been laid out lengthwise for the world’s eight best (and currently active) men’s tennis players as fans called out for autographs and selfies. Carlos Alcaraz in Louis Vuitton and Ben Shelton in Ralph Lauren walked among them; missing was the home favorite, Jannik Sinner, who qualified for the field but is sidelined with a knee injury. The scene delivered a surreal, Hollywood-esque half-hour of public stagecraft—paparazzi flashbulbs, police escorts—with all of it designed to celebrate the end of a very notable, and sometimes odd, year in men’s pro tennis.

Speaking of the dreamlike: the evening included an ATP-commissioned portrait session with the photographer Szilveszter Makó, a man who has skyrocketed to industry prominence for having shot multiple covers this year—including for the American, British and Italian editions of Vogue. Makó’s aesthetic itself is rather painterly; photographs as aged frescoes, both cerebral and unusual. Within Turin’s Inalpi Arena, he forged two vignettes with his signature box sets. We stepped in to take a look as Arthur Fils, wearing Balenciaga, was instructed to stand tall and lift his right foot, balancing it on the heel. (“It’s kind of weird, no?” Fils asked, before leaning in.) Makó lensed seven of the eight athletes; due to extenuating circumstances, Alcaraz was unable to stop by the makeshift studio.

But, no matter. In a mad dash between the Principi di Piemonte Hotel, the Piazza San Carlo, a jam-packed van ride across gridlocked roads, and, finally, the Arena, we caught up with all eight players, who together offer an apt representation of the deep and diverse present state of the world’s elite-most men’s tennis. What was discussed: everything from self-reflections to coaching change-ups to cellys to the popularity of the Maldives.

2026 was the biggest year of Zverev’s career: he won his maiden Slam at Roland-Garros, then followed it up with a victory at the US Open. The German also reached the world number 1 spot for the first time (it’s worth noting here that Zverev also holds a super-rare tennis title: an Olympic gold medal, from Tokyo). At 29, he is a half-generation older than the sport’s current dominant duopoly of Sinner and Alcaraz, but if he keeps his current level of play up, he’ll make a strong case for another “Big Three”(the nickname assigned to Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic during their long run of supremacy). Despite the settlement of a domestic abuse lawsuit involving his ex-partner Brenda Patea, a new case was brought to light just a few days ago: the tennis writer Ben Rothenberg reported that Patea has sued Zverev for public misrepresentations. It’s been a career year, but it has to be said that Zverev remains a polarizing figure.

The finest Canadian tuxedo I’ve ever seen.

When you wear head-to-toe denim, yes. You’ve had an incredible year. What worked—and is working—best for you mentally, looking back on it now?

I made a decision with my team last year to change my game style—changing the way we play. I think it was quite a bold move at the age of 29. But we said: it had been working, I’ve had a great career, but it wasn’t working at the final stage of Grand Slams. It hadn’t worked to achieve the dreams and the goals we had. So, sticking to the new game plan, I think that was the biggest thing. Sticking to it and being brave enough to accept it. I think, in the end, it paid off.

Definitely. Two Slams this year, the number one ranking. Are you happy with your game right now, or is there anything you want to improve in 2027?

No, I don’t think I’m complete at all. There are always things you have to improve—and at the end of the day, everybody else is improving, too, so you have to keep with it to stay relevant.

You had some frustration a few weeks ago in Paris in having to defend your number one ranking. Are you still reckoning with that?

I think in Paris it was all just quite new, and I was mentally a little bit tired. There were a lot of new things. And of course, it’s a different kind of pressure. But, I think it’s all settled down, and I’m very happy to be here among the best in the world. It’s an honor.

What’s your vacation plan once the season ends?

Alcaraz—men’s tennis’s brightest star—nicely bookended an otherwise turbulent 2026. The Spaniard, 23, won his first Australian Open all the way back in January, and has enjoyed a surge of recent title wins (in Vienna, Tokyo, and Paris) after returning to the tour from a bout with wrist tenosynovitis that kept him offline for nearly five months. His return at the US Open—where he reached the quarterfinals—brought with it a much-hyped collaboration with Nike’s Cactus Jack line and a tousled new hairstyle. One interesting note going into Turin: Alcaraz has not yet won an ATP Finals, and will be hungry to add that to his resume.

What’s your best 2026 memory off of the court?

Oh, well, I have a couple, to be honest. One of the highlights I had this year was attending the World Cup final. Seeing Spain win the World Cup was unbelievable. So yeah, I’m going to say that! Ferran Torres’s goal, that was the turning point of his career. From that, I would say his stock is really high.

You’ve come back from injury, and you’ve had a strong tail-end of the year, winning Tokyo and Paris. After being hurt, did your mentality change at all? Any hesitation?

I knew that, coming back, I needed matches. I needed competition. I need to feel I was back in the rhythm of competing, and I’m still [building that back]. I need to go out there and feel those nerves of competition. I’m still working on being strong for these difficulties.

With the season ending, what will you try to do in the offseason?

Well, I am not allowed to play golf yet, because my team [won’t let me]. Probably the first thing I’m going to do after the season is over is play golf.

Shelton, 24, had two standout moments on the court in 2026: he defended his Canadian Open title and reached his first Major final at the US Open. Though he lost to Zverev there, it was still a considerable level-up for the Florida-born phenom. Shelton made recent industry news by tapping Juan Carlos Ferrero—Alcaraz’s former coach—to join his team in 2027 (Shelton’s father, Bryan, will remain his coach as well).

You’re bringing on Juan Carlos Ferrero as a coach. Talk us through that decision.

Yeah. Even in the early stages, I think we’ve done a good job of putting together a schedule where I will have two coaches. I don’t want either of them to have to travel 40 weeks a year. So I think we’re putting together a really good formula where they’re both traveling about half the weeks. That’s the ideal scenario for us.

What’s the strongest, most resonant moment you’re taking with you from 2026?

Defending my title in Canada is one. I thought that was the best tennis I’ve played in my career. I didn’t drop a set all week. I was clinical. It was fun for me to see that I can play at that level. But, I have to say, walking out on court for a US Open final and feeling the energy of that stadium on that day, even though I took an L, was pretty special.

I’m just going to play it by ear. I might go on vacation with Arthur Fils, but we’ll see.

The tennis world is happy to see Medvedev, 30, back in elite form. After a less-than-stellar 2025, the lanky Russian has been playing significantly better in 2026, having won four titles and returned to the top 10. Yes, he still has outbursts, and yes, crowds will either go with him on them or boo relentlessly. But that’s just part of the Medvedev Experience. What’s helped on a deeper level: coaching change-ups, and a newfound self-assurance. Don’t forget: Medvedev is a Slam winner (US Open, 2021), a former world number one, and an ATP Finals winner (2020).

Looking back at 2026, what’s the most significant thing you fixed?

What I was looking for was probably finding confidence in myself. Sometimes that requires changing things, and I wanted to take a bit more responsibility. That was probably the biggest fix I managed to make, closer to the end of the year.

Was that rediscovering your old confidence, or was it something new?

Rediscovering in terms of tennis, yes. But more in terms of… I want to say, it’s more like confidence in a tennis life path. I was listening to my old coaches a lot rather than trusting myself fully. So there was always a bit of back-and-forth. Where do I trust them? Where do I trust myself? And now it’s more about trusting myself fully, and then discussing that trust with the team, if that makes sense.

You’re known for your heated interactions with crowds. At this stage in your career, how much of that is just a reaction versus a choice?

It’s never a choice. It’s always a natural reaction.

Any indulgences you’re looking forward to after the season ends?

I have a photo shoot with Lacoste, and then I’m in the Maldives the next day. I would love to go to Hawaii, I don’t know, or wherever. But it’s way too far from where I live.

Cobolli, 24, had the best year of his young career in 2026. His breakthrough: reaching the final of the French Open, where he lost to Zverev in five sets. In Turin, the Italian naturally received the loudest cheers on the blue carpet. With Sinner absent, he’s the home favorite. Cobolli is well-liked on social media, too; the ATP sometimes jokingly calls him their “admin.” He’s had some struggles with fatigue as the season nears its conclusion, but here’s hoping the Florentine can turn on the jets in Piedmont.

At Wimbledon this year, you made some headlines for doing Matheus Cunha’s “surfing” celebration. Should tennis have more cellys?

No, you know why? Two weeks ago, Cunha beat AS Roma. He beat my team, so I’m really pissed with him. [Laughs] But no… I think [for celebrations] if I have something on my mind, I just do it.

You’re the home favorite in Turin. What does that feel like?

It means a lot to me to play here and to win in front of the Italian crowd. Of course, we miss Jannik a lot. He deserves to be here. So I play for him, for the country, for my team, for myself, and for my family. I just want to play for everybody!

Fils, the 22-year-old Frenchman, struggled in the beginning of the year with a back injury that forced him out of the Australian and French Opens. But he had a strong enough summer to qualify for the year-end tournament, winning his first Masters 1000-level title at the Cincinnati Open. In tennis circles, many believe Fils has the natural talent to eventually challenge the Tour’s stalwart top three Sinner, Alcaraz and Zverev. But he’s already matched them if not exceeded them in aura: in Turin, Fils stepped out on the blue carpet in a full Balenciaga look—he has a deal with the brand—and space-like sunglasses. Audiences went wild.

What are you most happy with regarding your play this year?

I’m serving better, moving better. I mean, I knew I was a great competitor. But I didn’t know I could be that good in competitive moments.

When the season is said and done, what’s going to be your first indulgence?

I’m going on holiday in the States, so I think I’m going to go with… having some ribs.

Tell us a little about working with Balenciaga.

They’re changing [internally] now, I know. But I love the brand. It was kind of a dream when I was a kid to sign one day with a huge fashion label. I feel very comfortable wearing them. It’s a new world for me, but I enjoy it.

Tiafoe, 28, has reached the ATP Finals for the first time. It’s testament to his grit and commitment—what he calls a re-established sense of “showing up” day in and day out. “Big Foe,” as he’s endearingly called, has had a productive year; he won his first 500-level tournament in Halle, reached the semis at the US Open, and recorded the fourth-most match wins of any man on Tour. He was all smiles in an expertly tailored Giorgio Armani double-breasted suit on the blue carpet, too.

You’re having a great season. What are you most happy with, not necessarily numbers wise, but in terms of your play?

I think I just found a flow state. I found this peace, and I’m showing up every day. I think sometimes you try to figure out this whole thing of how to get to X to Y to Z, or how to do X, Y and Z together. And it’s kind of just: you show up, man.

Every day looks different, but you just go out there and give your best and be okay with the result. Every time I’ve been able to lay it out there and lost, I was cool with it, rather than having regret that I could have done a little more. I was also focused on my preparation, and once preparation meets opportunity, you get the results.

During the long season, what was a favorite memory away from the court?

I saw the Chris Brown and Usher concert in D.C. and it was out of control. One of the biggest things was getting to meet Matthew McConaughey at the US Open. He’s a special individual.

What are you looking forward to during the break?

Jodar, the youngest man in the Turin field, has been lightning in a bottle this year. He broke men’s tennis’s record for the quickness of his ascent: from his tour debut to hitting the top 10, Jodar needed only 296 days. With that in mind, the Spaniard can be forgiven for speed bumps along the way: a highly publicized outburst at a ball kid during the Shanghai Masters, and a gamesmanship debate around equipment changes. He’s among the youngest of tennis’s new guard—a quarter-generation behind Alcaraz and Sinner, even—and his future feels bright.

So much has been said about the speed of your year, and how quickly you’ve risen. Is there anything you wish would slow down?

Well, I think how it works is that if you do well on Tour, you’re going to have more expectations. That’s something you just have to deal with when you’re doing well. Not every day you’re going to be in a happy mood. But at the end of the day, you just have to handle the situation in the best way possible, and keep focusing on and trying to get better at the game.

What do you do with your limited free time?

I think I’d say spending some time at home and doing some activities in Madrid. Probably, the thing I want to do most is go to the Bernabéu to watch Real Madrid. That’s when I disconnect completely from tennis, and focus on the football game.

#6648. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6646. “It’s Crazy That We’re Allowed to Be Doing This”—Emily Dawn Long on her Limited-Edition Merch for Club Kid

Jordan Firstman’s film Club Kid is getting rave reviews and plenty of early awards-season buzz, not only for its tenderly expressed coming-of-age storyline, but for its vivid depiction of downtown New York’s contemporary creative milieu. To wit, Firstman’s character Peter is the kind of guy who lives in trendy Dimes Square, parties all night in Brooklyn, and wears the de facto uniform of cool kids who loiter around Canal Street in Chinatown: a screen-printed T-shirt from the designer Emily Dawn Long.

Indeed, Dawn Long’s popular “Take Off Your Clothes” tee makes its own cameo in the A24 movie, which tells the story of a hard-partying gay club promoter’s discovery that he fathered a son and is now responsible for him. To take the onscreen relationship a step further, the designer is dropping a line of merch to promote the film.

“The film is so quintessential New York,” Dawn Long said in a phone call. “And I’m sure you’ve heard everyone’s comparing it to Big Daddy or Uptown Girl, but it is its own thing now—it’s iconic.”

The T-shirts will be offered in limited edition quantities at a pop-up space hosted at a classic souvenir shop in Chinatown on Thursday, November 19, and then via the A24 website on November 24. To coincide with the film’s father-son theme, they come in adult and children’s sizes. As is her wont, the EDL shirts are offered in short supply: only 50 at the pop-up and 130 for the website, and will cost $150. Expect a feeding frenzy.

“I obviously knew that my T-shirt was in the movie,” the designer said. “And Jordan and I had been riffing in DMs, and he was, like, ‘We got to get you on the merch.’” Dawn Long had an existing relationship with A24 from when she designed a T-shirt for Zendaya and Robert Pattinson’s movie The Drama, earlier this year. “A24 and I were both on the same page, and they just let me do whatever I wanted, which was so nice. I’m obsessed with them. We’re fam.”

Printed on vintage tees from the 1950s to the ’80s, the EDL Club Kid T-shirt features a reference to one of Dawn Long’s favorite parts of the film, in which Firstman’s character wakes up his son to show him the New York skyline as they ride over the bridge into the city, telling him, “It’s like this every time.” The phrase, along with a hand-drawn rendering of downtown’s cityscape, is printed on the front of the shirt, and the film’s title is on the back.

That moment spoke to Dawn Long’s own feelings about the life and business she’s built here. “It’s insane that we live in New York and we get to see this,” she said, referring to magic moments like seeing the city skyline. “It’s insane that we live in New York, first of all. And for me, this film and everything that’s going on in my life right now … It’s crazy that we’re allowed to be doing this, and building this world. I resonated so much with that line in the film in terms of what I’ve built and how long I’ve been in the city. I have chills right now.”

Indeed, it’s been a banner year for the designer: two ready-to-wear collections, two A24 collaborations, two award nominations, one of them resulting in a runner-up win from the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund. It also aligns with a new concept that she’s working on, EDL Studios, which allows her to pursue creative ventures outside of her fashion practice—consulting, costume design, film, and more.

“At the New York screening, I was able to sit in a theater with 300 of my closest creative friends downtown, and then for them to see my T-shirt on the screen, and then they’re sitting in Dimes Square drinking a watermelon slushie—I don’t want to give everything away, but it’s everything that we … it’s so real. The film is so real. I think everyone who lives our life, all the downtown people, I think we all saw that, and it makes you cry. It makes you laugh. It’s everything.”

#6644. Robert Pattinson’s Hair Is Already 007 Material

Whether you like it or not (or placed bets on Kalshi), Robert Pattinson is our next James Bond. During the years-long process in casting 007, we used our best detective skills to narrow down the field to who would join His Majesty’s Secret Service. And if you were going by hair type alone, well, Pattinson makes a rather compelling case.

Let’s review the canon for a moment. In the 1957 novel From Russia, with Love, Bond creator Ian Fleming describes the spy’s mane thusly: “The hair was black, parted on the left, and carelessly brushed so that a thick black comma fell down over the right eyebrow.”

Pattinson’s hair might be naturally light brown, but a darker ‘do is hardly out of the question for the actor’s upcoming transformation. For his turn as Bruce Wayne in The Batman, he dyed his hair to a darker, almost pitch-black hue. The rest of Fleming’s description fits the actor nicely, particularly the bit about being “carelessly brushed.” In real life, the actor’s hair is rarely anything approaching immaculate. Even at more formal engagements, it tends to retain a certain studied dishevelment, with stray strands escaping an otherwise respectable comb-through. Fleming’s famous “comma,” after all, isn’t a carefully sculpted curl. It’s simply a lock of hair allowed to fall where it pleases, which just so happens to be very on trend in 2026.

We got our first glimpse of the 40-year-old actor taking on the role in a video posted by the official James Bond X account where he’s seen stepping out of the shadows pointing a gun at something (or someone) just outside the frame. It’s hard to tell whether the golden lighting is playing tricks on his hair color, but the accompanying promotional image certainly seems to suggest a shade of black. Plus, his hair’s parted on the correct side.

It’s worth noting that Daniel Craig’s casting as Bond was initially met with considerable resistance, much of it centered on one detail: He’s blonde. Fleming’s Bond, after all, was famously dark-haired, and Craig represented a departure from the physical template established by the novels and previous screen incarnations. We know how that turned out. Craig went on to deliver one of the most celebrated interpretations of 007, proving that a little deviation from the source material needn’t be a deal-breaker.

Pattinson will still need to prove himself to be agile in a tuxedo, nimble behind the wheel, and thirsty for a martini or two, but one thing’s sure: He's got the hair down pat.

#6643. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.
