#6641. 5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

Let's just say the health department had a few notes.

Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day. Sometimes, going out really pays off. It saves you time in the kitchen, cuts down on effort, and most importantly, lets you relax while someone else does the heavy lifting. Many families turn to fast food when they want an easy, quick meal or when time is of the essence. But where you go can really make a difference.

Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns. But beyond the macros, another factor to consider is cleanliness.

Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location. You may have seen headlines concerning less-than-stellar hygiene reports stemming from certain fast food locations over the years. Kitchen cleanliness is paramount to food safety (just look at this year’s Cyclospora outbreak), and some chains have faced more than their share of troubling headlines. Here are five fast food chains with a disappointing history of food safety issues.

I hate to break it to burrito-with-extra-guac fans, but Chipotle has a history of high-profile food safety issues. The company paid $25 million to resolve criminal charges related to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks between 2015 and 2018. According to the documents, Chipotle was charged with "adulterating food in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act," resulting in the largest criminal fine ever imposed in a food safety case at the time.

Records cited at least five foodborne illness outbreaks across several states, including incidents involving norovirus, that sickened more than 1,100 people. These outbreaks "primarily stemmed from store-level employees' failure to follow company food safety protocols." Personally, I'd rather have a side of hot sauce than a side of stomach flu.

In February 2025, a Massachusetts store was cited for nine core health code violations—including insufficiently cleaned ice machines, improperly stored produce, and missing thermometers in a walk-in cooler—along with one priority foundation violation. Such issues can raise concerns about food safety and sanitation.

In 2022, a health inspector described another location in the state as "very unclean." A year before that, workers at a Springfield, Missouri, location staged a walkout over poor working conditions. A subsequent health inspection found that "the floors in the food preparation area (especially under equipment and near drains), walk-in refrigerator and freezer, and dry storage areas were not clean," leading to a follow-up inspection. (Don't even get us started on some of the issues found overseas!)

Sorry, chalupa lovers. Taco Bell has also faced its share of food safety concerns over the years. Reports include an E. coli outbreak along the East Coast in 2006 resulting in 71 illnesses (53 of whom were hospitalized), two Salmonella outbreaks in 2010 affecting at least 155 people across 21 states, and a hepatitis A outbreak in 2000 that sickened 23 people and hospitalized 15.

More recently, a customer’s viral video appeared to show a Taco Bell kitchen strewn with food, garbage, and old boxes near food prep areas. Some commenters suggested that it was filmed during rush hour while the restaurant was understaffed and that employees were too busy to clean. Still, it's not a great look for in-store hygiene.

Big Mac lovers, look away. The Golden Arches have faced numerous lawsuits over food safety issues over the years, including a class action suit (plus several personal injury suits) filed in 2024 following a multistate E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounders. The outbreak ultimately sickened 104 people and killed one, with investigators identifying slivered onions as the likely source of contamination.

The Boston City Department of Inspectional Services found nearly 125 violations at seven different McDonald's locations between 2018 and 2019—everything from mismanaged storage to mold, rat droppings, and even live cockroaches. Complaints and lawsuits have also alleged undercooked meat and foodborne illnesses caused by cross-contamination.

Wendy's locations have racked up numerous health code violations, too (one Las Vegas restaurant in particular drew 27 demerits in a 2019 inspection for dirty soda nozzles, food left on the floor, raw food cross-contamination, and more). A 2023 "Dirty Dining" segment called out a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, location with an inspection that found insects all over the restaurant.

Perhaps most concerningly, a Michigan family filed a lawsuit in 2024 alleging their daughter developed hemolytic uremic syndrome following an E. coli infection they attributed to food from Wendy's. According to the lawsuit, the illness caused permanent brain damage, kidney failure, a seizure disorder, and other lasting health problems. Inspectors had found the location in violation of 17 different health and food codes just days before the family's visit, including moldy food, spoiled produce, dirty surfaces, and water leaks.

Even with these histories of violations, not every location should make you rethink your dining options—many restaurants are up to code and clean. While all this information is enough to convince me to stick to home-cooked meals for the rest of my life, I suggest checking your local restaurant's latest health inspection report before deciding whether or not to visit your chain of choice.

#6638. 12 Todd Snyder Gifts That Even Menswear Snobs Will Appreciate

There’s a certain kind of guy who’s impossible to shop for. Pleasing him might seem hopeless, but there’s a cheat code, and it’s called Todd Snyder. The brand has spent more than a decade quietly perfecting the American wardrobe: the sweaters, cords and jackets that look like they’ve been in his closet forever, only better.

Consider this your shortcut. I went shopping the way I always do and pulled the Todd Snyder gifts I’d be thrilled to unwrap. All that’s left for you to do is pick one and maybe hide the receipt, since he won’t be needing it. Fair warning: there’s a good chance you’ll end up buying something for yourself, too. ‘Tis the season.

A barn jacket gets an upgrade. Flocked denim gives it a velvety, suede-like surface, and the leather collar adds a nice bit of contrast. It’s rugged enough for a weekend upstate and polished enough for a swanky dinner in the city.

Cords are back in a big way, and it’s not just vintage obsessives wearing them: they’ve become the go-to cold-weather pant for guys who want something softer than denim. This straight leg camel pair is an easy way to add some warmth and texture to his wardrobe. He’ll wear them just like his favorite 501’s.

Colorful flecks of Donegal yarn take a simple black beanie somewhere much more interesting. It’s cashmere too, so he’ll actually want to wear it instead of stashing it away in a coat pocket in case of emergency.

Supple leather on the outside and cashmere on the inside: this is a cold-weather essential done right. It’s a grown-up upgrade over the gloves he’s been losing every winter since college.

An olive wool bomber with a plush shearling collar hits the sweet spot between a flight jacket and a proper winter coat. It works with everything from cords to tailored trousers. Bonus points since it will look better every season after some wear and tear..

For the guy who lives in dark denim, black cords are a smart switch. They’re just as versatile, much cozier, and dress up easier than you’d think.

Brushed cotton turns the camp collar into a fall shirt. The muted plaid and relaxed fit make it a great layering piece over a tee, or something to wear buttoned up on its own when the heat’s cranked indoors.

The waffle knit gives this navy sweater a depth and texture that a flat knit can’t match. It’s understated in the best way: the kind of piece that gets compliments without trying too hard.

Joshua Ellis has been weaving cloth in Yorkshire since the 18th century, and it shows. This bold red tartan is the coat accessory that does the most work, brightening up even the gloomiest January commute.

Pleats, a roomy leg and a flecked silk-Donegal fabric from Italy make this the dress pant for guys who don’t like dress pants. It’s sharp enough for the office party and relaxed enough to wear with a sweater the next morning.

#6637. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6636. Kate Middleton and Prince William Turn to Bollywood Fashion Royalty in Mumbai

The Prince and Princess of Wales’s second official visit to India reached its high point today, as William hosted the sixth annual Earthshot Prize ceremony in Mumbai. The event, which awards £1 million ($1.3 million) each to five winners tackling the world’s most pressing environmental challenges, was held on the subcontinent in recognition of the fact that it has offered more winners and finalists than anywhere else since the initiative was founded in 2020. It also marked Catherine’s first appearance at the awards since Boston in 2022, with the couple marking the occasion with a rare red-carpet (or, in this case, green) photo call.

And while the Princess’s wardrobe over the past few days has largely consisted of her tried-and-tested staples—a Roksanda dress here, an Edeline Lee suit there—tonight was the night to pull out all the stops. Catherine chose a hand-embroidered anarkali of sindoori-red georgette by New Delhi-based designer Mahima Mahajan, which she paired with a necklace and earrings from Queen Elizabeth II’s emerald tassel suite and a burgundy velvet Prada minaudière.

William similarly paid tribute to Indian design, wearing a black bandhgala by Mumbai-based Manish Malhotra—one of Indian cinema’s most influential costume designers, who later turned his hand to couture—and the man behind Simone Ashley’s custom lehenga for the evening. Also in attendance were actors Sonam Kapoor and Alia Bhatt, as well as the three remaining members of Take That.

Beyond today’s engagements, though, which included the inaugural Children’s Earthshot Awards—for which Catherine rewore a blue linen Gabriela Hearst suit last seen at Wimbledon earlier this year—the Prince and Princess will spend the remainder of their visit celebrating the deep cultural ties between Britain and India through cricket, film, and, of course, fashion. All while shining a light on the country’s remarkable environmental progress. (India reached its target of having 50% of its installed electricity capacity come from non-fossil fuel sources five years ahead of schedule, while its solar capacity has grown more than 50-fold in little over a decade.)

“Too often, the world’s emerging economies are presented with false choices: growth or the environment; prosperity or protection,” as William told a crowd of changemakers at the Earthshot Prize’s 2026 Impact Assembly yesterday. “But India shows us a different picture. A picture full of color, complexity, and possibility.”

#6635. Taco Bell Is Expanding Its Cantina Menu With Six New Steak Creations

Your usual order could be getting some serious competition.

Taste-testing Taco Bell's new FLAMIN' HOT menu items should've bought my stomach at least a few days off. Instead, the chain has already given me another reason to start thinking about my next order.

Taco Bell is testing a new carne asada protein across six menu items, giving its Cantina lineup another round of additions. But of course, there's a catch. As of November 12, it's only available in Nashville, Tennessee, and the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. So if you're lucky enough to live in either market, congratulations. I'll just be over here drooling over the pictures.

The steak itself sounds pretty different from what Taco Bell currently serves. It gets a marinade with citrus and savory seasonings before being cooked sous vide, then seared and cut into small chunks. Taco Bell says it's going for a deeper, more grilled flavor, and rather than giving it one or two menu appearances, the chain has come up with six ways to try it.

The Cantina Carne Asada Chalupa Lime Bowl is probably the most loaded of the bunch, piling steak, rice, black beans, guacamole, pico de gallo, cheese, and purple cabbage slaw together with chile-lime seasoned Chalupa Chips. There's also a Cantina Carne Asada Burrito, which wraps the meat in a new Sonoran-style flour tortilla with lettuce, cabbage, cheese, pico, and Spicy Ranch Sauce before getting grilled.

If tacos are more your speed, there are three options. The Cantina Carne Asada Crispy Taco comes in a fried corn shell with cheese grilled onto the outside, while the Cantina Carne Asada Soft Taco uses that same new flour tortilla with cabbage slaw and Spicy Ranch. Then there's the smaller Cantina Carne Asada Street Chalupa, which has a fried shell lined with crispy cheese.

Rounding things out is the Cantina Carne Asada Rolled Quesadilla, stuffed with steak, a three-cheese blend, and Spicy Ranch before being grilled and sliced. All six items also come with an Avocado Verde Salsa packet.

The rollout follows Taco Bell's push to give its Cantina menu more attention, including the slow-roasted chicken that's already made its way into items like the Cantina Chicken Mexican Pizza. This latest test could eventually put carne asada on the permanent menu, although there's no word yet on whether it'll expand beyond those two markets.

#6634. All About Amanda Seyfried’s Estranged Husband, Thomas Sadoski

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Amanda Seyfried has moved on from her days as Sophie in the Mamma Mia franchise (at least for now), and in 2021, she earned her first Oscar nod, a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nomination in the 2020 film Mank.

When it comes to her personal life, Seyfried is pretty private. But for years, she had a big love in her life: Thomas Sadoski.

In 2013, Seyfried spoke to ELLE about her love life and the importance of sexual attraction in a relationship.

“Everybody I’ve dated I’ve been sexually attracted to immediately,” she said then. “Sparks don’t grow—your vagina doesn’t become more inclined to wanting someone just because you’re around them.” At the time, she spoke about the person ELLE identified as her “crush”: “[He’s] someone separate from my industry life—I’ve known him since he was 16….I picture him as the father of my children all the time. But it is a fantasy right now.”

Later in 2013, Seyfried ended up dating actor Justin Long, but the two split in September 2015.

Seyfried and Sadoski met on the set of their first film The Way We Get By (2009), and by March 2016, they were a confirmed item. They were engaged by September 2016 and by early 2017, they were expecting their first child, their daughter, Nina.

In 2020, they shared that they had welcomed a son, Thomas. Their love story lasted for years. Ultimately, the pair announced their separation in September 2026 while reaffirming their commitment to each other as friends and co-parents.

On September 15, the two actors revealed they had privately separated some time ago after nine years of marriage. They said in a statement to People, “We have been separated for a while, and it’s proven to be the right move for us and our family unit. We’ve got each other forever—and it’s GOOD.”

Per WWD, Sadoski was born in Texas. When he was 4 years old, he and his parents moved to College Station, Texas, and by the time he was in high school, he knew he wanted to pursue acting. He tried college for three months: “Things didn’t really work out for me, and it didn’t really work out for them, so we had a mutual parting of ways.” He moved to New York, where he studied at Circle in the Square Theatre School.

Sadoski has spent much of his career onstage and got a Tony nomination for Reasons to Be Pretty (2009).

“For most of my career, I’ve held on really tightly trying to figure out what the hell I’m supposed to do next and controlling everything,” he told WWD. “I’ve gotten to a point in my life where I think that my job is to just follow the path that gets laid out in front of me.”

Sadoski is best known for his role as Jon Keefer in The Newsroom (2012–2014). You can also find him in John Wick (2014) and John Wick: Chapter 2 (2017), the TV series The Slap (2015), and the series Life in Places (2015–2019). Here’s his full IMDb for more.

Before Seyfried, Sadoski was married to Kimberly Hope for what was reportedly eight years. The two split in 2015.

In 2018, Seyfried told PorterEdit that when she met Sadoski while working on their Off-Broadway play The Way We Get By, she noticed how respectful he was of his then-wife. She said they were friends at first, and when she had panic attacks onstage, he helped her through them.

“We were both in bad relationships,” she said. She added that they “never flirted, never disrespected his wife. That was another reason why I thought, later on, that I could marry him.”

When they were both out of their respective relationships, Seyfried suggested Sadoski for her love interest in her 2017 movie, The Last Word with Shirley MacLaine. It was then that their romantic relationship grew. “It was amazing,” Seyfried said. “It felt healthy and freeing and clean. We can tell the story without any guilt.”Seyfried and Sadoski were married just before they welcomed their daughter. “I really wanted to have rings on in the hospital, you know?” she told PorterEdit. “And what if something goes wrong, and he’s not legally my husband?” The magazine reports that she bought a dress at Free People, they got married in Topanga, California, and then they went to a favorite neighborhood café on Sunset Boulevard, Cheebo.

In 2017, Seyfried said Sadoski was fired from a job after he publicly supported Jessica Walter, who claimed she was “verbally harrassed” by her Arrested Development co-star Jeffrey Tambor.

“Here’s a somewhat recent post from my husband who, in return for standing beside a badass woman who’d recently been bullied, recently lost out on a job because of this,” she wrote. “I’d rather speak up and lose out. Integrity, ladies and gentlemen.”

“This is Jessica Walter. She is a national goddamned treasure. It was an honor and a privilege to work with her. I don’t give a fuck who you think you are or how good you think you are or how awesome you think your buddy/daddy is: screaming at someone isn’t ‘part of the business.’ It’s bullshit. It’s unhinged bullshit behavior and it has NEVER been acceptable. It wasn’t cool in the ’70s or ’80s or whenthefuckever you ‘came up.’ It was bullshit then, it is bullshit now. And excusing that kind of behavior is pathetic. Just pathetic. I worked in shitty greasy-spoon kitchens growing up: it wasn’t acceptable behavior THERE and most of us were on HEAVY DRUGS. It certainly isn’t acceptable for some man-baby millionaire to do on a cozy ass tv show set. And it is even less acceptable for his male cast-mates to excuse it away IN FRONT OF THE PERSON THAT IT HAPPENED TO....(wait for it)....WHILE SHE IS TRYING TO EXPLAIN HOW TRAUMATIZING THE EXPERIENCE WAS. What in the halfpenny fuck is happening?!”

Back in 2017, Sadoski was admittedly “terrified” of becoming a parent, but he’s since embraced the role. After the birth of his first daughter, he spoke to Fatherly about his favorite part of being a dad: “When my daughter discovers something new. That’s the coolest thing in the world. That chokes me up every time she does it.”

Sadoski and Seyfried are ambassadors for the nonprofit War Child, which assists children living in areas of conflict. During the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, the couple led a huge donation campaign in support of the charity.

“The unfortunate reality is that there are people in this world who can literally not afford for the rest of us to turn a blind eye, and I don’t mean afford in an economic sense, but I mean their lives are literally at stake,” Sadoski told People. “That’s sort of why we’re finding ourselves drawn specifically to this organization in this moment.”

Sadoski added that fatherhood has inspired him to continue supporting War Child. “I think all parents should be able to relate to the suffering of innocent children. It’s just something that’s deeply, inherently part of who we are—that we want to protect our little ones.”

Seyfried recognized the milestone on Instagram, where she shared photos of her and Sadoski with the caption “Five fucking years.”

Seyfried and Sadoski shared the screen in Apple TV+ series The Crowded Room. The anthology’s first season is inspired by Daniel Keyes’s novel The Minds of Billy Milligan. Filming took place in 2022, and paparazzi managed to snap some photos of Seyfried and Sadoski on set together.

The couple ultimately attended the premiere together in June 2023, marking a rare joint event for them:

Seyfried rarely shares photos of Sadoski on Instagram, choosing instead to keep posts focused on her work and animals she raises with him on their upstate New York farm. She gave a little look into her world on Jan. 1, 2024, writing, “God I am concerned and anxious about this new year but thankful so many things can be true at once. I also feel lucky that my starting off point is right here with my family (not pictured except for my dad and the mountains I call home).”

Seyfried told Grazia in 2022 that “up until a few years ago I was working so much, and I was worried that if I gave myself a break, I wouldn’t be able to get back into it. But now I have a husband who, like me, loves his work and two children that need somebody to be with them. Because of this I only accept roles that I consider impossible to miss out on.”

In a rare public appearance, the couple attended the November 19 opening night of the Avett Brothers Broadway musical Swept Away at the Longacre Theatre in New York City.

In an interview with Who What Wear in December 2025, Seyfried shared a snippet about her personal life at home while reflecting on growing older.

“I know life is harder the older you get, but I also know that I’m pretty prepped because I’ve done a lot of work in the decade of my 30s,” she explained. “I’ve done a lot of couples therapy. I’ve done a lot of therapy alone. I’ve had insane amounts of conversations with psychologists and friends who are psychologists that I feel like I have a lot of self-knowledge. It’s not everything, but it certainly goes a long way.”

While attending the 2026 Critics Choice Awards on January 4, Seyfried spoke to E! about her husband’s praise of her performance in The Testament of Ann Lee. Sadoski had emailed E!’s reporter Justin Sylvester about different aspects of her work in the film, writing, “which she did brilliantly,” seven times in the note.

“What a sweetheart,” Seyfried said. “Thank you for doing that.”

Seyfried and Sadoski are both actors, and in her January Vogue digital cover story, she detailed how they navigate their careers while raising their family. “[He] sacrifices a lot for me,” she said. “He also knows that, in this moment, the opportunities I’m being afforded are insane.” She paused before adding, “I do say no a lot.”

She also revealed how her children—one in third grade and the other in kindergarten at the time—view her job. “My world’s moving so fast, and there’s so many things I have to do each day, and there’s no way I can express what I’m doing,” she said. “I just make very clear every day: ‘I really would rather be home with you.’”

She assures them, too, that she loves her career: “I’m having a great time, right? It’s not painful suffering.”

On September 15, Seyfried and Sadoski announced that they had separated after nine years of marriage. In a joint statement to People, the couple revealed that they had been living apart for some time.

“We have been separated for a while, and it’s proven to be the right move for us and our family unit. We’ve got each other forever—and it’s GOOD,” they said.

On November 8, Seyfried shared an Instagram Story featuring a post from divorce consultant Olivia Howell.

“The most radical thing we can do is make divorce boring. Make it normal. Make it accessible. Because the system thrives on confusion and stigma, on making you believe you’re the first one to ever walk this road. But when divorce becomes just another life transition—like a wedding, like a graduation—the patriarchy loses one of its most effective weapons,” the post read.

Seyfried then posted a black-and-white photo of herself and Sadoski hugging and smiling, tagging her estranged husband.

On November 15, Seyfried attended the opening night of Downstate on Broadway, which Sadoski stars in, and posed with him at the after-party in a sweet show of support for her ex.

#6633. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6632. Joaquin Phoenix Wasn’t Thinking About 'Her' When He Filmed This Intelligent Eyewear Campaign

It feels like a scene out of a sci-fi movie: Joaquin Phoenix is standing across from me, instructing me to speak into his eyeglasses in a foreign language.

“Let’s see what happens,” the Oscar winner says. “It could be any language.”

The idea we’re testing here is whether the glasses Phoenix is wearing—a dark-rimmed pair from the South Korean luxury eyewear brand Gentle Monster’s new Intelligent Eyewear collection—could live-translate these words into English. This is one of the glasses’ capabilities the actor was most delighted to discover while he was shooting their campaign film directed by another Oscar winner, Jonathan Glazer. The glasses were crafted in partnership with Google and Samsung, and feature AI-powered technology.

Joaquin Phoenix in the Jonathan Glazer-directed campaign spot.

The last time Phoenix appeared in a fashion campaign, it was 1997 and he was modeling moody suits for Prada. This time around, he stars in the Glazer-directed spot that Phoenix says was partially inspired by the 1969 documentary Salesman, in which vendors travel across New England selling Bibles. In the Gentle Monster ad, Phoenix’s character—who has an intense, quasi-manic energy—ventures into an unnamed hotel, where he falls into a deep sleep and meets colorful, large creatures at the end of a hallway. (One might even call them…Gentle Monsters.) Per a press release, the “intelligent eyewear becomes his way of understanding their language and communicating with them, opening up unexpected possibilities for connection.”

Phoenix had wanted to work with Glazer for a long time. “I’ve known him for years, and when we all approached him, we came up with this really interesting and offbeat idea that just [had so] much mood. He just gets super excited and inspired,” the actor says. During the shoot, the Zone of Interest filmmaker kept the camera rolling for prolonged periods of time, encouraging Phoenix to harness different emotions. A moment in the ad might last for “30 seconds, but we shot for 15 minutes,” he explains. “A whole range of things are happening in those 15 minutes, things that we were trying.”

In an email, Glazer reiterated that he was glad to have had a reason to work with Phoenix: “The first image I had was him asleep, maybe dreaming, with the glasses all wonky across his face. The rest kind of grew from there,” the director said.

When I meet the actor last Wednesday at 23 Wall Street in Manhattan—where Gentle Monster has staged an enormous activation for the Intelligent Eyewear launch, complete with fake horses with wagging tails and huge surreal sculptures—it’s hard not to think about his turn in the 2013 film Her, one of the most prophetic AI movies of our time. In the Spike Jonze near-future drama, Phoenix’s character, Theodore Twombly, chats with and subsequently falls for an AI-powered operating system voiced by Scarlett Johansson. If 2011’s Contagion foreshadowed the COVID-19 pandemic, Her’s depiction of chatbots feels eerily similar to the world of ChatGPT dots, Meta Muses, Claude Duets, and Gemini Sparks that we’re beginning to grow accustomed to.

Phoenix and his partner, actress Rooney Mara, wearing Intelligent Eyewear at the Gentle Monster event in Manhattan.

When I ask Phoenix if filming the campaign made him think of Her, he shrugs. “I wasn’t. It seems like I should have,” he says. “It’s funny because I think that sometimes films have more of, maybe, an impact on the people that view them than for me, but I hadn’t thought about that. Somebody just made a joke about it actually, and I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re right.’”

Phoenix, who most recently starred in 2025’s politically tinged neo-Western Eddington, leaves on his Intelligent Eyewear glasses—which are Gemini-embedded, sleek, and thick-rimmed—while we speak.

“The thing is,” he says, “I’m not even aware that I’m wearing them.”

#6631. Inside the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Premiere, Where the Odds Were in Everyone’s Favor

On Monday evening, Lincoln Center was temporarily transformed into the Capitol of Panem for the highly anticipated world premiere of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. The purple carpet, flanked by flames, was thronged with fans cheering as three generations of Hunger Games stars reconvened for a long-awaited reunion.

The dress theme for the evening, Make Them Remember You, encouraged attendees to dress in vintage-leaning silhouettes and rich textures, and to embrace a touch of theatricality. It was an assignment that the cast and attendees alike took seriously, donning looks that were hard to forget. Elle Fanning and Elizabeth Banks took on a battle of the Effies, with each actress indulging in an avant-garde approach to the mood board. McKenna Grace’s Mockingjay gown came complete with wings as a nod to Katniss’s costume from Catching Fire. The horde of onlookers surrounding the area also displayed their own interpretations of Capitol-inspired garb.

As the final guests were ushered into Alice Tully Hall, director Francis Lawrence invited what he described as “one of the most impressive casts in cinema” to rise one by one. Each familiar face from the original films—including Woody Harrelson, Josh Hutcherson, and Jennifer Lawrence—was greeted with thunderous applause. Francis even invited the audience to wish his assistant a quick “Happy Birthday” before the lights dimmed and the room erupted into more cheers as each member of the cast appeared on screen.

Following the screening, guests journeyed across Central Park to the historic Metropolitan Club for an opulent after-party. Indeed, the space felt reminiscent of the ball held in Catching Fire as people sauntered into a marble room complete with a sizable ice sculpture carved in the symbol of the film: a spiked sun rising over a songbird and snake. Attendees were also spoiled with their choice of Haymitch-style cocktails: a sweet floral vodka cocktail named “The Rascal” or the spicy, tequila-infused “All Fire.”

The stairs were decorated with extravagant floral arrangements, nodding to the flowers seen in the film’s arena, while mirrors on the wall were inscribed with quotes like “All machines can be broken” or “I love you like all fire.” Flags of Panem hung below a balcony filled with what appeared to be Capitol citizens inspecting guests from above. As servers strolled through the many decorated rooms distributing hors d’oeuvres of tuna tartare and ceviche, guests were truly made feel as if they were transported straight to the heart of the action.

The DJ played a wide variety of dance floor-filling tunes while decked out in full Effie Trinket attire, much to the delight of stars who’d arrived to join their fans. Some of the cast had changed into more comfortable clothing to relax and unwind—no one more so than Joseph Zada, who arrived in the infamous set of pajamas Woody Harrelson wore to the premiere of Mockingjay — Part 2. Meanwhile, Elle Fanning opted for a full in-character transformation as she bopped and laughed alongside her sister, Dakota, switching into a latex bodysuit and a brand-new metallic purple bob.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters on Friday, November 20.

#6628. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6627. More Men Are Getting Penis Filler Than You Think

In Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life, Eric Idle sings, “Isn’t it awfully nice to have a penis?”

But, according to the new documentary Manhood, the feeling is not universal. In the film men look between their legs with nothing but shame, regret, and self-pity. The subjects’ members—particularly their perceived smallness—are problems to be solved.

Enter Bill Moore, a Dallas-based med spa operator, whose PhalloFILL penis filler procedure can supposedly add meaningful girth without surgery. The film follows his eager patients, including Ruben, an aspiring comedian and father of five, and David, a gay ex-OnlyFans star whose penis was botched by a previous filler procedure.

Director Daniel Lombroso spent years filming Moore and his patients, , slowly building trust until they opened up and (quite literally) bared all to the camera. Watching Manhood, it is clear that getting penis filler is never just about being bigger. To the patients, this procedure represents an escape from middle-aged ennui, a break from a difficult past, or a life preserver for a sinking marriage. The fast-growing, nationwide penis enlargement industry is happy to help, at $6,000 worth of filler injections per dick.

GQ sat down with Lombroso, fresh off Manhood’s breakout premiere at SXSW, to find out how he convinced a male enhancement spa to let him film inside, why the penis filler industry is booming, and who’s already getting rich off it. Manhood is available to stream on November 17.

Daniel Lombroso: That’s a great question. I think the most squeamish moment is Ruben bombing at stand-up on stage, more so than the botched penises. But, it’s funny. In real life, I am incredibly squeamish. It’s hard for me to look at surgery. It’s hard for me to look at someone using the bathroom or throwing up. There’s something about when you’re making a film, when you’re behind a lens, it gives you a level of separation. It’s sort of a mediator between you and the world. I shoot a lot of my own work, and on this project I shot some and worked with an incredible cinematographer, Vittoria Campaner. So there’s something about having that intermediary between you and the world that gave me comfort and helped me get through it. The hardest moment was the penile reconstruction, but we did not put most of that in the film.

Yeah. David, the person who gets botched, had his penis fully degloved like a banana. They had to peel back the layers and scoop out the permanent dermal filler that’s living in nodes in the shaft of his penis. That was one of the most gruesome experiences of my life. We decided to spare the audience that horror. And David is okay, thank God.

It’s tough. That was the toughest one. I also used to work at The New Yorker and I made a film on the Brazilian butt lift, which was similarly gruesome. I mean, that is one of the most gruesome cosmetic surgeries in the world. It’s a fat transfer procedure. They suck out the fat from where you don’t want it, your stomach or your arms, and stick it in where you do want it, your butt.

I filmed and watched that, and edited it on my New Yorker computer in The New Yorker newsroom for six months, and I would see David Remnick walk by and be curious and confused, and continue with his day. So it’s not my first time being in those environments, and they are hard for me personally. But something about making a film, it just gives you this level of separation that helps you get through it.

I think it’s important for people to be braced with these images. It is shocking to me how difficult it is for people to look at just a regular penis, especially straight men and older straight men. Gen X and above feel like they’re getting hit with an atomic bomb when they see a penis. Younger men, queer men, and women have always been fine, but I cannot tell you how many pitch meetings we went into where, like, the female executives love the film, the queer executives love the film. Then it gets to a straight guy at the top who is hit with one dick, and certainly one botched dick, and is out. Or he has to make sure on the record that everyone knows that he doesn’t have that problem. That happened in quite a few meetings. So I think it’s important to confront people with those images.

My business partner Kerry [Mack] joked that this is the first time I don’t have a Holocaust connection. We were looking for a penis enlargement-to-Holocaust connection, but we couldn’t find one.

I started this film three and a half years ago. At the time, we were all inundated with stories about the male loneliness epidemic. It felt almost like a cliché. I know you’ve covered it super well, and I’m sure we both grew up on Vice. It’s also something that’s really hard to show, because you don’t necessarily want to… “Condone” is the wrong word. “Platform” is also the wrong word. I hate when that word is used. But it is a cultural phenomenon that needs to be covered and discussed, and it’s very hard to do it.

I couldn’t really find a good way. Around that time, I read about the explosion in penile enhancement, and specifically, penile girth enhancement. I was less interested in penis enlargement than using that as a canvas to explore this burgeoning cultural discussion. So I called, like, every urologist in the country doing versions of it. There’s the Penuma, which is a really gnarly implant.

Yeah, Ava Kofman wrote a great story about the Penuma, which, like, pokes through and makes you bleed. I spoke to the creator of the Penuma. I spoke to people doing more permanent dermal fillers. And all of them were reticent. You know, the way I make films is I embed for many years in these environments. When I made [the alt-right documentary] White Noise, I lived on the road with white nationalists for three or four years. And for this film, I lived in clinics for two years.

So I had to find a practitioner who was open. And finally I got to Bill Moore, this very classic American character. He’s a businessman, not a doctor, and he said, “Come on down to Dallas.” So I booked a one-way ticket, and I would just sit in the waiting room and introduce myself to different patients. With a story like this, it’s really the only way. These men are so ashamed, they’re not gonna open up to a random reporter who calls them. So I knew I would have to put in a lot of time. I would just sit there, usually with my camera in a different room, and introduce myself. Sometimes they’d say, “Come back,” some would say no, some would say yes.

On those first two shoots, I met a megachurch pastor getting his penis enlarged. He’s very famous, and I cannot say who it is. A border patrol agent in the film. A father of five, an OnlyFans star, someone with brain cancer.

Super hard, and I try to be very patient. You want to push your way in at the right times and with the right people, but this is not the kind of project where you want to be coercive in any way. The last thing you want is someone saying that they were forced to appear naked in a film. So all of these men consented in different forms. Some said, “Change my voice.” Some said, “Anonymize my face.” Some said, “Just shoot my dick.” Some said, “You can shoot my face, but not my dick. I can talk about having a small dick, but don’t show it.”

There was kind of every version and permutation. But when I started to look for the main characters who could carry a film, I needed someone who was comfortable with me filming their family. Usually I’m doing vérité, like direct cinema. Really in their lives for at least a year and a half. I feel like this is front of mind for everyone now because of the Lance Oppenheim Nathan Fielder movie [You Can See Everything]. But you need someone who’s willing to invite you into their home and play the game with you, and Bill was willing to do that from the beginning.

Ruben was the next person who signed on. He’s a father of five on his second marriage. And it doesn’t go the way he might have hoped. The hardest one, I think, which speaks to your question, was David Smith. David is a pseudonym. He’s an OnlyFans star, and he had never told his story before. You would not know this from watching the film, but it actually took the entire production to get him to show his face. It was such an incredible story. I’ve never heard someone talk so openly about their botched penis and growing up evangelical and the horrors of being a male porn star.

We had a very small budget, but we saved a tiny bit of money up until the SXSW deadline. We were about to work with a face replacement company in France because that was his wish, and we thought it spoke to the theme of shame. We were starting to explore, do we hire an actor? And around that time we said, “You know what?” I used to work at The New Yorker, where you don’t really screen things. But I said, “Let’s just take a chance.” So we flew David to New York. We said, “You have no editorial control.” None of the subjects in any of my work ever have any editorial control, including my grandmother. But let’s just show him the film and see what he thinks.

And he was so blown away, he cried in the room. He called his brother, and has since opened up to his family about everything. He’s touring with the film. He came to SXSW. That took until literally a week before the premiere at SXSW, and it’s an ongoing process. He continues to become more and more open.

Yeah. I mean, it’s funny. He was a porn star. You’d think that he had such a level of exposure that he would be comfortable with this. But I think this speaks to the film. Somehow talking about your body is easier than talking about your feelings. Having to talk about his shame, his insecurity, his issues with faith, and with his parents is super, super hard for him. He needed to see the final cut to decide to go forward with it. It was the biggest gamble of my career and, thank God, it paid off.

That’s a great point. So many of the men—this takes me back now—like, I was more nervous than them. I felt like I was being potentially intrusive. I didn’t want to appear coercive in any way, as I mentioned. I wanted them to feel comfortable. But many of them felt grateful to have what you might call a third space to talk about how they feel, because most of them are not opening up to their partners, believe it or not. I don’t know how they come home with a soup can and explain that. And many of them are paying cash. There’s no credit card transaction fee. Many of them are finding ways to anonymize what they’re doing.

But at the same time, they want to talk to someone about it, which is so strange. They just don’t want the people that are part of their daily life to know, but they want Bill to know, and I think Bill deserves a lotta credit for that. He’s a queer man treating these oftentimes right-wing Texans, holding their dicks and enlarging them and making them feel comfortable.

And they wanted to talk to me, and if they wanted it to be off record, that was fine. If they wanted to be on record, that was fine. I think for many of them that was a relief. It’s so common when you work on intense stories that people start to see you as a friend or a collaborator. People see you as someone who understands their plight, and I think whenever I felt like it was starting to get there, I would remind them I’m a journalist. The world is gonna see this. Anything that is private or uncomfortable, just make sure you’re comfortable sharing before it goes in front of the world.

These guys feel so alone. Going back to White Noise, my first film, the single biggest motivator for joining those white nationalist movements wasn’t ideological conviction. I mean, some of them are gnarly racists or antisemites, but a lot of them just, like, want to be part of a club. I saw that in a lot of these men too. They just feel isolated. They want someone to talk to, and felt relieved that Bill was there to listen and that I was there to listen.

I think men, and particularly straight men—I say this as a straight man who probably struggles with this myself—have an underdeveloped sense of self oftentimes.

I’ve done these types of stories for ten years now. When I’ve interviewed women or gay men, they’ve had to think about who they are and their place in the world from such a young age. Especially queer men, from their earliest memories or certainly when they started to understand their sexuality, have had to grapple with who they are and how they appear publicly. I think that because there’s this lack of communication or lack of internal dialogue in a lot of these men, they’re internalizing so much constantly, and they’re not reaching out to those around them.

The reason I got so excited about Tuben as a character is he felt emblematic of everything we were talking about during Trump’s last re-election. You have the. disaffected conservative man who maybe voted for Trump. He would never tell me. He wouldn’t say whether he did or he didn’t, but he thinks all politicians are corrupt, and he’s living in this world on his phone that goes from Andrew Tate to porn to Nick Fuentes.

And, then here comes along a doctor, or not even a doctor, that says, “All of the things that you’re feeling can be fixed with this shot.” If you’re Ruben and you’re already feeling so alone and you haven’t spent your life thinking about who you are and your place in the world, you see a chance to fix all of your problems.

And when Ruben and Lana, his partner, had deep conversations, or when Ruben is on stage doing comedy, connecting with an audience, he feels so much better about himself. But then when he’s back to his phone, he’s feeling horribly alone, like he needs to change something. I think that’s something we all feel.

When I’m talking to my fiancée about how I’m nervous about this or that, I feel great. I feel connected. But then I go back to my phone, and I feel like shit again. So yeah, the ones who have those conversations are in a much better place.

That was by design. Every kind of man is getting this. Anecdotally speaking, Bill says that about two-thirds of the patients are straight and one-third are queer, which is surprising. Sometimes he even says three-quarters are straight, and anecdotally from my experience, that’s accurate. I’ve seen patients as young as early 20s. I mean, David was in his late teens when he got botched, or maybe right around 20 years old. He’s 24 in the film.

Yeah. I also filmed with men in their 70s. I’ve spoken to practitioners who’ve done penis enlargements for men in their 90s.

Men have been trying to enlarge their penis all the way back to the days of the cavemen, as the movie says. But now there’s this extra layer of social pressure, and technology makes it possible. It doesn’t mean that it’s safe, but it makes it possible. Every kind of man is doing this, and I felt like I needed an avatar for both.

You have the guy who’s completely seduced by bullshit online. We all know that guy. I have friends I went to college with who are that guy now. Certainly people from high school who are that guy. And then David is a little bit more heartfelt coming from OnlyFans and dealing with the scars of his experience.

There’s always something bigger. No pun intended. I really tried not to be reductive. For Bill, it was a partner who called him a “little dick motherfucker” 15 or 20 years ago, and then he started changing every part of his body. He has fake balls. He has silicone balls. He has his [fake] pecs, all of it. For David, it was growing up evangelical. For Ruben, it was dealing with abuse and being Mexican-American and things like that.

But there are ordinary people. Believe it or not, the most ordinary person I met was the megachurch pastor. He claimed he was just doing it for his wife, who he loves very much. I hope that that’s true. But almost everyone else would start that way, and then you know how it goes. It’s the old Errol Morris trick: you just kind of stay quiet and let them continue. Then they’d be like, “Oh, and also it’s this, and that, and this kid who said this fucked up thing to me 15 years ago. And by the way, my wife and I don’t have sex anymore.”

Look at implants. Whenever Dolly Parton got hers, they were sort of the medical frontier. I’m sure whoever was the version of me and you at the time was dealing with the same sort of fun, gonzo stories.

And there was probably a Dr. Loria at that time [a penis enlargement provider in the film] who was botching breast implants. It’s a lot safer now, and we know how those work. This is a—maybe unregulated isn’t the right word—but under-regulated frontier. You have people like Dr. Loria operating with impunity in Florida.

This is a guy who designs his own proprietary blend of who knows what. He literally will not tell me. It’s some kind of silicone oil. He says he’s “a hobbyist pharmacist,” and he likes to come up with his own proprietary solutions which he creates in Florida at his office. And the results you see in the film are egregious. I have yet to talk to a Loria patient who has had a positive outcome, and he is still practicing in the state of Florida.

The movie intentionally tries to leave that in a gray zone. But even the better technologies like hyaluronic acid, which is lip filler, the FDA has never said that you can inject that into someone’s dick. [But] it hasn’t said you can’t. It’s fine for off-label use. It’s all sort of the Wild West right now, and I think people don’t realize that the American medical system has all these gray areas and openings.

Bill is not a doctor. He just has to be under the supervision of a doctor, meaning a doctor came to his facility at some point and sanctioned it. Where I see the trouble is that all of these urologists who are trained to do really important medical procedures, like someone struggling with ED or who has issues after prostate cancer, they see a way to make money doing this. I saw literally dozens of urologists flock to Bill because they realize they can make a few thousand dollars in twenty minutes doing penile enhancement. Is that what they should be doing with their time? Probably not. Is that a way that they can make a lot of money? Certainly.

Business looks good. And sorry, one last point is that the penis is different also because it’s invisible. Men already don’t talk about their feelings, as you and I know. But other types of female work are visible. The media has been objectifying women from the beginning of time.

This is something that almost feels personal to men. They’re not telling their partners. Many of them say they’re doing it for themselves. Some of them literally tell me they just want it to poke bigger through their pants at the gym, or they want to show it off in the locker room. So it’s a personal choice, I think, in a way that I’m skeptical of, that’s also different from other medical procedures or kinds of plastic surgery.

[Long breath] I don’t know if you can put “long breath” in the transcript, but… I believe in a kind of documentary filmmaking that doesn’t impose a takeaway. I think we now live in this streamer era where movies are designed to be “two screen” documentaries. It’s a Netflix term, where you can fold laundry [while watching], and they tell you every third of the movie what it’s about and what the takeaway is. The movie is not pro-penis enlargement. It’s not anti-penis enlargement. It’s using that as a canvas to explore all of these things and I think that’s where I like to start. That said, I would not recommend my friends do it. Bill tried to get me to do it, by the way.

Many times. And I am willing to do anything for my stories, like be in bed with Nazis for years or whatever the fuck. I was not willing to do that. The simple fact is that this is a medical gray area. No one knows how safe it is. Filler migrates, and the problem is in your penis.

Whoever that friend is, I would be like, “What issue are you having in your marriage, with your kids, with your self-esteem, with your body?” And I would really welcome the chance to get close to that friend again, you know? As you get older, people are around less, people have kids, people are also more isolated. They’re in their family. And those moments actually can lead to incredible breakthroughs when your friend is like, “I’m scared that my dick is not good enough.”

I would have just been gifted with the most exciting conversation that I’ve had in months, and I would welcome that. We would go on a hike, or have a beer, and talk about why he doesn’t like his dick. I think we as a society would be better if we did that more often.

#6624. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6623. Cynthia Erivo Brought the House Down at Lincoln Center’s Arts for All Benefit Concert

If there was ever a reason to get dressed up on a chilly Monday night, Cynthia Erivo made the case. The award-winning actress and singer brought her powerhouse vocals to Lincoln Center’s annual Benefit Concert, drawing a glitzy crowd to David Geffen Hall for an evening where culture, couture, and cocktails took center stage—all in support of the institution’s Arts for All initiative.

The festivities began with a lively reception along the Grand Promenade, where guests mingled over sparkling pours, a generous sushi spread, and food stations dishing out hanger steak, chicken roulade, and wild mushroom farro. Among those in attendance were Zac Posen, Tony Award winner Caissie Levy, and stylist June Ambrose, alongside a fashionable mix of New Yorkers, all gathered to toast the power of the arts.

For Posen, the evening was also something of a homecoming. “I grew up here in New York City. I first came to Lincoln Center as a young child for its concerts for kids, and my grandparents would also come here for the symphony. So I have a long history with this place. Music is a great connector and an emotional unlock,” he told Vogue on the red carpet.

The designer also has a special connection to the woman of the hour. “Cynthia is a very close friend. We’ve been working together since she first started doing press for The Color Purple,” Posen said. “She came to the studio and we lent her clothing for her whole press tour. We’ve had amazing collaborations, and she’s one of the world’s greatest performers and artists.”

Beyond the glamour, a meaningful mission permeated the occasion. The benefit spotlighted Lincoln Center’s commitment to making the arts accessible to all through its free and Choose-What-You-Pay programming. Since launching in 2022, the initiative has welcomed more than three million people to its campus for performances, educational events, and festivals. At its heart is a belief that the arts should be an essential part of everyday life—not a privilege reserved for a select few.

“Every dollar we raise tonight makes everything else possible,” Dr. Mariko Silver, president and CEO of Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, told Vogue ahead of the performance. “We want to ensure that cultural experiences remain available not only to New Yorkers, but to audiences from around the world, because the arts are the beating heart of humanity. The arts tell us how to see one another, help us to feel, help us to build community.” In an increasingly digital world, Silver believes there’s no substitute for experiencing live performance together. “Those in-person moments are essential to our humanity,” she said. “AI can’t replicate that. Nor should we want it to.”

Then came the main event. Barefoot in a burgundy floral-motif gown, Erivo commanded the stage with a 10-song set that put her extraordinary vocal range in the spotlight. Her interpretation of Whitney Houston’s “I Wanna Dance with Somebody (Who Loves Me)” had the crowd on its feet, while her soulful rendition of Sting’s “Fields of Gold” offered a more tender moment. An exuberant performance of Phil Collins’s “In the Air Tonight” brought another surge of energy, prompting a standing ovation.

“I just sing the songs that I like, and you’re just here along for the ride,” she shared to the audience at the top of the show. “So I always start by saying thank you for indulging me. And along this journey, you might notice some songs—join me and sing along.”

Erivo also performed Bryan Adams’s power ballad “(Everything I Do) I Do It for You.” Before launching into the number, she told the crowd how she sees it as “the most beautiful love song ever written.” Fittingly, on the day that the new James Bond was announced, she also launched into Gladys Knight’s “Licence to Kill,” the title track from the 1989 film of the same name. “I really want to do a James Bond theme song. It’s a dream,” she revealed. “Since I haven’t been able to do it yet, hopefully it’s something I can do. Is anyone listening?”

For the grand finale, Erivo turned to “I Will Always Love You,” the beloved classic written by the late Dolly Parton and immortalized by Whitney Houston. As she unleashed its soaring final notes, the hall erupted, bringing the evening to a spectacular close.
