#6595. Robert Pattinson, I’m Begging You For a Quirked-Up James Bond

Our long international nightmare is finally over: two-time Meme of the Year nominee Robert Pattinson has been chosen as Daniel Craig’s James Bond successor, bringing an end to an exhausting series of “reports” and “leaks” about Amazon’s search for a new 007. Finally we can stop the debates and fan-casting and let Patts and Denis Villeneuve cook until they’re ready to present their new vision. But that would require a level of restraint that the internet doesn’t typically exercise. Immediately after the protracted process of casting Bond concluded, the internet moved on to naming its dream picks for Bond Girls and Bond Villains (sometimes, to brilliant effect.) I can’t say I have a dog in either fight, at least not right now. My Bond WishList is of a different magnitude altogether: can we make James Bond silly again? Just a little, even, 15 percent goofball?

In the hands of another (read: more limited) actor, I’d never suggest such a risky swerve. But the best thing about Pattinson is his range. Sure, if Villeneuve and co. want to render Bond as the stoic and taciturn gentleman he’s generally been this century, Rob has proven he can do that, as every Tenet truther has been gleefully preaching for the last 24 hours. But more often than not, Pattinson is keen to get weird, whether that’s going Full Freak, as he does in Primetime, or approaching certain archetypal parts with a silly, goofy mood (like his conniving suitor in The Odyssey). He can do a “voice” (Mickey 17), he can do scumbag grime (Good Time), he can do hapless screwball (The Drama). Why not make what’ll be his biggest role to date a little cocktail of all his best elements? (Okay, he can leave the Mickey 17 voice behind.)

20 years ago, Casino Royale was a refreshing reset and a crucial corrective to the overflowing ridiculousness of the Piece Brosnan era. But in the past two decades, the pendulum has swung back—the gritty reboot has become studios' stock-in-trade. I feel the same way about Batman; the actual risky choice would be to make something less like Nolan’s series that, instead, hewed a little closer to, say, Batman Forever, or even the gothic camp of Tim Burton’s two films.

Of course, Robert Pattinson was at the center of a Batman reboot as well, and the result was a movie that felt more like a spiritual cousin to David Fincher’s Se7en; audiences ate it up so much that the hunger for a sequel persists even after endless delays. When it comes to franchises as high-stakes as Batman or Bond, you can’t trust these increasingly sauceless execs to make anything but the basic choice. There’s no reason to expect Jeff Bezos isn’t texting Denis screenshots from Skyfall for reference from his megayacht at this very moment.

But if there’s anybody capable of putting a little English on the handle while still giving the mainstream what it wants, it’s Big Bob Pattinson. He could easily make his James Bond a little off, or he could go full seductive cad who smiles like Neil Tenet, has a ki with Q, and charms women with some playful banter instead of simply brooding them into submission. I’m not looking for invisible cars and sharks with lasers, or a Lothario like Roger Moore who speaks in puns. All I’m asking is that we give camp a chance. Because ultimately, the most exciting thing Villeneuve and Pattinson can do to set their Bond apart would be to loosen him up a little.

#6593. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6592. Homemade Mac & Cheese

The perfect mac & cheese will have you dreaming about its cheesy goodness for days after you eat it. Obviously, the cheese has to be top-notch, but the real secret to the best version is the perfect crunchy topping. My recipe delivers on all of that and more, so you won't even think about reaching for another mac & cheese recipe for the rest of your gatherings. From weeknight dinners to potlucks and holidays, this is the classic side dish everyone will be reaching for.

What People Are Saying:"Always a huge hit with friends and family! This is my go-to if I'm bringing a dish to a holiday dinner with friends. I've rarely had leftovers to take home!" - Zafire_Shadows

"This is exactly what mac and cheese dreams are made of. Love the gruyere funk and the mustard powder (so clever!)." - Pastagofer

First, you’ll boil the pasta. Start with a big pot of salted water (and I mean super salty, it should taste like the ocean), then add your pasta and cook it until before al dente—I’m talking still-has-a-ring-of-hard-white-pasta-in-the-middle-when-you-bite-in uncooked. You want it to meld and absorb with your cheese sauce in the oven, not turn into mush. Undercooking now guarantees the perfect bite when you pull it out of the oven.

Then it’s cheese sauce time, and that means making a béchamel. You’ll start by melting your butter in a pan over medium heat, then sprinkling the flour over the top and stirring everything together until it starts pulling away from the pan slightly. You’re looking for what’s called a “blonde roux,” which has a slightly yellow tint and should smell a bit like baked goods. You don’t want it super dark (so keep an eye on the heat!), but you definitely don’t want it as light as it started.

Next, add the milk in slowly, stirring constantly so you don’t get thick lumps. Want to shortcut this process a bit? Heat your milk ahead of time to room temperature or even slightly warm. You’re going to cook it until it’s thick and bubbly (about 2 minutes), so having your milk warm will help you get there faster. It’s going to get a LOT thicker when you add the cheese, so if it’s still a little thin but you want to get on with it, that’s okay too.

Once you’re ready to add the cheese, it’s very important to take it off the heat before so that the sauce doesn’t start to separate. That said, if you’ve been at it for a minute and are still having trouble getting your cheese to melt, pop your pot back on the heat for just a few seconds to bring the temperature up and help the process along.

Once it comes together, you can stir in the macaroni until every noodle is coated.

At this point, you could eat this mac & cheese right now, and it would taste wonderful. But! If you want exceptional mac & cheese, you’ve gotta bake it. So pour it into a pan, then get ready for the best part—the topping. To make it, you’ll combine some breadcrumbs and the remaining half cup of Parmesan in a bowl, then add the olive oil and mix it all up. Sprinkle it on top of the mac and cheese in the casserole dish.

All you have to do is pop it into your preheated 375° oven and bake it until it's golden brown on top. Go ahead, snag a bite before it's fully cooled—you'll really be able to taste all your extra effort.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

If you’re looking to make this dish ahead of time, prepare the mac & cheese up until step 4, then cover it in your baking dish and refrigerate it up to 3 days (or freeze it up to 2 months). When ready to serve, add the Parmesan and panko mixture, bake, and serve. If baking from frozen, allow to thaw in the refrigerator overnight before baking.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for around 3 days.

#6590. Upgrade Your Basics: Best Undershirts for Men in 2026

Just because you don't see a building's foundation doesn't mean it isn't holding everything up. In much the same way, the best undershirts for men are the humble base layer of countless great outfits. Many GQ staffers, in fact, wear-test theirs daily, and yet they're often overlooked, even though they've long-perfected their role: to be the protective layer between your gross body and your steezy, attention-hungry shirts and polos.

And while they're certainly good for some added warmth in the winter, there's a common misconception that they can make the wearer too hot. In fact, lightweight, moisture-wicking undershirts made from fabrics like modal, or cotton blends can actually transfer the sweat away from your body, speeding up your cooling down. All that's to say: Undershirts are more than just men’s underwear. They’re the cornerstone of a hall-of-fame fit.

An undershirt is an undershirt is an undershirt. If you want the most straightforward version, the kind that you’re picturing in your head is most likely from Calvin Klein. It’s a classic crewneck undershirt that’s made of a lightweight jersey that’s 100% cotton which has a smooth, very slightly brushed hand that feels worn-in in the best way possible. The slim fit won’t cause any weird bunching or bulging and it’s got enough length to stay tucked even when you’re out on the town cutting rugs.

My colleague, GQ senior commerce editor Avidan Grossman, has been wearing CK's genre-defining undershirts since his high school years. (He could do without the logo at the hem, but has made his peace with it, given that you never see it once it's tucked.) Otherwise, he prizes Calvin Klein's riff for its simple, pared-down design and blessed lack of modern-day frills. After all, not every shirt needs to moisture wick or odor block. If you just want an undershirt that gets the job done, don't overthink it.

Sometimes, sleeves are just too much undershirt. That’s where tanks come in. Also known as A-shirts, the humble, sleeveless tank has been rocked by every heartthrob and neighborhood grandpa as far back as anyone can remember. And while the low neck and lack of sleeves means you’ll practically never see them underneath a button-up, the irony is that they look great shown off with an unbuttoned camp shirt or on their own.

For the money, we think Hanes takes the cake with their multipack of undershirts. The stretchy ribbed jersey is made of 100% cotton and fits snug with a low neck that’s slightly squared off compared to most tanks. They may cost just under twenty bucks for a pack of six, but they look like a million bucks. “I’ve had buyer's remorse over many a menswear garment over the years,” explains GQ editor Jordan Bowman, "but the one thing that has never let me down is the humble tank top from Hanes. They nailed the fit and the material, and the great thing is, you can buy a pack just about anywhere."

If every part of your wardrobe has to be fit for a king, down to the most basics of basics, then CDLP is what we’d recommend, my liege. The reality is that most luxury tees don’t offer much more than the regular stuff. It’s diminishing returns after a certain price point, but CDLP is the notable exception. My colleague, our contributing editor Louis Cheslaw, has put his same CDLP cottons through the ringer year after year, and says they still haven't lost their luster.

It’s a pricey undershirt, for sure, but the high-quality fabric has a silky hand and lightweight feel that’s unparalleled. (It really feels like you’re almost wearing nothing.) Thanks to a wider neckline, you’re a lot less likely to see the tee poking out, too. And if you feel like such a nice T-shirt is wasted as underwear, don’t worry—the cut and shorter length means it looks great untucked, and can double as your regular T-shirt too.

Mack Weldon’s silver series of garments is what happens when you get nerdy about chemistry and fashion (in the best possible way). The Ionic+ technology embeds silver charged silver ions which are naturally antimicrobial into the fabric itself. Essentially, that means bacteria and odor is neutralized, which means you can take it easy on the deodorant. Beyond that, the tees are made of super long staple Supima cotton and a smidge of lycra for an extra silky fee, comfortable stretch, and long-lasting wear.

The main bummer is that they’ll cost you more than most tees, so stocking up for the week can get pricey. Still, it’s one of those undershirts that makes you realize you’ve been settling for squalor—plus, you can bundle up and get 10% off to help offset the sticker shock.

Not everything at Uniqlo is a great value. But when it comes to upgraded basics at an affordable price, you’d be hard-pressed to find brand that does it better. When you need an airy, breathable undershirt that's truly lightweight, the Japanese mega-retailer’s AIRism tees are legendary. They’re crafted from a smooth and breathable cotton-polyester-spandex blend that dries quickly, feels cool to the touch, and fights odors—a triple threat that’ll have sweaty days in a headlock. I personally wear these—they're a failsafe way to save my expensive dress shirts from dreaded pit stains, but they’re also perfect for wearing as a gym shirt. And at just $15 per tee, there’s no other undershirt that can do as much for the price.

GQ contributor Evan Malachosky was always a little skeptical of Skims, but the brand's tees won him over. He found that Skims’s proprietary fabrics are silky on the skin, and are neither too thin (and therefore exposing), nor too thick (and therefore too hot). Pleasingly, the brand has applied just as much care to its undershirt, even though—or perhaps because—it's designed to look invisible under your clothes. (The design team even thought about cleaning up the seam lines, so nothing would show through.) Made from 100% cotton, and available in an incredibly wide range of sizes, our favorite detail is that it's a little bit longer than the brand's standard tees, so that there's no risk of any unsightly seams being visible at the hemline, either.

If the purpose of an undershirt is to fly under the radar, then it stands to reason that a V-neck one—which remains invisible even when you unbutton your shirt collar—might be the most efficient of all the styles here. You'll still want to trust the classic makers here, which is why our favorite comes from Calvin Klein. Like the Calvin Klein crewneck option above, the fabric is smooth, slightly brushed, and 100% cotton. It's also affordable, and available in not just white, black, and gray, but also a multipack comprising all three. Lastly, CK's trademark slimmer fit means no bunching or bulging risk.

Are these “undershirts” far heavier than the usual ones? Yes. But they never lose their shape, and if you live in a bitterly cold climate, you'll want even your undershirt to max out its warming properties.

The luxury car of undershirts, Falke's premium undershirts go on just as smoothly (and last just as long) as the beloved German brand's famous socks.

You heard it here first: Ralph Lauren's Pony has become the coolest label in menswear again.

When James Bond—well, Daniel Craig as James Bond—needs an undershirt, he wears Sunspel's.

Kirkland Signature is somewhat of a fashion industry secret. These are made of soft, long-staple Egyptian cotton, and they're tube knit, meaning you don't have to worry about any uncomfortable side seams.

Made from rayon and polyester, Hanes’ moisture-wicking undershirts are fast-drying, cool to the touch, and silky smooth, all for just $5 a pop.

If you wanna let your clavicles shine uninhibited by any undershirt peek-age, a V-neck is the best way (short of a tank) to do it.

Cut from a premium cotton, this lightweight undershirt is going to feel a little thicker and warmer than others on this list, purely because Reigning Champ's premium cotton fabrics tend to lean towards the beefier end of the spectrum.

Though Mack Weldon’s 18-Hour Rib Tank doesn’t come with the microbe-smashing odor technology as their Silver crew neck undershirt, it does have an even silkier fabric and plenty of stretch.

The first thing I noticed when I met Wythe's founder was not his jeans, or amazing western shirt. It was actually this ribbed tank.

Undershirts are meant to be that intermediate layer between your outermost layers and your body, a protective guard that keeps your star garments fresh and free of sweat. Therefore, it's materials, construction, and fit that are the main components that determine how good an undershirt (and, well, every garment) actually is.

Above all else, your undershirt's fabric should be breathable, soft, comfortable, and, ideally, sweat-wicking. We primarily love undershirts and tanks that are made from high-quality 100% cotton, which has many of those characteristics naturally, but we also feel like there’s a time and place for synthetics, which are often used for their ability to wick away moisture and dry easily—especially for those who run particularly hot. And note: Stretchy materials like Spandex are helpful for comfort, but their elasticity will eventually degrade over time.

Undershirts should almost always fit closer to the body than your regular T-shirts. This is because they’ll be layered underneath another shirt or sweater, and can bunch in odd ways if too baggy. They don’t need to be skin-tight, but they should be slim enough to layer comfortably and long enough to tuck into your shirt. In fact, Peter Middleton, founder of Wythe, even told us that they should fit slim to start, since they are cotton and are knit, and will therefore stretch a little over time. If they are loose to start with, they are only going to become looser and saggier, which is really not the point.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6588. Andy Baraghani's Ditto Café Is His Most Personal Project Yet

Andy Baraghani is more afraid of becoming stagnant than he is of dying. Stagnancy, he’s quick to clarify, is different from stillness. Stagnancy is like a fetid pond; stillness is meditative. Baraghani seems to be at risk of neither.

It is late morning on the first actually chilly day of autumn and we are staring one another down across a stainless-steel prep table, which has been dragooned into use as an island in his outrageously good-looking kitchen. He is about to make me scones—salty-sweet ones with dates and lemon zest, an offering under development for his forthcoming café Ditto. But first, we’ll need to pop out for cream.

Quite literally in motion since I arrived, Baraghani finishes his point on stagnancy: He fears a life in which he is not learning, moving, or evolving “as a writer, a cook, and a good gay,” he says.

He lives just a few blocks from the Union Square Greenmarket, where niche pepper varieties are currently splayed in colorful fractals across folding tables. We have just completed a ground floor tour of the apartment that the chef-cum-writer-cum-chef shares with his husband, Keith Pollock. Now he moves across the kitchen and pauses at the Crittall-style window. It gives me 30 seconds to take inventory of his countertop alliums.

These details feel important. Baraghani has become a sort of standard-bearer for exquisite seasonal produce and the exquisite life one can lead preparing such stuff. I clock a couple of shallots, which sit in a Swid Powell bowl beside five heirloom tomatoes. It occurs to me that even onions are more beautiful in Baraghani’s universe.

“Oh,” he says casually, following my gaze. “Torpedo shallots.” As if all of our countertops look like this.

In the decade or so since he became a household name for a certain set of a certain era (food-obsessed aesthetes who love an acidic drizzle and a hard, salty cheese), as a video star for a certain magazine—okay, this one—his fandom has only continued to explode.

His debut cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be, was a New York Times bestseller and the recipient of a James Beard Award. He has more than 370,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok. He’s been called “the Internet boyfriend of our dreams.” Vogue covered his wedding. The New York Times published his ideal Thanksgiving menu. In the last 24 hours alone, Baraghani has been busy beating out creative director Terrence O’Connor for a Best Body prize at the podcast How Long Gone’s inaugural “Goneies” Award Show, (Baraghani was asked to remove his blazer to reveal a formfitting Dario Vitale–era Versace pink tank top) before running into David Tanis while shopping for groceries.

When Baraghani announced he would be opening a restaurant this fall near Union Square with restaurateur Michael Silber, publications began tripping over themselves to cover the news. Still, he says, few have pushed him on the true meaning of the name Ditto. Perhaps they were too busy trying to keep up.

Baraghani takes a seat on one of the iron stools beside the prep table and there is a rare, brief silence, which is broken almost immediately by the tinny opening notes of a techno song emanating from the crew performing a renovation on the lower floor. I inquire about his cortisol levels as he juggles opening Ditto a few blocks away, the second cookbook he has just shot in this apartment, and now the remodel below us.

Baraghani grins. “I feel calm,” he insists. “If something goes wrong, I can fix it, because I feel pretty clear on what I want to achieve.”

He has spent the last 10 years peppering his recipes with caveats. “I know that my food may be a touch too lemony for some,” he writes in The Cook You Want To Be. “And that I use what has been called a ridiculous amount of herbs.”

His background too. Years ago, he penned an essay for this magazine about growing up Iranian in a post-9/11 America; he started to go by Andy instead of Andisheh and bought an “Italian Stallion” T-shirt. He wrote about learning to accept his sexuality in restaurant kitchens, where he rarely encountered other gay men, and in his family life. He grew up in the Bay Area, the son of parents who had emigrated from Iran to Berkeley in 1977. The piece ended with an admission: “So as nice as it would be for this story to end with that Iran feature or getting my dream job at Bon Appétit, the truth is that I’m still trying to figure things out. It’s not always steady progress.”

Since I had a baby six weeks ago, I have been walking around floored that the adults in my life could have ever been children, but with Andy, I don’t have to work too hard to picture it. He has a particularly cheerful sense of wonder. When I ask about it, he says it comes from his upbringing. His parents were political activists. Andy’s mother worked as an aesthetician (yes, he established his famous skin-care routine early). He grew up surrounded by a diverse community of immigrants who would invite his family to their celebrations and into their homes, where a young Baraghani got to taste dishes from far-flung places. After he landed in New York, he would take respite in stints abroad, traveling from hostel to hostel so he could eat his way across Vietnam, Lebanon, and Turkey.

Now, though, Baraghani says he is done footnoting his vision. In the intervening years since that essay, Baraghani has written and cooked and tasted at warp speed. He was bound to self-actualize in the same timeframe it took the rest of us to figure out how to style barrel-leg pants. Or perhaps it’s the reality of having to reckon with what he can’t change: In 2024, after a battle with small-cell lung cancer, his beloved father passed away. Baraghani tells me that before it was stagnancy, his greatest fear was losing a parent. He has since learned that loss isn’t something to solve, but a tremendous void one must learn to live with.

“There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see [at Ditto,]” he says. The dishes will weave together all of the threads of Baraghani-ism: seasonal vegetables prepared deftly with Persian flourishes, blending tart and sour and aromatic with a firm point-of-view. If the specifics seem hard to picture, I think that might be the point. Baraghani has thrived historically by taking a straightforward-seeming dish and twisting it just off-kilter, so it is a few degrees punchier and much more beautiful than you were expecting. The result is food that is as much about the people and places evoked by the flavors as it is about aesthetic provocation. (That Italian Stallion shirt, he tells me, is long gone.)

Literally speaking, Ditto will be a revival of the sort of counter-service restaurant Baraghani has long adored, from Gjusta in Los Angeles to City Bakery in New York. He and Silber sprang for a shiny rotisserie oven, for what they’re calling a “beyond chicken program,” with plans for spit-roasted porchetta, romanesco, and cabbage.

The goal is dishes that are palpably human, in a space Baraghani hopes will seem accessible to everyone. It was important for both owners to find a space in a hub neighborhood. With the storefront they chose, a former Agnès B. on 16th Street, Greenmarket shoppers can stop by for a selection of California-ish sides and salads displayed Yotam Ottolenghi–style, counter pastries, or just to peruse marketplace provisions: tahini, harissa, dates (and, for now, no tinned fish). Maybe, one day, they’ll stay open for dinner service, but for now the plan is breakfast and lunch.

Suddenly Baraghani is moving again, reaching for his phone to show me a photo of a dish he would have loved to serve, had Con Ed turned on the gas in time for a September opening: a mound of spicy tuna salad piled perkily in a blanched tomato with a turret of scallion greens.

The sight makes me hungry, and I realize we still haven’t gone out for that cream. Ninety minutes have passed and I have yet to ask any of the questions I’d prepared for Baraghani, who keeps surprising me with disclosures. (Such as: He did not speak until he was three years old.)

Suddenly, it is time to head to Ditto for a tour, cream and scones be damned.

As we walk over, I ask about the restaurant’s name. He asks if I’ve seen the movie Ghost. I have, but not for a while. “It’s another way to say ‘I love you,’” he says simply, before disappearing to join a meeting.

Later I dig up that scene Baraghani mentioned and press play. In it, Whoopi Goldberg tries to convince a frustrated Demi Moore that her recently deceased boyfriend has returned as a ghost. Moore jumps up in disbelief to flee the restaurant as Patrick Swayze, the boyfriend, scrambles to find a way to prove to her that he’s right there. “Tell her ‘ditto,’” he urges Goldberg, who screams “ditto” after Moore as she bolts. “Ditto!” It’s their code word for “I love you too.”

Moore stops in her tracks and turns, her gaze connecting with a man she misses, who she isn’t totally sure is there.

And for the first time in a while, she is no longer in motion. She is still.

#6587. I Can't Wait to Play Grand Theft Auto VI—For the Fashion (Yes, Really)

I’m never one to out myself on main, but I’m here to declare: I am a proud (but once-closeted) gaymer.

As someone who rarely watches the latest movies or TV shows, people always retort: “Well, how do you spend your free time?” The answer is, and always has been: By booting up my Xbox. I’ve long found joy in immersing myself in a virtual world. When I was younger, it was through Super Mario on the Nintendo 64. (Aging myself much. . . I need a new night cream.) In my teen years, things evolved to the Resident Evil and Grand Theft Auto franchises. Even now, well into my early thirties, I still find myself slipping on a headset after a stressful day and blocking out the real world—by recently playing video games like Dead by Daylight, where one teams up with three fellow survivors to escape a blood-thirsty killer. That’s my idea of fun.

This week, however, my attention is shifting back to Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto series—mainly, because Grand Theft Auto VI is finally releasing on Thursday. Over a decade in the works, the buzzy new game is one of the most anticipated (and pre-ordered) games in history—so much so that it’s already surpassed the $1 billion mark before it’s even out.

There’s certainly a lot to be excited for: The new installment introduces two new characters, Jason and Lucia, and promises its biggest map to date (twice the size of GTA V’s world), interactive features (how strong Jason and Lucia’s relationship is depends on you), and even a star-studded soundtrack (featuring tracks by Cardi B, Travis Scott, Yung Lean, and Tove Lo, not to mention in-game radio commentary from notable names like Alex Consani and Lana Del Rey).

Sure, all of these innovative elements may have been what coaxed me to shell out $99.99 for the game’s ultimate edition ahead of Friday—but most of all, I’m excited to play around with all of the customizable fashions. (Yes, really.)

Some may choose to play Grand Theft Auto for the high-stakes speed racing or dangerous crime missions, but I personally play it to flex cute outfits while doing it. Customizing your character’s look, after all, has long been an integral part of the GTA fun: Over the years, having the ability to choose your character’s ensembles, hairstyles, tattoos, and more has been one of the best parts of the game.

I’ve spent countless hours perfecting my saucy in-game ’fits—running around and causing chaos in my sleek biker jackets or stiletto booties. I don’t spend hours completing missions or bank heists to save money for my (virtual) savings account: I rack up the cash to spend it on the lavish fashions, duh! And the good news for me is: GTA VI is rumored to have several clothing, shoe, and jewelry shops to explore across Leonida. Meaning, if I’m going to become the most ruthless crime lord in town, I’m going to be able to look good doing it. (And yes, I will be maining Lucia, who is bound to have the cuter options.)

Lucia in a “Vice City Style” outfit from Grand Theft Auto VI.

It hasn’t taken high-fashion brands long to catch onto this idea that gaming can be glamorous. In Grand Theft Auto V, for one, your character could sport pieces from real-life streetwear labels such as Civilist, MISBHV and Born x Raised. And it’s not just GTA that’s been getting more and more into the fashion space. Over the years, video games have slowly becoming a high-fashion playground in general—releasing purchasable skins that can make your character feel completely tailored to you. Balenciaga has collaborated with games like Fortnite, Louis Vuitton with League of Legends, and Burberry with Roblox. Makes sense: Why shouldn’t your avatar reflect your personal tastes and likes?

So yes, come Thursday, I will be crashing cars, shooting absurdly-violent weapons, and being overall mischievous—but those are all side quests, because come launch day, the very first thing I will be doing is securing cash (perhaps a quick corner store robbery?) to buy me some new chic shoes. Priorities, people.

The real question is. . . Who do we think will be the first luxury designer to get on board and collaborate with Grand Theft Auto VI? Demna, for one, has proven he is a gaming fan: Can we expect a Gucci x GTA wardrobe sometime soon? I, for one, wouldn’t mind running the streets in this fab faux-fur coat from spring 2027.

#6586. We Found The 6 Strongest Drinks At Starbucks, Ranked By Caffeine

Each of these bevvies delivers a serious buzz.

I would love nothing more than to be the type of person who jumps out of bed with the sunrise—without the lure of a steaming hot and very caffeinated cup of coffee waiting for me. But I need to smell the freshly brewed espresso before I can muster the strength to get out from under the duvet.

Even as decaf this and half-caf that have become all the rage in our high-cortisol society, you can pry the double cappuccino out of my cold, dead hands! Sometimes you just need a 350-milligram latte to keep you chugging through the day (unless your doctor says otherwise, in which case, ignore me).

In the spirit of staying fueled, I analyzed the Starbucks menu and narrowed it down to the most caffeinated bevvies you can buy in a grande size. However, everything is customizable and may differ slightly in caffeine content—you can always ask for more or fewer espresso shots, or opt for a larger size.

There’s a reason you might feel extra jittery after a morning Cold Brew. It’s packed with caffeine because it uses almost twice as many coffee grounds as regular brewed coffee. It is diluted with water, though, to temper the buzz.

A Caffè Americano—hot or iced—packs a similar punch as a Cold Brew. It’s not all that different, TBH, except instead of brewed coffee, it combines water and espresso to give it a littleeeee more edge.

If you love a sweet latte but want more caffeine, the Iced Brown Sugar Shaken Espresso is your ticket at roughly 255 milligrams for a grande.

If you’re craving a Cold Brew with a kick, go Nitro. It uses a higher coffee-to-water ratio in the cold steeping and dispensing process, and it is served without ice (so, again, less dilution). The result: bold flavor and about 280 milligrams of caffeine.

There’s a reason I’m a drip-coffee loyalist, and it’s not just the flavor. It’s also about the 310 milligrams of caffeine that a grande Pike Place delivers, which earns the medium roast coffee a solid second spot on this list.

Drumroll, please! The most caffeinated beverage on Starbucks’ menu is the Blonde Roast Brewed Coffee at 360 milligrams. Why does it differ from the medium and even the dark roast? It’s pretty simple: Blonde usually tests higher because Starbucks brews it with a little more coffee, and lighter roasts can pack more grounds into the scoop. That means more caffeine makes its way into your cup.

#6585. Maple Pumpkin Overnight Oats

“I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.)

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

#6582. Beyond the Blueprint: The Art of Building an Architectural Legacy

What does it take to create something that truly endures? How can luxury leaders balance heritage with innovation and create spaces that are not only beautiful but meaningful to the people who inhabit them? Against the backdrop of London’s iconic Tower Bridge, some of the leading names in luxury gathered aboard one of the world’s most extraordinary superyachts, Kismet, for an afternoon spent discussing the legacies they hope to leave behind.

These questions brought together influential leaders across fashion, jewelry, architecture, real estate, retail, and technology for an exclusive Vogue Business gathering in collaboration with Shanna Collective. Held on October 14, with London's historic skyline as its setting and the superyacht itself offering a compelling example of ambitious design, the event explored what it takes to create spaces, brands, and experiences that transcend generations. Hosted by Shanna Khan, founder and CEO of Shanna Collective, the afternoon opened with remarks from Vogue Business head of advisory and custom insights Anusha Couttigane, followed by a panel moderated by Vogue Business features director Lucy Maguire. Speakers included Sergei Mosunov, CEO of Fabergé; Jade Holland Cooper, founder and creative director of Holland Cooper; and Dr Valerie Vaughan-Dick MBE, chief executive of the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA).

“Hosting this gathering with Vogue Business aboard Kismet was a wonderful opportunity to convene thought leaders from architecture, hospitality, real estate, and retail, each bringing a distinct perspective on the future of design and placemaking to build an enduring legacy,” said Khan. “What struck me was the shared understanding that creating something truly exceptional requires more than a vision for the space itself; it requires an understanding of its wider context, its people, and the legacy it can leave behind. Anusha and I were delighted to bring this group together, and I left feeling inspired by the ambition, openness, and collective thinking in the room,” she added.

Left to right: Lucy Maguire (features director, Vogue Business), Jade Holland Cooper (founder and CEO, Holland Cooper), Anusha Couttigane (head of advisory and custom insights, Vogue Business), Shanna Khan (founder and CEO, Shanna Collective) and Dr. Valerie Vaughan-Dick MBE (CEO, RIBA).

Opening the discussion, Couttigane drew parallels between London’s architectural history and the role of private enterprise in shaping cities.

“If you look out across the city, you can observe centuries of architectural ambition, entrepreneurship, and reinvention.” she began. “It’s a reminder that the great cities we inherit today weren’t shaped by architects and politicians alone. They were also shaped by entrepreneurs, investors, and business leaders who saw opportunities to create something bigger than themselves — investing in the physical landscape, advancing commerce and culture, and creating places that would serve communities for generations,” she continued.

The English capital also holds a symbolic place in Khan’s business philosophy. “It was no coincidence that we gathered in the heart of London, a city that shaped that modern world and one that hosted us for discussions on how we can collectively steward the future,” Khan said. Having recently been interviewed by Couttigane for Vogue Business, Khan’s own work includes the regeneration of Chicago’s Fulton Market district and Jacksonville’s Shipyards development, where design, commerce, and community intersect.

“What I find particularly compelling about Shanna’s approach is her conviction that exceptional design should do more than create beautiful buildings and interiors. It should contribute something enduring to the places and people around it. It should honor the past and the history of a place, while making it relevant for modern users. It’s a philosophy that resonates strongly with our discussion today,” Couttigane added.

Anusha Couttigane delivering the opening remarks.

Beginning the panel, Maguire asked Mosunov how Fabergé is translating the hallmarks of the brand, such as craftsmanship, detail, and surprise into the physical realm, given its ambitions to expand physically. “The previous owner had a business model that was focused on B2B. It didn’t have its own retail distribution. When I bought Fabergé, I decided that we needed to expand the direct-to-consumer business, with the main instrument being our own boutiques,” Mosunov explained.

The challenge is creating spaces that communicate the maison’s heritage while supporting its contemporary ambitions. “We needed to express this historical story through the boutiques, showcasing pre-1970 pieces and sharing the story about Peter Carl Fabergé, the founder of the company. This way, you get a real sense of the company.” Mosunov also shared how the brand is designing jewelry iterations of its iconic egg motifs, inspired by the fifty Imperial Eggs that secured the maison’s acclaim between 1885 and 1916.

As Fabergé expands its international retail footprint, Mosunov is adapting the design of its boutiques to local preferences. “For example, in the Middle East, we have a store in the Dubai Mall. They like very opulent forms in that region so we need to adapt the execution to the local marketplace.”

Vaughan-Dick reinforced the importance of cultural context in architecture. Referencing Norman Foster’s work in the Middle East, she highlighted the influence of climate, environment and local requirements on architectural decisions. “You cannot have this homogenous view of design. You have to think about culture, sustainability, and building safety. You have to look at the different requirements for that country and for that particular society,” she added.

Turning to Holland Cooper, Maguire asked about how she was creating environments that would resonate with the world of the brand. As a business that has grown from stalls at Badminton Horse Trials to a £100m+ company with flagship boutiques and a new 70,000-square-foot HQ in the Cotswolds, Holland Cooper spoke about the importance of making the brand experience as special as possible.

Left to right: Lucy Maguire (features director, Vogue Business), Dr. Valerie Vaughan-Dick MBE (CEO, RIBA), Sergei Mosunov (owner and CEO, Fabergé) and Jade Holland Cooper (founder and CEO, Holland Cooper).

“Although we don’t have a lot of shops, the ones that we do have are so important.” she explained. “For me, the importance of retail is making that physical experience as special as we possibly can. I think there’s a narrative that retail is dead, that bricks and mortar is dead, but I think we’re just getting too lazy about the experience that we’re creating for the customer…what we’ve done in our physical retail spaces is really understand that the service and environment are paramount to that experience,” she added.

Holland Cooper’s retail philosophy draws inspiration from brands including Ralph Lauren and Abercrombie & Fitch, whose distinctive environments left a lasting impression on her as a young shopper: “I am pedantic about music volume, lighting, smell, hanger presentation, visual merchandising, how the staff and the service levels are, because the minute you walk through those doors, you want it to be immersive, and you want people to forget the outside world. That’s why they call it retail therapy.”

Maguire then highlighted a tension in the theme: “Buildings need to endure, but the people, communities, and lifestyles they serve are constantly changing. How should brands, architects and developers design for longevity without becoming trapped by the tastes or assumptions of the present?” she asked.

For Vaughan-Dick, the guiding architectural principle is “long life, loose fit”: creating buildings capable of adapting to future needs. “I do think that individuals recognize that when you’re designing buildings, they don’t know what a building is going to look like in 100 years time, but every architect, every engineer, everyone here needs to think: what we design now needs to have that longer life,” she stated.

Left to right: Tom Pascall (communications manager, the Chancery Rosewood), Joanna Gunn (chief brand officer, Rosewood), Shanna Khan (CEO and founder, Shanna Collective) and Naomi Sebley (the Chancery Rosewood).

For Mosunov, Fabergé’s design legacy distinguishes between timeless beauty, modern beauty, and more transient aesthetic preferences when considering its future. Holland Cooper similarly sees heritage as an enduring source of differentiation: “I am obsessive about heritage, classic shapes and just reinventing them to be appealing to the modern audience, and that doesn’t mean ripping the rulebook up entirely. I pay homage to all the beautiful British aesthetics, and that’s the romanticism of what we’re doing, really,” said Holland Cooper.

As a consequence, British manufacturing remains fundamental to the brand’s identity and ambitions. “All of our tailoring is made in London. All of the wool is woven in the UK, and I’ve done that since day one. And I was told that it wouldn’t be possible to scale a business and do that, and I have, and it is. And I’m really passionate about the UK manufacturing industry. So that’s a big part of our heritage,” she explained.

For Khan, these principles of detail, experience and emotional connection are paramount: “Jade shared her belief that every detail matters to drive an exuberant retail experience. Elements that may seem subtle influence how a place is experienced, remembered, and valued. For me, that is where design becomes truly meaningful: when we can transport guests in time and place, it moves beyond aesthetics to create an emotional connection that endures long after the initial experience itself.”

Left to right: Andrea Latten, (chief business officer, Condé Nast Britain), Shanna Khan (CEO and founder, Shanna Collective) and Christopher Warren (UK head of industry, Condé Nast Britain).

The afternoon concluded with a tour of Kismet, whose interior design was led by Shanna as chief creative director. The superyacht is an example of the extraordinary experiences that thoughtful design can create. For an industry deeply rooted in heritage, the gathering raised a pertinent question: what are today’s luxury leaders creating that will remain relevant and meaningful to future generations?

For Shanna Khan, working together across disciplines is central to answering this question. “Our collaboration with Vogue Business creates a valuable opportunity to bring different disciplines into our conversations and explore how ideas from across creative landscapes can inform one another. The future of luxury lies in creating places and experiences with substance, soul, and generational value,” she said. But she reflected: “Ultimately, building in an enduring way is defined by creating something that feels relevant today, salutes the heritage of the past, and has the potential to become part of a legacy for generations to come.”

#6581. 23 Healthy Breakfasts That'll Keep You Full Till Lunch

When it comes to healthy breakfasts, free yourself to eat more than plain yogurt and granola bars. And honestly, those $19 acai bowls from the smoothie shop aren’t that nutritious. A truly healthy breakfast has plenty of carbs for energy (this includes fiber-rich ingredients like whole grains, berries, legumes, and seeds); muscle-and-bone-supporting protein; and plenty of healthy fats for nutrient absorption. Many of these recipes can easily be made ahead and doled out from the freezer, so before you swing by the drive-through for bland egg muffins, consider these more flavorful options. When it comes to healthy breakfast ideas, my mind immediately goes to oats. Also chia seed pudding. So the newest edition of my column Good for You is a chia seed–overnight oat hybrid, which also uses up a can of pumpkin purée (I bet you have one in the pantry).

Frozen or fresh berries work great in these accidentally vegan pancakes (thanks, silken tofu!) from Good for You. A good drizzle of maple syrup is all they need for accompaniment, but since I’m not vegan, I enjoy them with a swipe of Greek yogurt.

Another Good for You hit is this speedy, protein-and-collagen-rich soup, which is something in between Italian stracciatella and Chinese egg drop soup.

Okay, after this one, I’ll stop shamelessly promoting my column. But seriously, don’t sleep on this hydrating mixed berry smoothie, especially if you’re lukewarm on eating plain cottage cheese.

This tricked out avocado toast is loaded with hot smoked salmon and creamy scrambled eggs.

You maybe haven’t seen an omelet filled with sliced apple and cheddar, but I recommend trying before knocking.

Oatmeal is an ideal choice in the morning for carbs and fiber. I like to slowly stir in egg whites while it’s simmering on the stove for extra protein and top it with ground flaxseed.

A great option for weekend mornings. You could top it with feta or yogurt, dunk whole wheat toast in the sauce, or spoon it over rice, anything goes.

Nothing hits quite like a breakfast burrito, but I can’t buy one every day and still pay rent. DIY to the rescue: I line the tortilla with salsa or hot sauce and sometimes add leftover refried beans if I have them.

The texture of chia seed pudding took me some time to get used to, but now I’m obsessed. Strange how the body adapts! I love that this recipe makes enough for a workweek of breakfasts. Head here for our favorite matcha powders.

If you don’t have time to make the hot honey mixture, these simple breakfast tacos are great with any hot sauces or chile-based condiments that happen to be in the fridge.

This Persian egg dish is similar to a frittata, which means it makes for great meal prep. It takes awhile to wash all the herbs, so make sure you have time, but leftovers will last a few days in the fridge. I like it cold with a swipe of Greek yogurt, but you do you.

Meet the bran muffins you’ll actually crave. Squidgy dates and chopped chocolate make these more like a hearty breakfast cake than the dense pucks you may have eaten in the past.

If it’s not heirloom tomato season, opt for smaller cherry or Campari tomatoes in this recipe—your taste buds will thank you.

To bulk up this green smoothie into a filling meal, add some nut butter and cottage cheese or plain yogurt, plus a scoop of protein powder if you have it.

Leftover cooked quinoa mocking you in the fridge? Stir it in to these blueberry muffins. Win-win.

Speaking of leftover quinoa, if you’re looking for a savory option instead of sweet, throw together this morning salad with a few boiled eggs and smoked trout.

While I personally love mushy porridge, I understand that cakey is a more pleasant texture for many. If that’s the case for you, baked oatmeal is the solution.

Serving brunch to a crowd? Make this breakfast casserole. Just grab a nice loaf of sourdough to slice alongside.

If you haven’t yet tried fried eggs that were based with turmeric oil, now is your moment.

For the savory oatmeal fans out there, try simmering with instant dashi powder and salt-softened vegetables.

A homemade gluten-free loaf that you’ll dream about. Try it with butter and a slice of aged cheese like cheddar or cream cheese and smoked fish.

#6579. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6577. Office Hours: Saie’s Laney Crowell on the Beauty of Doing Good

For Laney Crowell, “feel good, do good” is not just the core philosophy of her beauty brand, Saie, but how she lives her life. “So much of beauty is not only who you are on the inside, but the actions that you take,” she says, emphasizing “the importance of taking action, especially in things that you are excited and passionate about.”

The driving force behind Saie was Crowell’s growing desire to make beauty better by creating formulas that are not just safe for your skin but also good for it. She wanted to create products that spoke to her as a self-professed “expert consumer.” “I’ve always struggled with really sensitive, acne-prone skin,” she says. “I had an aha moment where I realized that my makeup was what was making me break out. I started a blog [called The Moment] to have the conversation. It was niche, but at the same time, I was one of the only people having this conversation.” Saie was born from this community building seven years ago.

The brand has steadily expanded since then, without ever straying from its mission. Each new product follows the same principles: It’s formulated to nourish the skin, is noncomedogenic, and is clinically tested and dermatologist tested. “When you try Saie, you immediately feel the textures and how hydrating they are. Then as you continue to use them, you realize how happy your skin is. You’re really seeing benefits over time.”

Saie’s innovations, however, haven’t come without growing pains. Working with a long list of ingredients to avoid, including silicones, the team has found that developing long-lasting products takes a long time. “I only ever want to launch something if it’s perfect,” Crowell says. Take its City Set setting spray, for example. When it debuted in December 2025, no setting spray claimed 16-hour wear.

“I make beauty products for women who get ready in five minutes, just like me,” says Crowell, who is gearing up to solve another customer request. Saie’s next launch, CityStick, took two years to perfect and is set to debut later this year. “I’m always on the go, so I wanted something I could throw in my bag, swipe on for a bit of radiance, and know I was also doing something good for my skin. That’s CityStick—my makeup and skin care in one quick step.” It’s 50% makeup, 50% skin care; expect the sheer, soft-focus, radiant coverage of a skin tint with the benefits of nourishing skin care.

Helming a cosmetics brand—not to mention pioneering an entire category—requires vision and tenacity, two things Crowell has in equal measure. The last seven years have shown her just how resilient she is. “The most important attribute of a founder and entrepreneur is the ability to keep going,” she says. The other thing she’s learned? How much she loves to improve. “I am always thinking about how I, the brand, and everything that we do get 1% better every day.”

Beyond formulating, leading, and championing a host of climate initiatives (the brand has Planet Beautiful, an annual sustainability and plastic-recovery campaign in partnership with Sephora and RePurpose Global), Crowell is also a mother of two. She’s as passionate about Saie’s commitment to our planet (read: making systemic change regarding the billions of units of plastic the beauty industry generates each year) as she is about showing up for her two little girls.

“My weekdays are crazy, but I love it,” she says with a laugh. Days at her home upstate start with a 6:30 a.m. matcha (Rocky’s ceremonial-grade matcha with steamed oat milk and simple syrup she makes herself) and a workout (weight training or Pilates) before the kids wake up. After getting them ready and taking them to school (her favorite part of the day), she’ll make another matcha, then settle in for a marathon of Zoom calls before spending the evening with the kids. She comes into the city once a week to meet with her team in person; The Mercer is her home away from home.

As an entrepreneur, she’s keen to take care of herself by consciously putting herself first, including upholding her boundaries. “When you do something that you really love, I think that is also a really beautiful commitment to yourself,” she says.

Having started her business at the tail end of 2019, Crowell worked tirelessly during the pandemic, when she also gave birth to her second child, Rosie. “I think back on the success of Saie, and a big part of it is that for two years I basically worked the amount that most people do in, like, six years,” she says. Her days were a balance of work and breastfeeding, and she only really left the house to go for walks. “After that, my immune system was a mess,” she adds. Working with holistic coach Jill Ketner Villa was her saving grace. Years later, Crowell says Villa is her “secret weapon” as a founder. Through her work with the practitioner, she’s developed her supplement ritual; she takes approximately 15 a day. Her assortment includes magnesium, zinc, iron, and vitamins C, A, and D—all housed in a beautiful leather pill case.

She’s also been meditating for 12 years. Nowadays, she loves Gabrielle Bernstein’s guided meditations, which last 10 to 20 minutes. “I get a lot of clarity out of it, and I find it to be the best way to calm anxiety.” Sleep, of course, is another tranquil practice; practice is the operative word because Crowell does a lot to ensure she gets a good night’s sleep. She takes magnesium or CBD before bed and uses the Truvaga device to stimulate her vagus nerve system and regulate her circadian rhythm. “Then I have my humidifier, face mask, earplugs, always a thick lip balm—that usually does it.” (The humidifier also makes its way to her weekly stays at The Mercer.)

Otherwise, she says going on a walk in nature helps her be her best self. “If I can fit a walk in between Zooms, that is a good day. I have my best ideas on walks.”

Crowell’s skin philosophy is appropriately minimalist, largely to suit her sensitive, dry, acne-prone skin. “I don’t use a ton of products, and I don’t use anything that’s super active. Generally, ‘less is more’ is what’s right for my skin, with a heavy focus on hydration.” As someone so knowledgeable and passionate about formulation, she’s gotten her skin-care regimen down to a science and has a couple of brands she knows work well for her skin.

First is Medik8, which she turns to for a suite of products: cleansers, a hydrating serum, and its Crystal Retinal. “Their retinol is the only retinol I can use. I use either level one, two, or three. I don’t really go above that. I also really love Sofie Pavitt’s line—it’s really wonderful if you have acne-prone skin.” Specifically, she gravitates toward the Omega Rich Moisturizer, Clean Clean Cleanser, and Mandelic Clearing Serum to spot-treat breakouts. Otherwise, she loves the Dr. Barbara Sturm toner for extra hydration, Alloy’s estrogen-powered face cream to boost skin’s plumpness, and Colorescience’s tinted mineral sunscreen if she’s skiing or in the sun, though her daily SPF is Saie’s Slip Tint. For extra protection, you’ll likely find her in a hat.

Crowell likes to keep her makeup routine quick. “I am not a makeup artist,” she says. “So all of our formulas are easy and effortless. I really love looking like myself.” Her five-minute regimen always starts with Saie’s Glowy Super Gel, which “gives [her] the most beautiful lit-from-within glow,” followed by Slip Tint for moisturizing coverage with sun protection. After a bit of Slip Tint concealer and a thoughtful dusting of the collection’s setting powder, she moves on to blush. At night she might layer the liquid Dew Blush and the powder SuperSuede blush, but for daytime it’s one or the other paired with the SuperSuede Baked Bronzer. Next, she brushes up her brows with gels by Kristie Streicher or Rare Beauty. Then she adds a mist of City Set setting spray, a few coats of Mascara 101, and her go-to lip combo (lip liner in shade Flirt, plus Glossybounce lip oil in shade Dip) for the finishing touches.

Hydration is key to keeping her thick, long brown hair, which can sometimes be dry, looking its best. “I don’t get a lot of haircuts, so I’m always hydrating the roots,” she says. Roz’s Milk Hair Serum comes with her everywhere, as does the brand’s Santa Lucia Styling Oil. “I really love her formulas,” she says. K18’s post-shower leave-in delivers molecular repair, while Arrey’s Not Today, Grey supplement slows early graying and supports fullness. “It’s 100% made a difference. When I stopped taking them, I noticed it.”

Another product she doesn’t leave home without is Dae’s styling wand, which comes in handy for taming flyaways. For her beloved beach waves, she swears by T3’s curling iron (specifically the 1-inch and 1.5-inch barrel sizes) and a bit of Dae’s styling cream.

Crowell is as thoughtful with her style as she is with her skin care and makeup. “I definitely believe in quality over quantity, so I wouldn’t say I buy a lot,” she says. When she does shop, however, she always asks herself if the item fits her “’90s, a little sporty, and minimalist” ethos. That said, she gravitates toward pieces from The Row, Khaite, and Kallmeyer or really special vintage finds. Most days, you’ll find her in jeans, a T-shirt, and Adidas sneakers—or Manolos to dress things up.

#6574. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6571. Too Busy for Breakfast? Make These Pumpkin Overnight Oats

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

I’m not going to tell you that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. Humans have been on the planet for hundreds of thousands of years and our ability to thrive simply isn’t rooted in whether we eat first thing in the morning. In fact, the cliché is barely a century old, stemming not from nutritional science but good old-fashioned advertising.

Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, advocates for breakfast cereal used religious rhetoric and maternal guilt to fuel their marketing efforts, while public relations executives at a pork company convinced doctors to recommend a heartier breakfast of bacon and eggs for sustained energy, aimed at working families.

Yet today breakfast is one of the most commonly skipped meals. So instead of wagging my finger at you about missing something so “important,” I think it’s worth asking: Why did you miss it in the first place?

On a jam-packed holiday like Thanksgiving, there are plenty of reasons. You have a turkey to roast. The table has to be set. Someone needs to pick up the wine. And oh, there’s still the pie dough to roll out! Maybe you even want to “save room” for the glorious feast you’re putting so much effort into.

But skipping this meal does come at a cost. Even if you aren’t ravenous, it’s metabolically valuable to eat in the morning. Breakfast stabilizes energy, and studies have shown that forgoing it leads to a reduced consumption of important nutrients like fiber, potassium, iron, and calcium, often found in morning staples like fruit, whole grains, and dairy. Without some food to start the day, you risk an energy dip, brain fog, and downright hanger. Which, let’s be honest, we don’t need in a kitchen overflowing with dirty dishes and extended relatives.

I have an easy solution. Making breakfast on Thanksgiving (or any day, really) doesn’t have to be a last-minute hassle. It can be quick to assemble and still feel special—like you’re really taking care of yourself, because you are. Take this overnight oats–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes the night before you plan to eat it.

Open up a can of pumpkin purée—odds are you bought extras that didn’t become a pie. Mix it with oats, maple syrup, and whichever milk you have in the fridge. A scoop of chia seeds adds bonus nutrition and prevents the oats from turning gluey as they hydrate overnight.

The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you. It’ll keep you full and firing on all cylinders for a day of turkey roasting, potato mashing, and vibe managing. It may not be the most important meal of the day—at least on Thanksgiving—but it will be delicious.

#6569. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)
